items.title: Sc-structures, sc-Banach spaces, sums and level shifts

book.label: §1.1, Definition 1.1, p. 6
book.statement: An *sc-structure* on a Banach space $E$ is a decreasing sequence of Banach spaces $E = E_0 \supset E_1 \supset E_2 \supset \cdots$ such that (1) every inclusion $E_{m+1} \to E_m$ is compact and (2) $E_\infty = \bigcap_m E_m$ is dense in every $E_m$. A Banach space with an sc-structure is an *sc-Banach space*; points of $E_\infty$ are *smooth*, points of $E_m$ have *regularity $m$*. A finite-dimensional space has exactly one sc-structure, the constant one. A subset $A$ inherits the filtration $A_m = A \cap E_m$, and $A^k$ is $A_k$ with the filtration $(A^k)_m = A_{k+m}$. The direct sum $E \oplus F$ has levels $E_m \oplus F_m$.
book.note: Example 1.2, the weighted Sobolev spaces $H^{m,\delta_m}(\mathbb R \times S^1)$, is not formalized (G.1).

lean.statement: A *scale* is an indexed family of real Banach spaces $E_m$, $m \in \mathbb N$, with injective compact continuous linear inclusions $E_{m+1} \to E_m$; the composite $E_m \to E_0$ is written $\iota_m$, and $E_\infty \subseteq E_0$ is the subspace of points that lift to every level, $E_\infty \cap E_m$ its preimage in $E_m$. An *sc-Banach space* is a scale in which $E_\infty \cap E_m$ is dense in $E_m$ for every $m$; then the image of $E_{m+k}$ is dense in $E_m$. For a finite-dimensional space $V$ the constant family $E_m = V$ with identity inclusions is an sc-Banach space, all of whose points are smooth. For sc-Banach spaces $E$, $F$ the family $E_m \times F_m$ with the product inclusions is an sc-Banach space $E \oplus F$, whose smooth points are the pairs of smooth points; the family $E_{m+1}$ is an sc-Banach space $E^1$, with smooth points those of $E$ seen in $E_1$, and $E^k$ is the $k$-fold iterate. For $U \subseteq E_0$ the level set $U_m \subseteq E_m$ is the preimage of $U$ under $\iota_m$.

chips: injectivity of the inclusions a field
only one structure in finite dim. (V1.31)
diff: The text's $E_m$ are subsets of one space $E$; the formal scale is a family of separate Banach spaces with injective compact inclusions, and "$x \in E_m$" for $x \in E_0$ means $x \in \iota_m(E_m)$. The two pictures are equivalent, and nothing in Chapter 1 uses more than the family.
Injectivity of the inclusions, implicit in "$E_{m+1} \subset E_m$", is a field of the structure; continuity is part of being a compact operator in Mathlib's sense.
Condition (2) is taken exactly as stated, density of $E_\infty \cap E_m$ in every $E_m$. The weaker "$E_{m+1}$ is dense in $E_m$" is derived, not assumed.
That a finite-dimensional space has *only* the constant structure, and that the constant sequence on an infinite-dimensional space is not an sc-structure, are proved separately (V1.31).

items.title: Sc-operators and sc-isomorphisms

book.label: §1.1, Definition 1.3, p. 7
book.statement: A linear map $T : E \to F$ between sc-Banach spaces is an *sc-operator* if $T(E_m) \subset F_m$ and the induced $T : E_m \to F_m$ is continuous for every $m$. A *linear sc-isomorphism* is a bijective sc-operator whose inverse is an sc-operator.

lean.statement: An *sc-operator* $T : E \to F$ is a family of continuous linear maps $T_m : E_m \to F_m$ commuting with the inclusions, $\iota^F_m \circ T_{m+1} = T_m \circ \iota^E_m$. The family is determined by its base map $T_0$, and a continuous linear $T_0 : E_0 \to F_0$ *is an sc-operator* when for every $m$ there is a continuous linear $T_m : E_m \to F_m$ with $\iota_m T_m = T_0 \iota_m$; the two notions correspond. Sc-operators compose and add, and map smooth points to smooth points. An *sc-isomorphism* is a family of continuous linear equivalences $E_m \simeq F_m$ commuting with the inclusions; its inverse and composites are sc-isomorphisms. A continuous linear $T_0 : E_0 \to F_0$ with $T_0(E_m) \subseteq F_m$ for every $m$ is an sc-operator (the continuity of $T_0 : E_m \to F_m$ is the closed graph theorem), and an sc-operator bijective on every level is an sc-isomorphism (the open mapping theorem).

chips: the level maps are the data
continuity on the levels is automatic
diff: In the family picture an sc-operator carries its level maps as data; the text's "one linear map $T$ mapping $E_m$ into $F_m$ continuously" is the predicate `IsScOperator` on the base map, and the two are interchangeable (`ScOperator.isScOperator`, `IsScOperator.toScOperator`).

An sc-isomorphism is given by level-wise continuous linear equivalences; that the inverse of a bijective sc-operator is continuous on each level (the open mapping theorem) is built into this definition, and proved separately (`ScIso.ofBijective`). Likewise the continuity of $T : E_m \to F_m$ asked by Definition 1.3 is automatic for a bounded $T_0$ that maps $E_m$ into $F_m$ (`isScOperator_of_mapsTo`, the closed graph theorem; Findings, Chapter 3, item 233). Updated in the third addendum of this page.

items.title: Sc⁺-operators are sc-compact

book.label: §1.1, Definition 1.4, p. 7
book.statement: An sc-operator $S : E \to F$ is an *$\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator* if $S(E_m) \subset F_{m+1}$ and $S : E \to F^1$ is an sc-operator. Since the inclusion $F_{m+1} \to F_m$ is compact, an $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator is *sc-compact*: $S : E_m \to F_m$ is compact for every $m$.

lean.statement: An *$\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator* $E \to F$ is an sc-operator $E \to F^1$ into the level shift, i.e. a family of continuous linear maps $S_m : E_m \to F_{m+1}$ commuting with the inclusions. Composing with the inclusion $F^1 \to F$ (itself an sc-operator) gives the underlying sc-operator $E \to F$, whose level-$m$ map $E_m \to F_m$ is a compact operator for every $m$; in particular $S$ raises the level, $x \in \iota_m(E_m) \Rightarrow S_0x \in \iota_{m+1}(F_{m+1})$.

chips: the first condition is the second
diff: Of the text's two conditions, "$S(E_m) \subset F_{m+1}$" is contained in "$S : E \to F^1$ is an sc-operator", so the formal definition keeps the latter alone; the text's remark that $S$ is then sc-compact is a proved lemma.

items.title: Sc-subspaces, sc-complements, sc-splittings

book.label: §1.1, Definition 1.5, p. 7
book.statement: A subspace $F$ of an sc-Banach space $E$ is an *sc-subspace* if $F$ is closed and $F_m = F \cap E_m$ defines an sc-structure on $F$. An sc-subspace $F$ has an *sc-complement* if there is an algebraic complement $G$ such that $G_m = G \cap E_m$ is an sc-structure on $G$ and $E_m = F_m \oplus G_m$ is a topological direct sum on every level; $E = F \oplus G$ is then an *sc-splitting*.

lean.statement: For a subspace $A \subseteq E_0$ its level-$m$ part $A_m \subseteq E_m$ is the preimage of $A$ under $\iota_m$; it is closed when $A$ is. $A$ is an *sc-subspace* if $A$ is closed and, for every $m$, $A_m$ lies in the closure of $A_m \cap E_\infty$ (the smooth points of $A$ are dense in every level). A closed $A$ with the induced filtration is a scale, with the restricted inclusions compact, and an sc-subspace is an sc-Banach space with this filtration. $E = F \oplus G$ is an *sc-splitting* if $F$ and $G$ are sc-subspaces and $F_m$, $G_m$ are complementary subspaces of $E_m$ for every $m$; then $F_m$ is closed complemented in $E_m$ (the sum is topological), and the splitting is symmetric.

diff: Of the conditions in "$(F_m)$ is an sc-structure on $F$", the closedness of $F_m$ in $E_m$ and the compactness of $F_{m+1} \to F_m$ follow from the closedness of $F$ (restriction of a compact operator), so `IsScSubspace` asks only for closedness and the density of $F \cap E_\infty$ in each $F_m$; the sc-Banach space $F$ is then built (`ScBanach.ofSubspace`).

"Topological direct sum $E_m = F_m \oplus G_m$" is read as: $F_m$ and $G_m$ are complementary closed subspaces of $E_m$; by the closed graph theorem the sum is then topological, which is recorded as a consequence (`IsScSplitting.closedComplemented`). The text's "$G$ an algebraic complement with $(G_m)$ an sc-structure" is the requirement that $G$ be an sc-subspace.

items.title: Finite-dimensional sc-subspaces

book.label: §1.1, Proposition 1.6, p. 7
book.statement: A finite-dimensional subspace $F$ of an sc-Banach space $E$ is an sc-subspace if and only if $F \subset E_\infty$. A finite-dimensional sc-subspace always has an sc-complement.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be an sc-Banach space and $F \subseteq E_0$ a finite-dimensional subspace. Then $F$ is an sc-subspace if and only if $F \le E_\infty$. If $F \le E_\infty$, there is a subspace $G \subseteq E_0$ with $E = F \oplus G$ an sc-splitting.

diff: The proof follows the text: a continuous projection $p : E_0 \to F$ (Mathlib's closed complementation of finite-dimensional subspaces, i.e. Hahn–Banach) is lifted to each level through $F_m \cong F$, $G = \ker p$, and the density of $G \cap E_\infty$ in $G_m$ comes from $g = (1 - P_m)g$ with $P_m$ the level projection, exactly as on p. 8.

items.title: Quotients of sc-Banach spaces

book.label: §1.1, Proposition 1.7, p. 8
book.statement: If $E$ is an sc-Banach space and $A \subset E$ an sc-subspace, then $E/A$ with the filtration $E_m/A_m$ is an sc-Banach space, where $E_m/A_m = \{(x + A) \cap E_m : x \in E\}$.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be an sc-Banach space and $A \subseteq E_0$ a *closed* subspace. The family of quotient Banach spaces $E_m / A_m$, with the inclusions $E_{m+1}/A_{m+1} \to E_m/A_m$ induced by $\iota$, is an sc-Banach space $E/A$ (the induced maps are injective and compact, and the smooth points are dense on every level), and the quotient maps $E_m \to E_m/A_m$ form an sc-operator $E \to E/A$. As a statement: there are an sc-Banach space $Q$ and an sc-operator $q : E \to Q$ with every $q_m$ surjective and $\ker q_m = A_m$.

diff: The text assumes $A$ is an sc-subspace; the proof uses only that $A$ is closed, and so does the formal statement (`ScBanach.quotient` takes `IsClosed A`).

The levels $E_m/A_m$ are the abstract quotients; the text's identification of $E_m/A_m$ with a subset of $E/A$ is the injectivity of the induced inclusion, which holds because $A_m$ is the full preimage of $A$.
The text's description of $(E/A)_\infty$ as the classes of points of $E_\infty$ (p. 9) is proved separately, with the Mittag-Leffler argument it needs (V1.33).

items.title: Sc-Fredholm operators and their index

book.label: §1.1, Definition 1.8, p. 9
book.statement: An sc-operator $T : E \to F$ is *sc-Fredholm* if there are sc-splittings $E = K \oplus X$ and $F = C \oplus Y$ with (1) $K = \ker T$ finite-dimensional, (2) $C$ finite-dimensional and $Y = T(E)$, (3) $T : X \to Y$ an sc-isomorphism. Then $K \subset E_\infty$, $T(X_m) = Y_m$, $E_m = K \oplus X_m$ and $F = C \oplus T(E_m)$. The index is $\operatorname{ind}(T) = \dim K - \dim C$.

lean.statement: An *sc-Fredholm splitting* of an sc-operator $T : E \to F$ consists of subspaces $K, X \subseteq E_0$ and $C, Y \subseteq F_0$ with $E = K \oplus X$ and $F = C \oplus Y$ sc-splittings, $K = \ker T_0$, $Y = \operatorname{range} T_0$, $K$ and $C$ finite-dimensional, and $T_m$ a bijection of $X_m$ onto $Y_m$ for every $m$. $T$ is *sc-Fredholm* if it has such a splitting. Its *index* $\dim K - \dim C$ equals $\dim \ker T_0 - \dim(F_0/\operatorname{range} T_0)$, so it does not depend on the splitting. Consequences: $K \le E_\infty$; $\ker T_m = K_m$ and $\operatorname{range} T_m = Y_m$ on every level; and every $T_m : E_m \to F_m$ is a Fredholm operator in Mathlib's sense.

diff: Condition (3), "$T : X \to Y$ is an sc-isomorphism", is taken as: $T_m$ restricts to a bijection $X_m \to Y_m$ for every $m$. The continuity of the inverses is automatic (open mapping theorem between the closed subspaces $X_m$, $Y_m$), so nothing is lost.
The text's "$F = C \oplus T(E_m)$" (a slip for $F_m$) is the level-$m$ part of the splitting $F = C \oplus Y$ together with $\operatorname{range} T_m = Y_m$.

The index is defined by the splitting as in the text and shown equal to $\dim\ker T_0 - \dim\operatorname{coker} T_0$, which the text does not state; the level-wise Fredholm property, the first line of §1.4.1, is a lemma.

items.title: Sc-Fredholm operators are regularizing

book.label: §1.1, Proposition 1.9, p. 9
book.statement: An sc-Fredholm operator $T : E \to F$ is regularizing: if $e \in E$ and $T(e) \in F_m$, then $e \in E_m$.

lean.statement: Let $T : E \to F$ be an sc-operator with an sc-Fredholm splitting, $e \in E_0$ and $m \in \mathbb N$. If $T_0 e \in \iota_m(F_m)$, then $e \in \iota_m(E_m)$. As a property: an sc-Fredholm operator is *regularizing* (`ScOperator.IsRegularizing`). Conversely, an sc-operator $T$ with $T_0$ Fredholm and $T$ regularizing is sc-Fredholm (V1.9); so $T$ is sc-Fredholm if and only if $T_0 : E_0 \to F_0$ is Fredholm and $T$ is regularizing.

diff: The hypothesis is the data of Definition 1.8 (a splitting) rather than its existence; the two are interchangeable, since the conclusion does not mention the splitting.

The converse, not stated in the text: together with “$T_0$ Fredholm”, being regularizing characterizes the sc-Fredholm operators (`isScFredholm_iff`). It is the construction of §1.4.1 with the two properties used there as hypotheses (V1.9), and the tool for the text's unargued “is sc-Fredholm” for operators obtained by conjugation and restriction in Chapter 3 (V3.8, V3.46, V3.96; Findings, Chapter 3, item 233). Updated in the third addendum of this page.

items.title: Compact perturbation of sc-Fredholm operators

book.label: §1.1, Proposition 1.10, p. 10 (proof §1.4.1, pp. 14–15)
book.statement: Let $E$ and $F$ be sc-Banach spaces. If $T : E \to F$ is sc-Fredholm and $S : E \to F$ is an $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator, then $T + S$ is sc-Fredholm.

lean.statement: Let $T : E \to F$ be an sc-Fredholm operator and $S : E \to F$ an $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator. Then the sc-operator $T + S$ (with $S$ read as an sc-operator $E \to F$) is sc-Fredholm. Along the way: $T + S$ is regularizing, and every level map $(T+S)_m$ is a Fredholm operator. The construction is also proved as a criterion: an sc-operator that is Fredholm on level $0$ and regularizing is sc-Fredholm, and every level map is then Fredholm of the level-$0$ index.

chips: needs a bootstrap the text omits
diff: §1.4.1 says "since $T$ is regularizing, $e \in E_m$"; the hypothesis gives only $Te = y - Se \in F_1$, so the regularizing step must be iterated $m$ times (`ScPlus.regularizing_add`). The same bootstrap gives $K_m = K_{m+1}$.

The complement $C$ is built from a linear right inverse of $F_0 \to F_0/Y$ with values in the smooth points rather than from a lifted basis; condition (3) of Definition 1.8, which the text does not verify, is proved as the bijectivity of $(T+S)_m : X_m \to Y_m$.

The classical fact that opens §1.4.1, a compact perturbation of a Fredholm operator is Fredholm, is not in Mathlib and is proved here (V1.25). The text does not record that the index is preserved; the formalization proves it separately (V1.30).

§1.4.1 uses two properties of $T + S$ only: it is Fredholm on level $0$, and it is regularizing (so its kernel lies in $E_\infty$, it maps $E_m$ onto $Y \cap F_m$, and its range has a complement spanned by smooth points). With these as hypotheses the construction is a criterion for sc-Fredholm operators (`isScFredholm_of_isRegularizing`), not stated in the text (Findings, Chapter 3, item 233). Updated in the third addendum of this page.

items.title: Partial quadrants and the tuples $(U, C, E)$

book.label: §1.1, Definition 1.11, p. 10
book.statement: A *partial quadrant* in an sc-Banach space $E$ is a closed convex subset $C \subset E$ such that there is an sc-isomorphism $T : E \to \mathbb R^n \oplus W$ with $T(C) = [0,\infty)^n \oplus W$. One considers tuples $(U, C, E)$ with $U$ a relatively open subset of the partial quadrant $C$.

lean.statement: The *quadrant* of $\mathbb R^n \oplus W$ (with $\mathbb R^n$ carrying its constant structure) is, on every level, the set of $(a, w)$ with all $a_i \ge 0$; it is closed and convex with non-empty interior, and its level sets are the quadrants of the levels. $C \subseteq E_0$ is a *partial quadrant* if $C = T_0^{-1}(\text{quadrant})$ for some $n$, some sc-Banach space $W$ and some sc-isomorphism $T : E \to \mathbb R^n \oplus W$. Then every level set $C_m$ is closed and convex with non-empty interior in $E_m$ and has unique differentiability at each of its points; the whole space is a partial quadrant ($n = 0$). $(U, C, E)$ is a *tuple* if $C$ is a partial quadrant and $U = O \cap C$ for an open $O \subseteq E_0$.

chips: closed and convex derived, not assumed
diff: "Closed convex" is a consequence of $C = T^{-1}([0,\infty)^n \oplus W)$ and is proved rather than assumed; since $T_0$ is a bijection, $T(C) = Q$ and $C = T^{-1}(Q)$ say the same.

The text uses constantly, without stating it, that $C_k$ is a partial quadrant in $E^k$ (so that $TC = C^1 \oplus E$ makes sense); this is proved with Chapter 2 (V1.36). What the proofs of §§1.2–1.3 need from the tuple is carried by the level-wise notion of an sc-domain (V1.27).

items.title: Sc⁰ maps

book.label: §1.1, Definition 1.12, p. 10
book.statement: For tuples $(U, C, E)$ and $(U', C', E')$, a map $f : U \to U'$ is *$\mathrm{sc}^0$* (sc-continuous) if $f(U_m) \subset U'_m$ and the induced maps $f : U_m \to U'_m$ are continuous for all $m \ge 0$.

lean.statement: For $f : E_0 \to F_0$ the level map $f_m : E_m \to F_m$ sends $x$ to the unique $y$ with $\iota_m y = f(\iota_m x)$ when it exists (a junk value otherwise). $f$ is *$\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U \subseteq E_0$* if for every $m$ and every $x \in U_m$, $f(\iota_m x) \in \iota_m(F_m)$, and $f_m$ is continuous on $U_m$. Then $f$ is continuous on $U$; if moreover $f(U) \subseteq V$ then $f_m(U_m) \subseteq V_m$; $\mathrm{sc}^0$ depends only on the values of $f$ on $U$, passes to subsets, and the composition of $\mathrm{sc}^0$ maps is $\mathrm{sc}^0$. The identity and every sc-operator are $\mathrm{sc}^0$, with level maps the $T_m$.

diff: Maps are total functions $E_0 \to F_0$ and only their values on $U$ matter; the target tuple plays no role in the definition beyond $f(U) \subseteq U'$, so it is not an argument of `IsSc0` (the text's own definition writes "$f(U_m) \subset V_m$" with $V$ meaning $U'$).
The level map $f_m$ is defined through the injectivity of $\iota_m$, and the condition "$f(U_m) \subset F_m$" is the first field of `IsSc0`.

items.title: The tangent of a tuple

book.label: §1.1, Definition 1.13, p. 10
book.statement: The *tangent* of $(U, C, E)$ is the tuple $T(U, C, E) = (TU, TC, TE)$ with $TU = U^1 \oplus E$, $TC = C^1 \oplus E$, $TE = E^1 \oplus E$. It is again a tuple: $TU$ is relatively open in the partial quadrant $TC$ of the sc-Banach space $TE$.

lean.statement: The *tangent* $TE$ of an sc-Banach space is $E^1 \oplus E$, the sc-Banach space with levels $E_{m+1} \times E_m$; for $U \subseteq E_0$, $TU \subseteq (TE)_0 = E_1 \times E_0$ is the set of $(x, h)$ with $x \in U_1$, and its level-$m$ part is $U_{m+1} \times E_m$. $TU$ is monotone in $U$. If $U$ is an sc-domain (open-in-convex levels with unique differentiability, V1.27) so is $TU$ in $TE$, and $T(U^1) = (TU)^1$.

diff: $TU$ and $TE$ are the text's. That $TC = C^1 \oplus E$ is a partial quadrant in $TE$, i.e. that $T(U, C, E)$ is again a tuple (which needs an sc-isomorphism $(\mathbb R^n \oplus W)^1 \oplus (\mathbb R^n \oplus W) \cong \mathbb R^n \oplus W'$), is proved with Chapter 2 (V1.36). The proofs of §§1.2–1.3 carry instead the level-wise regularity `IsScDomain`, which $T$ preserves, and this is all the chain rule and §1.2 need.

items.title: Sc¹ maps and the tangent map

book.label: §1.1, Definition 1.14, pp. 10–11
book.statement: $f : U \to U'$ is *$\mathrm{sc}^1$* if (1) $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$; (2) for every $x \in U_1$ there is a bounded linear $Df(x) : E_0 \to F_0$ with $|f(x+h) - f(x) - Df(x)h|_0 / |h|_1 \to 0$ as $|h|_1 \to 0$, $h \in E_1$, $x + h \in U_1$; (3) the *tangent map* $Tf : TU \to TU'$, $Tf(x, h) = (f(x), Df(x)h)$, is $\mathrm{sc}^0$. In general $x \mapsto Df(x)$ is not continuous into $\mathcal L(E_0, F_0)$ with the operator norm, but it is with the compact-open topology; the $\mathrm{sc}^1$ maps between finite-dimensional spaces are the $C^1$ maps.
book.note: The text writes $Df(x)$ as if it were unique.

lean.statement: For a family $D : E_1 \to \mathcal L(E_0, F_0)$ the tangent map $T_Df : TE \to TF$ is $(x, h) \mapsto (f_1(x), D(x)h)$. $f$ is *$\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with derivatives $D$* if (1) $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U$; (2) for every $x \in U_1$ the map $f \circ \iota_1 : E_1 \to F_0$ has derivative $D(x) \circ \iota_1$ at $x$ within $U_1$ (Mathlib's `HasFDerivWithinAt`); (3) $T_Df$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $TU$. $f$ is *$\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$* if such a $D$ exists; `scDeriv` is a chosen one, and `tangentMap` the tangent map built from it. If $U_1$ has unique differentiability at $x \in U_1$, any two derivative families satisfying (2) agree at $x$ (the inclusion $E_1 \to E_0$ has dense range); on an sc-domain the chosen derivative therefore agrees with any admissible one on $U_1$, and the tangent map on $TU$. Being $\mathrm{sc}^1$ depends only on the values on $U$. Level $0$ of (3) says $(x, h) \mapsto D(x)h$ is continuous on $U_1 \times E_0$, and this gives uniform continuity of $D$ on compact subsets of $E_0$; for maps between finite-dimensional spaces on an open set, $\mathrm{sc}^1$ is $C^1$. The derivative need not be norm continuous: on $E = \mathbb R \oplus X$, with $X$ the sc-Banach space whose level $m$ consists of the sequences with $(k+1)^m x_k \to 0$, normed by $\sup_k (k+1)^m|x_k|$, the map $f(t, x)_k = \cos(kt)x_k$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ into $X$, and for every derivative family $D$ of $f$, $x \mapsto D(x)$ is not continuous on $E_1$ into $\mathcal L(E_0, X_0)$ with the operator norm.

diff: Condition (2) is Mathlib's differentiability of $f : U_1 \to F_0$ at $x$ within $U_1$, with derivative $Df(x)|_{E_1}$; the limit over $h \in E_1$ with $x + h \in U_1$ is exactly this.

The text speaks of "the" operator $Df(x)$ and "the" tangent map; both need $Df(x)$ to be unique, which the text does not discuss. The formal definition takes the family $D$ as an explicit parameter (`IsSc1With`), proves uniqueness on $U_1$ where $U_1$ has unique differentiability (relatively open subsets of partial quadrants have it, V1.10) using the density of $E_1$ in $E_0$, and defines `tangentMap` through a choice that is then shown immaterial.

The remark on the compact-open topology is formalized here as the uniform continuity of $x \mapsto Df(x)$ on compact sets of $E_0$, and as an equivalence with level $0$ of (3) in V1.34; the remark on finite dimensions is proved on open sets in `Polyfold/Test.lean` and on relatively open subsets of quadrants, with boundary, in V1.35. That $x \mapsto Df(x)$ need not be norm continuous is proved by an example, which the text does not give: $f(t, x)_k = \cos(kt)x_k$ on $\mathbb R \oplus X$, $X$ the weighted $c_0$ scale (the project's first infinite-dimensional sc-Banach space); the factor $k$ of the $t$-derivative is absorbed by one level, $(\pi/(n+1), 0) \to 0$ in $E_1$, but $\|Df(\pi/(n+1), 0) - Df(0, 0)\| \ge 2$, and the derivative is unique on $E_1$, so no derivative family is norm continuous (Findings, Chapter 1, follow-up item 1; formerly G.3). Updated in the third addendum of this page.

items.title: Sc^k and sc-smooth maps

book.label: §1.1, Definition 1.15, p. 11 (unnumbered in the preprint)
book.statement: Inductively, an $\mathrm{sc}^0$ map $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^2$ if it is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ and $Tf : TU \to TV$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$; then $T^2f = T(Tf)$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$, and $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^3$ if $T^2f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$, and so on. $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^\infty$, or *sc-smooth*, if it is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ for all $k \ge 0$.
book.note: The preprint's numbered Remark 1.15 (partial cones) is not formalized; the inductive definition that precedes it is numbered 1.15 here, as the Lean files do.

lean.statement: $f$ is *$\mathrm{sc}^k$ on $U$* by recursion on $k$: $\mathrm{sc}^0$ means $\mathrm{sc}^0$; $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$ means $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with the tangent map $Tf$ (built from the chosen derivative) $\mathrm{sc}^k$ on $TU \subseteq TE$. $f$ is *sc-smooth* if it is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ for every $k$. Then $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$ implies $\mathrm{sc}^k$ (and $\mathrm{sc}^l$ for $l \le k$); $f$ is sc-smooth iff it is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with sc-smooth tangent map; on an sc-domain, $\mathrm{sc}^k$ depends only on the values on $U$.

diff: The recursion uses the tangent map built from the chosen derivative `scDeriv`; on relatively open subsets of partial quadrants the choice does not matter (V1.13), so the notion is the text's.

items.title: Sc¹ in terms of the levels

book.label: §1.2, Proposition 1.16, p. 12
book.statement: Let $U$ be relatively open in a partial quadrant of $E$ and $F$ an sc-Banach space. An $\mathrm{sc}^0$ map $f : U \to F$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ if and only if (1) for every $m \ge 1$, $f : U_m \to F_{m-1}$ is $C^1$, so that $df : U_m \to \mathcal L(E_m, F_{m-1})$ is continuous; and (2) for every $m \ge 1$ and $x \in U_m$, $df(x)$ extends to a bounded $Df(x) : E_{m-1} \to F_{m-1}$ with $(x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h$ continuous on $U_m \oplus E_{m-1}$. In particular, at a smooth point $x \in U_\infty$ of an $\mathrm{sc}^1$ map, $Df(x) : E \to F$ is an sc-operator.

lean.statement: Let $U$ be an sc-domain in $E$ and $f$ $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U$. Then $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ if and only if there is a family of operators $D_m(x) \in \mathcal L(E_m, F_m)$, $x \in U_{m+1}$, such that for every $m$: $f_m \circ \iota : U_{m+1} \to F_m$ is differentiable within $U_{m+1}$ at every $x \in U_{m+1}$ with derivative $D_m(x) \circ \iota$, and $(x, h) \mapsto D_m(x)h$ is continuous on $U_{m+1} \times E_m$. For such a family, $x \mapsto D_m(x) \circ \iota$ is continuous $U_{m+1} \to \mathcal L(E_{m+1}, F_m)$ in the operator norm, so $f : U_{m+1} \to F_m$ is $C^1$; and $\iota_m \circ D_m(x) = D_0(\iota x) \circ \iota_m$, so the $D_m(x)$ are the restrictions of one operator $Df(x) = D_0(x)$. For an $\mathrm{sc}^1$ map with derivatives $Df$, the family is given by the *level operators* $Df(x) : E_m \to F_m$ (V1.26). At a point $x \in U_1$ that is smooth, $Df(x) : E_0 \to F_0$ is an sc-operator.

diff: The text's one symbol $Df(x)$ for the extensions on all levels becomes an explicit family $D_m(x)$; that they are restrictions of a single operator (Lemma 3.H of the exposition), which the text does not state and which the direction (⇐), called "clear" in the 2010 paper, needs, is proved (`IsSc1Levels.toBase_apply`).

The text's (1), the $C^1$ property and the continuity of $df$ in the operator norm, is a consequence of the formal conditions rather than part of them; it is proved for both directions (`IsSc1Levels.contDiffOn`, `IsSc1Levels.continuousOn_clm`, and for an $\mathrm{sc}^1$ map directly in V1.26).

The hypothesis "$U$ relatively open in a partial quadrant" is weakened to `IsScDomain` (V1.27), which is all the proof uses. The "in particular" is proved as stated, for the derivative family of Definition 1.14 at a smooth point of $U_1$.

items.title: Lifting the index: sc^k on $U^1$

book.label: §1.2, Proposition 1.17, p. 12
book.statement: Let $U$ and $V$ be relatively open subsets of partial quadrants in sc-Banach spaces and $f : U \to V$ an $\mathrm{sc}^k$ map. Then $f : U^1 \to V^1$ is also $\mathrm{sc}^k$.

lean.statement: Let $U$ be an sc-domain in $E$ and $f$ $\mathrm{sc}^k$ on $U$. Then the level-$1$ map $f_1 : E_1 \to F_1$ is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ on $U^1 = U_1$ as a map between the shifted spaces $E^1$ and $F^1$. For $k = 0$ no hypothesis on $U$ is needed; for $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with derivatives $Df$ the derivatives of $f_1$ are the level-$1$ operators $Df(x) : E_1 \to F_1$, $x \in U_2$; and sc-smooth maps lift to sc-smooth maps.

diff: The target $V$ plays no role (the formal map goes into $F^1$; values in $V^1$ follow from $f(U) \subseteq V$). The hypothesis on $U$ is the weaker `IsScDomain`.
The induction uses $T(U^1) = (TU)^1$ and that the tangent map of $f_1$ is the level-$1$ map of $Tf$, which rests on the uniqueness of derivatives (V1.13).

items.title: Sc^k maps are $C^k$ from $U_{m+k}$ to $F_m$

book.label: §1.2, Proposition 1.18, p. 13
book.statement: Let $U$ and $V$ be relatively open subsets of partial quadrants in sc-Banach spaces. If $f : U \to V$ is $\mathrm{sc}^k$, then for every $m \ge 0$ the map $f : U_{m+k} \to V_m$ is of class $C^k$; moreover $f : U_{m+l} \to V_m$ is $C^l$ for every $0 \le l \le k$.

lean.statement: Let $U$ be an sc-domain in $E$ and $f$ $\mathrm{sc}^k$ on $U$. Then for every $m$ the map $f_m \circ \iota : U_{m+k} \to F_m$ is $C^k$ within $U_{m+k}$ (Mathlib's `ContDiffOn`), and $f_m \circ \iota : U_{m+l} \to F_m$ is $C^l$ for $l \le k$; in particular $f \circ \iota_k : U_k \to F_0$ is $C^k$. An sc-smooth map is $C^k$ from $U_{m+k}$ to $F_m$ for all $m$, $k$.

chips: $C^k$ within the set, in Mathlib's sense
proved for all levels at once
diff: "Of class $C^k$" on a relatively open subset of a quadrant, which the text never defines, is Mathlib's $C^k$ within the set; on these sets derivatives are unique.

The 2010 paper proves the case $m = 0$ and lifts it with Proposition 1.17; the formal proof treats a general level directly, with a compatible level-lowering operator $\rho : E_{m+k} \to E_m$ as a parameter, and uses the compact-open lemma (V1.26) in place of the multilinear maps $\Gamma(x)$ and differentiation under the integral sign.

items.title: Sc^{k+1} from classical smoothness on the levels

book.label: §1.2, Proposition 1.19, p. 13
book.statement: Let $U$ be relatively open in a partial quadrant of $E$ and $F$ an sc-Banach space. Assume that for every $m \ge 0$ and $0 \le l \le k$ the map $f : U \to F$ induces a map $f : U_{m+l} \to F_m$ of class $C^{l+1}$. Then $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$.

lean.statement: Let $U$ be an sc-domain in $E$ and $f$ $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U$. If for every $m \ge 0$ and $0 \le l \le k$ the map $f_m \circ \iota : U_{m+l} \to F_m$ is $C^{l+1}$ within $U_{m+l}$, then $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$ on $U$; if this holds for every $l$, then $f$ is sc-smooth. Also proved, under the stronger hypothesis that every level map $f_m : U_m \to F_m$ is $C^{k+1}$: $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$; for $k = 0$, where the two hypotheses agree, with $Df(x)$ the derivative of $f : U_0 \to F_0$ at $x$; and if every $f_m$ is $C^\infty$, $f$ is sc-smooth.

diff: "$f$ induces a map $f : U_{m+l} \to F_m$" is the $\mathrm{sc}^0$ hypothesis (the values on $U_m$ lie in $F_m$; continuity then follows from the case $l = 0$); "of class $C^{l+1}$" is Mathlib's $C^{l+1}$ within $U_{m+l}$, as in V1.17. The text's relatively open subset of a partial quadrant is a special case of an sc-domain (V1.27).

The proof is the 2010 paper's induction $(\mathrm S_k)$ on the elementary maps $(x, h_1, \dots, h_j) \mapsto d^jf(x)(h_1, \dots, h_j)$ on mixed levels (V1.37, V1.38), with $f$ the elementary map with $j = 0$. It cannot be run on the hypothesis itself: if $f$ satisfies it with $k$, then $Tf$ in general does not satisfy it with $k - 1$, its second component $(x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h : U_{m+l+1} \times E_{m+l} \to F_m$ being only $C^l$.

The earlier version under the stronger hypothesis "$f : U_m \to F_m$ is $C^{k+1}$ for every $m$" (`proposition_1_19`, `IsScSmooth.of_contDiffOn_levels`) is kept: there the level maps of $Tf$ are $C^k$ and the induction needs no $(\mathrm S_k)$. For $k = 0$ the two hypotheses agree (`proposition_1_19_zero`).

items.title: Maps into $\mathbb R^N$

book.label: §1.2, Corollary 1.20, p. 13
book.statement: Let $U$ be relatively open in a partial quadrant of an sc-Banach space and $f : U \to \mathbb R^N$. If for some $k$ and all $0 \le l \le k$ the map $f : U_l \to \mathbb R^N$ is $C^{l+1}$, then $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$.

lean.statement: Let $U$ be an sc-domain in $E$, $V$ a finite-dimensional normed space with its constant sc-structure and $f : E_0 \to V$. If for some $k$ and all $0 \le l \le k$ the map $f \circ \iota_l : U_l \to V$ is $C^{l+1}$ within $U_l$, then $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$ on $U$. If $f \circ \iota_l$ is $C^{l+1}$ within $U_l$ for every $l$, then $f$ is sc-smooth; if $f$ is $C^\infty$ within $U$, then $f$ is sc-smooth. Also proved, under the stronger hypothesis: if $f \circ \iota_m$ is $C^{k+1}$ within $U_m$ for every $m$, in particular if $f$ is $C^{k+1}$ within $U$, then $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$; for $k = 0$ this is the text's hypothesis.

diff: The corollary is Proposition 1.19 (V1.18) for the constant structure: $f : U_{m+l} \to V$ is the restriction of the $C^{l+1}$ map $f : U_l \to V$, and $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ because each $f : U_m \to V$ is the continuous $f : U_0 \to V$ composed with the inclusion, so no $\mathrm{sc}^0$ hypothesis is needed. $\mathbb R^N$ is any finite-dimensional normed space.

The two sc-smooth statements are the exposition's ("$C^{l+1}$ on $U_l$ for every $l$", and "$C^\infty$ on $U_0$"), not the text's; the second gives the bump functions the theory uses. The earlier versions under the stronger hypothesis $C^{k+1}$ on every $U_m$ (`corollary_1_20`, `corollary_1_20_base`) are kept.

items.title: The chain rule

book.label: §1.3, Theorem 1.21, p. 13 (proof §1.4.2, pp. 15–16)
book.statement: Let $U \subset C \subset E$, $V \subset D \subset F$ and $W \subset Q \subset G$ be relatively open subsets of partial quadrants in sc-Banach spaces and $f : U \to V$, $g : V \to W$ be $\mathrm{sc}^1$. Then $g \circ f : U \to W$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ and $T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf$.
book.note: Remark 1.22: differentiability is guaranteed only with the loss of one level, yet the composition loses only one; the compactness of $E_{m+1} \to E_m$ saves the day.

lean.statement: Let $U \subseteq C \subseteq E$ and $V \subseteq D \subseteq F$ be relatively open subsets of partial quadrants, $f$ $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with $f(U) \subseteq V$, and $g$ $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $V$ (with values in any sc-Banach space $G$). Then $g \circ f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ and $T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf$ on $TU$. With derivatives made explicit: if $g$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with derivatives $Dg$ and $f$ with derivatives $Df$, and $V_1$ is the intersection of an open and a convex set, then $g \circ f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with derivatives $x \mapsto Dg(f_1(x)) \circ Df(x)$; this existence part needs no hypothesis on $U$. Iterated: the composition of $\mathrm{sc}^k$ maps between sc-domains (in particular between relatively open subsets of partial quadrants) is $\mathrm{sc}^k$, and sc-smooth maps compose to sc-smooth maps.

chips: proved by the mean value inequality
diff: The text's third tuple $W \subset Q \subset G$ is not needed and is dropped; $T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf$ is an equality of maps on $TU$, which for the chosen derivatives rests on the uniqueness of $D(g \circ f)(x)$ on $U_1$ (so the quadrant structure of $U$ enters only there).

The two integrals of §1.4.2 are replaced by the one-variable mean value inequality for $t \mapsto g(y_t) - t\,Dg(f(x))(f(x+h) - f(x))$ on $[0, 1]$, and the first integral is not needed at all since $Dg(f(x))$ is bounded on $F_0$. The step "$y_t \in V_1$ for $|h|_1$ small" uses that $V_1$ is open-in-convex and that $f : U_1 \to F_1$ is continuous, which the text does not say; the uniform convergence on the compact set $\overline{Df(x)(\iota B_1)}$ is `IsCompact.eventually_forall_of_forall_eventually` instead of the subsequence argument.
The text's "$f : U_1 \to F$ is $C^1$ by Proposition 1.18" is not used.

items.title: The degeneracy index of a partial quadrant

book.label: §1.3, Definition 1.23, p. 14
book.statement: Let $C$ be a partial quadrant in $E$ and $T : E \to \mathbb R^k \oplus W$ an sc-isomorphism with $T(C) = [0,\infty)^k \oplus W$. For $x \in C$ with $T(x) = (a_1, \dots, a_k, w)$ put $d_C(x) = \#\{i : a_i = 0\}$. The map $d_C : C \to \mathbb N_0$ is the *degeneracy index*; points with $d_C = 0$ are interior, with $d_C = 1$ boundary points, with $d_C \ge 2$ corners.

lean.statement: For $p = (a, w) \in \mathbb R^n \oplus W$ let $\#(p)$ be the number of indices $i$ with $a_i = 0$, and for a presentation $T : E \cong \mathbb R^n \oplus W$ of a partial quadrant let $d_T(x) = \#(T_0 x)$. The *degeneracy index* $d_C(x)$ of $x \in E_0$ is $d_T(x)$ for an arbitrarily chosen presentation $T$ of $C$ (and $0$ if $C$ is not a partial quadrant); by Lemma 1.24 it equals $d_T(x)$ for every presentation $T$ and every $x \in C$. On the quadrant $[0,\infty)^n \oplus W$ itself, $d(p) = \#(p)$.

diff: The text defines $d_C$ on $C$ through a fixed $T$ and then shows independence; the formal $d_C$ is a total function on $E_0$ defined through a chosen presentation, with the independence theorem (`degIndex_eq`) making it the text's on $C$. The classification into interior, boundary and corner points is terminology, not formalized in Chapter 1 (Chapter 2 defines the boundary of an M-polyfold).

items.title: The degeneracy index does not depend on the presentation

book.label: §1.3, Lemma 1.24, p. 14 (proof §1.4.3, p. 17)
book.statement: The map $d_C$ does not depend on the choice of the linear sc-isomorphism $T$.

lean.statement: Let $T : E \cong \mathbb R^n \oplus W$ and $T' : E \cong \mathbb R^{n'} \oplus W'$ be sc-isomorphisms with $C = T_0^{-1}(Q_n) = T_0'^{-1}(Q_{n'})$. Then $d_T(x) = d_{T'}(x)$ for every $x \in C$, and $n = n'$. Core form: a continuous linear equivalence $S : \mathbb R^n \times W_0 \to \mathbb R^{n'} \times W'_0$ carrying the quadrant onto the quadrant preserves the number of vanishing half-line coordinates at every point of the quadrant.

chips: only level $0$ and linear algebra are used
$k = k'$ derived from the lemma at $x = 0$
diff: The core statement is proved for any continuous linear equivalence of the base levels carrying one quadrant onto the other; the sc-structure plays no role, as the exposition observes.

The text first proves $k = k'$ and then the index equality; the formal proof does not need $k = k'$ and derives it afterwards as the index of the origin. The codimension of $E_x$ is made precise as $\dim(V/E_x) = \#I(x)$, with $E_x$ the kernel of $(b, v) \mapsto (b_i)_{i \in I(x)}$, and $S$ induces an isomorphism of the quotients; the text's "since $S$ is an isomorphism, equality" is the symmetric inclusion for $S^{-1}$.

items.title: Boundary recognition

book.label: §1.3, Theorem 1.25, p. 14
book.statement: Given tuples $(U, C, E)$ and $(U', C', E')$ and a germ $f : (U, x) \to (U', x')$ of a local sc-diffeomorphism with $x' = f(x)$, then $d_C(x) = d_{C'}(f(x))$. (The text cites [20], Theorem 1.19, for the proof of a more general result; sc-smooth diffeomorphisms recognize boundary points and corners, homeomorphisms only boundaries.)

lean.statement: Let $U \subseteq C \subseteq E$ and $U' \subseteq C' \subseteq E'$ be relatively open subsets of partial quadrants, $f : E_0 \to E'_0$ $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with $f(U) \subseteq U'$, $g : E'_0 \to E_0$ $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U'$ with $g(U') \subseteq U$, $g \circ f = \mathrm{id}$ on $U$ and $f \circ g = \mathrm{id}$ on $U'$. Then $d_C(x) = d_{C'}(f(x))$ for every $x \in U$. At points $x \in U_1$ this is proved directly; a general $x \in U$ is approximated by level-$1$ points of $U$ with the same index, and $d_{C'}$ is upper semicontinuous.

chips: sc¹ suffices, the text has sc-smooth
germ = sc¹ map with sc¹ inverse on $U$, $U'$
proved, not cited; by the §2.3 argument
diff: The text's "germ of a local sc-diffeomorphism" is undefined in Chapter 1; it is read as an $\mathrm{sc}^1$ map $f : U \to U'$ with an $\mathrm{sc}^1$ inverse $g : U' \to U$, where $U$ and $U'$ may be taken as small as one likes (relatively open neighbourhoods of $x$ and $f(x)$). Only $\mathrm{sc}^1$ is needed, where the text has sc-smooth: the statement is stronger.

The text gives no proof. The formal proof is the argument of §2.3 (Lemma 2.29, Theorem 2.31, Corollary 2.32) specialized to the identity retraction: for $x \in U_1$ and $v \in E_x \cap E_1$ the sign argument gives $Df(x)v \in E'_{f(x)}$, density extends this to $E_x$, and the codimensions $\dim(E/E_x) = d_C(x)$, $\dim(E'/E'_{f(x)}) = d_{C'}(f(x))$ compare through the chain rule; general points are reached by approximation with level-$1$ points of the same index (smooth points are not needed) and the upper semicontinuity of the index. The file sits in Chapter 2 because it uses the retraction vocabulary.

items.title: Fredholm operators between Banach spaces, and Riesz–Schauder

book.label: §1.4.1, p. 14 (quoted as classical)
book.statement: The proof of Proposition 1.10 opens with "since $S : E_m \to F_m$ is compact for every level, the operator $T + S : E_m \to F_m$ is Fredholm for every $m$", and later uses that the image of a Fredholm operator is closed. The classical theory of Fredholm operators and compact perturbations is taken for granted.

lean.statement: For real Banach spaces $E$, $F$: a continuous linear map with closed range is a strict map (open mapping theorem), and one with finite-dimensional kernel, closed range and range of finite codimension is Fredholm in Mathlib's sense (the remaining conditions, strictness and complementedness of the kernel, are automatic). A finite-rank operator is compact. **Riesz–Schauder:** for a compact operator $c$ on $E$, $1 + c$ has finite-dimensional kernel, closed range and range of finite codimension, hence is Fredholm.

diff: No counterpart as a statement: Mathlib has the notion of a Fredholm operator (with quasi-inverses) but not the theorem that $1 + \text{compact}$ is Fredholm, nor that compact perturbations preserve the property. Both are proved here, the finite codimension of the range by a chain of closed subspaces and Riesz's lemma.

items.title: Compact perturbations of Fredholm operators

book.label: §1.4.1, p. 14 (quoted as classical)
book.statement: "The operator $T + S : E_m \to F_m$ is Fredholm for every $m$" because $S$ is compact on every level: the stability of Fredholm operators under compact perturbations, used without citation.

lean.statement: Let $E$, $F$ be real Banach spaces, $u : E \to F$ a Fredholm operator and $k : E \to F$ a compact operator. Then $u + k$ is Fredholm.

diff: Proved from Riesz–Schauder with a quasi-inverse $v$ of $u$: $v(u + k) = 1 + c_1$ and $(u + k)v = 1 + c_2$ with $c_1$, $c_2$ compact. The invariance of the index, which the exposition states (Kato IV.5.26) and the text does not, is V1.28.

items.title: The compact-open lemma and the level operators $Df(x) : E_m \to F_m$

book.label: 2010 paper, Propositions 2.1–2.3 (the compactness argument)
book.statement: The proofs of Propositions 1.16–1.18 in the 2010 paper rest on one argument: for unit vectors $h_n$ of $E_{m+1}$ a subsequence converges in $E_m$ (compactness of the inclusion), so the continuity of $(x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h$ on $U_{m+1} \times E_m$ gives the continuity of $x \mapsto Df(x)$ into $\mathcal L(E_{m+1}, F_m)$; and on the integral identity $f(x + h) - f(x) = \int_0^1 Df(x + \tau h)h\,d\tau$.

lean.statement: **Compact-open lemma.** Let $s \subseteq X$ be the intersection of an open and a convex set with unique differentiability at each point, $\iota : Y' \to Y$ a compact operator and $A : X \to \mathcal L(Y, Z)$ with $(x, y) \mapsto A(x)y$ of class $C^k$ on $s \times Y$. Then $x \mapsto A(x) \circ \iota$ is $C^k$ on $s$ into $\mathcal L(Y', Z)$; for $k = 0$, continuity on $s \times Y$ suffices and no hypothesis on $s$ is needed. **Level operators.** For an $\mathrm{sc}^1$ map with derivatives $Df$ and $x \in U_{m+1}$ there is a unique continuous linear $Df(x) : E_m \to F_m$ with $\iota_m \circ Df(x) = Df(\iota x) \circ \iota_m$ (the second component of the level-$m$ tangent map); $(x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h$ is continuous on $U_{m+1} \times E_m$, $x \mapsto Df(x) \circ \iota$ is continuous $U_{m+1} \to \mathcal L(E_{m+1}, F_m)$, and on an sc-domain $f_m \circ \iota : U_{m+1} \to F_m$ is differentiable within $U_{m+1}$ with derivative $Df(x) \circ \iota$, hence $C^1$; if $f_m : U_m \to F_m$ is differentiable at $x$ its derivative is $Df(x)$.

diff: No counterpart as a statement: the lemma isolates the one analytic mechanism behind §1.2 and its $C^k$ version (by induction with the mean value inequality) replaces the multilinear maps $\Gamma(x)(h_1, \dots, h_k, h)$ and the differentiation under the integral sign of the 2010 paper's Proposition 2.3.

The integral identity is formed as a Bochner integral in $F_m$ directly and identified with $f(x+h) - f(x)$ through the fundamental theorem of calculus for the $C^1$ map $f : U_1 \to F_0$; the 2010 paper forms it in $F_0$ and notes that the integrand is continuous into $F_m$.

items.title: Sc-domains: what the proofs use of a tuple

book.label: §1.1, pp. 10–11 (the tuples $(U, C, E)$)
book.statement: Every statement of §§1.2–1.3 is made for $U$ relatively open in a partial quadrant $C$ of $E$, and the tangent construction is said to produce again such a tuple.

lean.statement: $U \subseteq E_0$ is an *sc-domain* if, for every $m$, the level set $U_m$ is the intersection of an open and a convex subset of $E_m$ and has unique differentiability at each of its points. A relatively open subset of a partial quadrant is an sc-domain; if $U$ is an sc-domain then so are $TU$ in $TE$ and $U^1 = U_1$ in $E^1$.

diff: No counterpart as a statement: the text iterates its definitions on tuples and asserts that $T(U, C, E)$ is a tuple; the formalization iterates on sc-domains, for which the stability under $T$ is a two-line proof, and every theorem of §§1.2–1.3 is stated for sc-domains, hence in particular for the text's tuples.

items.title: The Fredholm index and its invariance under compact perturbations

book.label: §1.4.1, p. 14 (quoted as classical)
book.statement: Not stated. The proof of Proposition 1.10 uses that $T + S : E_m \to F_m$ is Fredholm; that its index is that of $T$ is the classical invariance of the index under compact perturbations, which the text does not invoke.

lean.statement: For a linear map $u$ over a field, $\operatorname{ind}(u) = \dim\ker u - \dim(F/\operatorname{range}u)$; if $u$, $v$ have finite-dimensional kernel and cokernel, so has $v \circ u$ and $\operatorname{ind}(v\circ u) = \operatorname{ind}(u) + \operatorname{ind}(v)$; a bijection plus a finite-rank map, in particular $1$ plus a finite-rank map, has index $0$. For real Banach spaces, a Fredholm operator has finite-dimensional kernel and cokernel; if $v$ is a quasi-inverse of $u$ ($vu - 1$, $uv - 1$ of finite rank) and $\|v\|\|s\| < 1$, then $u + s$ has finite-dimensional kernel and cokernel and $\operatorname{ind}(u + s) = \operatorname{ind}(u)$; if $u$ is Fredholm and $k$ compact, $\operatorname{ind}(u + k) = \operatorname{ind}(u)$.

diff: Infrastructure Mathlib v4.33.1 lacks: Mathlib has Fredholm operators but no index. The exposition cites Kato IV.5.26 for the invariance; the formal proof shows first that the index is locally constant (a small perturbation $u + s$ satisfies $v(u+s) = (1 + vs) + (vu - 1)$, a bijection by the Neumann series plus a finite-rank map) and then that $t \mapsto \operatorname{ind}(u + tk)$ is locally constant, hence constant, on $\mathbb R$.

items.title: The level operators of an sc-Fredholm operator

book.label: §1.1, Definition 1.8, p. 9
book.statement: After the definition: $K \subset E_\infty$, $T(X_m) = Y_m$, $E_m = K \oplus X_m$ and "$F = C \oplus T(E_m)$" for all $m$; the index is $\dim K - \dim C$. That $T : E_m \to F_m$ is Fredholm with this index on every level is not stated.

lean.statement: Let $T$ have an sc-Fredholm splitting $(K, X, C, Y)$. Then $K \le E_\infty$ and $C \le F_\infty$; a subspace $A \le E_\infty$ has $\dim A_m = \dim A$; and for every $m$ the level map $T_m : E_m \to F_m$ is Fredholm with $\dim\ker T_m - \dim(F_m/\operatorname{range}T_m) = \dim K - \dim C$, which is the index $\dim\ker T_0 - \dim(F_0/\operatorname{range}T_0)$ of $T$.

diff: The text records the splittings on every level but not the index of $T_m$; the formal statement (the exposition's Lemma 2.D) adds that every $T_m$ is Fredholm of index $\operatorname{ind}(T)$, using $\ker T_m = K_m \cong K$ and $F_m/\operatorname{range}T_m = F_m/Y_m \cong C_m \cong C$ (V1.7).

items.title: Compact perturbation preserves the index

book.label: §1.1, Proposition 1.10, p. 10 (proof §1.4.1, pp. 14–15)
book.statement: If $T : E \to F$ is sc-Fredholm and $S : E \to F$ is an $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator, then $T + S$ is sc-Fredholm. (The index of $T + S$ is not mentioned.)

lean.statement: Let $T : E \to F$ be an sc-Fredholm operator and $S : E \to F$ an $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator. Then $\operatorname{ind}(T + S) = \operatorname{ind}(T)$, with $\operatorname{ind} = \dim\ker(\cdot)_0 - \dim\operatorname{coker}(\cdot)_0$; and for every $m$ the level map $(T+S)_m : E_m \to F_m$ is Fredholm of index $\operatorname{ind}(T)$.

diff: The text proves only that $T + S$ is sc-Fredholm (V1.9). The equality of indices, which the exposition adds, is proved on level $0$ by V1.28 ($S_0$ is compact) and transported to every level by V1.29 applied to $T + S$.

items.title: Finite-dimensional spaces carry only the constant structure

book.label: §1.1, after Definition 1.1, p. 6
book.statement: A finite-dimensional Banach space has precisely one sc-structure, the constant one $E_m = E$; on an infinite-dimensional space the constant structure is not an sc-structure, because property (1) fails.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be an sc-Banach space with $E_0$ finite-dimensional. Then every point of $E_0$ is smooth, every inclusion $\iota_m : E_m \to E_0$ is bijective, and the $\iota_m$ form an sc-isomorphism of $E$ onto $E_0$ with the constant structure. For any scale, if one inclusion $E_{m+1} \to E_m$ is surjective then $E_m$ is finite-dimensional.

chips: an onto inclusion forces finite dimension
diff: With sc-Banach spaces as families, "$E_m = E$" becomes "$\iota_m$ is bijective", and "precisely one structure" becomes: the identity of $E_0$ extends to an sc-isomorphism with the constant structure, so all the level norms are equivalent. "The constant structure is not an sc-structure" becomes: an onto inclusion forces finite dimension (open mapping theorem, then the identity is compact).

items.title: Sc-splittings are sc-projections

book.label: §1.1, Definition 1.5 and the proof of Proposition 1.6, pp. 7–8
book.statement: An sc-splitting $E = F \oplus G$ is a topological direct sum $E_m = F_m \oplus G_m$ on every level. In the proof of Proposition 1.6: the map $P$ with $P \circ P = P$, continuous on every $E_m$, "is a sc-projection", and $G := (1 - P)(E)$ is then an sc-complement.

lean.statement: If $E = A \oplus B$ is an sc-splitting, the projections of $E_m$ onto $A_m$ along $B_m$ are continuous and form an sc-operator $P$ with $P_m^2 = P_m$, $P_m(E_m) = A_m$ and $\ker P_m = B_m$ for every $m$. Conversely, if $P : E \to E$ is an sc-operator with $P_0^2 = P_0$, then $P_m^2 = P_m$ and $P(E)_m = P_m(E_m)$ for every $m$, and $E = P(E) \oplus \ker P$ is an sc-splitting. So $E = A \oplus B$ is an sc-splitting iff there is an sc-operator $P$ with $P^2 = P$, $P(E) = A$, $\ker P = B$.

chips: used, not stated, in the text
diff: The text uses the equivalence in the proof of Proposition 1.6 without stating it (the exposition's Lemma 2.B). The formal proof of Proposition 1.6 (V1.5) builds the complement directly and does not depend on this item. The complement is written $\ker P$, the same subspace as the text's $(1 - P)(E)$.

items.title: The smooth points of a quotient

book.label: §1.1, Proposition 1.7, p. 9
book.statement: In the proof: "$(E/A)_\infty = \bigcap_j (E_j/A_j)$ consists of all elements of the form $x + A_\infty$ with $x \in E_\infty$."

lean.statement: Let $A$ be an sc-subspace of $E$ and $x \in E_0$. If for every $j$ some point of $E_j$ differs from $x$ by an element of $A$, then some smooth point of $E$ differs from $x$ by an element of $A$. Equivalently, the class of $x$ is a smooth point of the quotient $E/A$ if and only if $x + A$ contains a smooth point of $E$.

diff: The text asserts the equality without proof; only the inclusion "$\supseteq$" is needed for Proposition 1.7 (V1.6). The converse is the exposition's Lemma 2.C: correct the choices $x_j \in (x + A) \cap E_j$ by smooth elements of $A$ so that the corrections form a series converging on every level (density of $A_\infty$ in every $A_j$, completeness, and a bound for the norms of the inclusions).

items.title: Continuity of $Df$ for the compact-open topology

book.label: §1.1, after Definition 1.14, p. 11
book.statement: The map $U_1 \to \mathcal L(E_0, F_0)$, $x \mapsto Df(x)$, will in general not be continuous for the operator norm, but it is continuous for the compact-open topology.

lean.statement: Let $X$ be a metric space, $Y$, $Z$ real normed spaces, $s \subseteq X$ and $A : X \to \mathcal L(Y, Z)$. Then $(x, h) \mapsto A(x)h$ is continuous on $s \times Y$ if and only if, for every $x \in s$, every compact $K \subseteq Y$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$, $\|A(x')w - A(x)w\| < \varepsilon$ for all $w \in K$ and all $x' \in s$ near $x$. In particular, for $f$ $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with derivatives $Df$, $x \mapsto Df(x)$ is continuous on $U_1$ in this sense. The negative half holds by an example (V1.13): there is an $\mathrm{sc}^1$ map $f$ on a relatively open $U$ in a partial quadrant such that, for every derivative family $D$ of $f$, $x \mapsto D(x)$ is not continuous on $U_1$ into $\mathcal L(E_0, F_0)$ with the operator norm.

diff: The compact-open topology on $\mathcal L(Y, Z)$ is written out as uniform convergence on compact sets, and the remark is strengthened to an equivalence (the exposition's Lemma 3.F): it is exactly level $0$ of condition (3) of Definition 1.14. That norm continuity fails in general is proved by a sequence-space example (V1.13; formerly G.3), not by the shift map of the exposition (§6), which needs weighted Sobolev spaces (G.1). Updated in the third addendum of this page.

items.title: In finite dimensions sc¹ is $C^1$, also at the boundary

book.label: §1.1, after Definition 1.14, p. 11
book.statement: The $\mathrm{sc}^1$-maps between finite-dimensional Banach spaces are the familiar $C^1$-maps.

lean.statement: Let $V$, $W$ be finite-dimensional real normed spaces with their constant sc-structures, $f : V \to W$, and $U \subseteq V$ an sc-domain, in particular a relatively open subset of a partial quadrant of $V$. Then $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ iff $f$ is $C^1$ within $U$, i.e. differentiable within $U$ at every point of $U$ with $x \mapsto \mathrm{fderivWithin}\,f\,U\,x$ continuous on $U$; and $f$ is sc-smooth on $U$ iff it is $C^\infty$ within $U$.

diff: The text does not say what $C^1$ means at boundary points of a quadrant; the formal statement uses Mathlib's $C^1$ within $U$, whose derivative at a boundary point is the derivative along $U$ (the one-sided derivative), unique because the quadrant has interior. Any sc-structure on a finite-dimensional space is the constant one up to sc-isomorphism (V1.31).

items.title: Level shifts and tangents of tuples are tuples

book.label: §1.1, Definitions 1.11 and 1.13, p. 10
book.statement: "$T(U, C, E)$ is a tuple consisting again of a relatively open subset $TU$ in the partial quadrant $TC$ in the sc-Banach space $TE$"; tacitly, $C^1 = C \cap E_1$ is a partial quadrant in $E^1$ and $U^1$ is relatively open in it.

lean.statement: If $C$ is a partial quadrant in $E$, presented by $T : E \to \mathbb R^n \oplus W$, then $C_1$ is a partial quadrant in $E^1$ (presented by the level shift of $T$) and $TC = \{(x, h) : x \in C_1\}$ is a partial quadrant in $TE$, presented by $T_1 \times T_0$ followed by the reassociation onto $\mathbb R^n \oplus (W^1 \oplus (\mathbb R^n \oplus W))$. If $U$ is relatively open in $C$, then $U_1$ is relatively open in $C_1$ and $TU$ in $TC$; and $(TU)_1 = T(U_1)$.

chips: the reassociation of summands made explicit
diff: The text asserts both facts; the formal proofs (the exposition's Lemmas 3.A(2) and 3.B) live in the Chapter 2 files, where retracts first need them. The statement for $C^k$ is the $k$-fold iterate. The proofs of §§1.2–1.3 do not use these facts but the sc-domain property (V1.27).

items.title: The derivative tower: one $d^jf(x)$ on all levels

book.label: 2010 paper, Proposition 2.4, pp. 51–53 (the derivatives $d^jf(x)$)
book.statement: The proof of Proposition 1.19 in the 2010 paper writes $d^jf(x)$ for the $j$-th derivative of $f$ on whichever level pair $U_{m+l} \to F_m$ the argument needs, with one symbol for all of them: the derivatives taken with a finer domain level or a coarser target level are tacitly identified.

lean.statement: A *derivative tower* of order $k + 1$ for $f : E_0 \to F_0$ on $U$ consists of base-level maps $\Phi_i(x)(h_1, \dots, h_i)$ with $\Phi_0 = f$ and, for $x \in U_{m+l}$, continuous $i$-linear maps $\Psi_{i,m,l}(x)$ on $E_{m+l}$ with values in $F_m$ ($i \le l + 1$, $i \le k + 1$) such that: $\Psi_{i,m,l}(x)(h)$ seen in $F_0$ is $\Phi_i$ at the images of $x$ and $h$ in $E_0$; $\Psi_{i,m,l}$ is continuous on $U_{m+l}$; and for $i \le l$, $i \le k$ it is differentiable within $U_{m+l}$ with derivative $\xi \mapsto \Psi_{i+1,m,l}(x)(\xi, \cdot)$. If $U$ is an sc-domain, $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ and $f : U_{m+l} \to F_m$ is $C^{l+1}$ within $U_{m+l}$ for all $m$ and $l \le k$, then the iterated derivatives within the level sets form a derivative tower of order $k + 1$. Two values of a tower with the same images in $E_0$ agree.

diff: No counterpart as a statement. The tower records exactly what $(\mathrm S_k)$ uses of the hypothesis of Proposition 1.19: $d^if(x)$ exists and is continuous on $E_{m+l}$ into $F_m$ for $i \le l + 1$, and is differentiable with derivative $d^{i+1}f(x)$ for $i \le l$.

The compatibility across levels is proved from the chain rule for compositions with continuous linear maps (the inclusions), applied to Mathlib's iterated derivative within a set, which is unique on the sc-domain's level sets. For $l > k$ the hypothesis is used with order $k + 1$, by restriction from $U_{m+k}$.

items.title: Elementary maps and the induction $(\mathrm S_k)$

book.label: 2010 paper, Proposition 2.4, pp. 51–53 (the statement $(\mathrm S_k)$)
book.statement: $(\mathrm S_k)$: if $f : U_{m+l} \to F_m$ is $C^{l+1}$ for all $m \ge 0$ and $0 \le l \le k$, then $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$, and every component $\pi \circ T^{k+1}f : T^{k+1}U \to F^l$ is a linear combination of maps $\Gamma : U^{k+1} \oplus E^{n_1} \oplus \cdots \oplus E^{n_j} \to F^l$, $\Gamma(x, h_1, \dots, h_j) = d^jf(x)(h_1, \dots, h_j)$, with $j + l - 1 \le n_i \le k$. Each such $\Gamma$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with derivative $d^{j+1}f(x)(\delta x, h) + \sum_i d^jf(x)(h_1, \dots, \delta h_i, \dots, h_j)$, and the components of $T^{k+2}f$ are again of this form.

lean.statement: *Elementary data* on an sc-Banach space $X$: an sc-operator $\pi_0 : X \to E^p$ (the base point), sc-operators $\pi_a : X \to E^{n_a}$, $a = 1, \dots, i$ (the vectors), and a target shift $m$; the *elementary map* is $z \mapsto d^if(\pi_0 z)(\pi_1 z, \dots, \pi_i z) : X \to F^m$ on $\pi_0^{-1}(U_p)$, with $d^if$ from a derivative tower of order $k + 1$ (V1.37). Under the conditions $m + i \le p$, $m + i \le n_a + 1$ and $i \le k$: the elementary map is $\mathrm{sc}^0$; it is $\mathrm{sc}^1$, by the level criterion of Proposition 1.16 (V1.15), with derivative $(\delta z) \mapsto d^{i+1}f(\pi_0 z)(\pi_0\delta z, \pi z) + \sum_a d^if(\pi_0 z)(\pi z \text{ with } \pi_a z := \pi_a\delta z)$; on $TX$ its tangent map is the pair of an elementary map of type $(p + 1, m + 1; n_a + 1)$ and the sum of an elementary map with $i + 1$ vectors and $i$ elementary maps with $i$ vectors, all satisfying the conditions (the one with $i + 1$ vectors provided $i + 1 \le k$). Hence, if the domain $\pi_0^{-1}(U_p)$ is an sc-domain and $i + s \le k + 1$, the elementary map is $\mathrm{sc}^s$. The shifts $E^p$ have $(E^p)_l = E_{p+l}$, with $E \cong E^0$ and $(E^p)^1 \cong E^{p+1}$.

chips: induction on $s$ over all elementary maps
diff: The 2010 paper's $(\mathrm S_k)$ describes the components of $T^{k+1}f$; the formal induction runs instead on $s$, over all elementary maps on all sc-Banach spaces $X$ at once: an elementary map is $\mathrm{sc}^{s+1}$ because it is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ and its tangent map is the pair of an elementary map and a sum of elementary maps, all $\mathrm{sc}^s$ by the induction hypothesis. Proposition 1.19 (V1.18) is the case $i = 0$, $p = m = 0$, $X = E$. The text's $\Gamma$ is the case $X = E^{k+1} \oplus E^{n_1} \oplus \cdots \oplus E^{n_j}$ with the projections as $\pi_0, \pi_1, \dots, \pi_j$.

The index conditions are $m + i \le p$ (the text's $j + l \le k + 1$, which the text derives from its bounds), $m + i \le n_a + 1$ (the text's $j + l - 1 \le n_i$) and $i \le k$; the upper bound $n_i \le k$ of $(\mathrm S_k)$ plays no role. That the new indices satisfy the conditions ("one checks" in the 2010 paper) is checked for each of the three kinds of terms.
The sums in the tangent map are handled by the sum rule for $\mathrm{sc}^k$ maps and the Leibniz rule by the derivative of the multilinear evaluation (V1.39).

items.title: Sums of sc^k maps; the derivative of multilinear evaluation

book.label: 2010 paper, Proposition 2.4, pp. 52–53 (the terms of $T^{k+1}f$ and the derivative (11))
book.statement: The proof of Proposition 1.19 in the 2010 paper shows that $T^{k+1}f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ by showing that "any of the terms" of its components is, i.e. uses that a sum of $\mathrm{sc}^1$ maps is $\mathrm{sc}^1$; and it obtains the derivative (11) of $(x, h_1, \dots, h_j) \mapsto d^jf(x)(h_1, \dots, h_j)$ by the product rule, without stating either.

lean.statement: On an sc-domain, the constant map $0$ is $\mathrm{sc}^k$, the sum of two $\mathrm{sc}^k$ maps is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ and so is any finite sum. The evaluation $(A, h) \mapsto A(h_1, \dots, h_n)$ of continuous multilinear maps is differentiable at every $(A, h)$ with derivative $(B, \eta) \mapsto B(h) + \sum_a A(h \text{ with } h_a := \eta_a)$.

chips: Leibniz rule for $(A, h) \mapsto A h$
diff: The sum $g_1 + g_2$ is the composite of the pairing $(g_1, g_2)$, which is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ (one direction of the exposition's Lemma 3.G(3), proved in the Chapter 2 files), with the sc-operator $(y_1, y_2) \mapsto y_1 + y_2$, which is sc-smooth, so the chain rule (V1.20) applies. Scalar multiples, the rest of "linear combinations", are not needed.
The derivative of the evaluation is written through Mathlib's derivative of a continuous multilinear map in its arguments and the linearity in $A$; Mathlib has no lemma in this form.

items.title: Sc-smooth retractions

book.label: §2.1, Definition 2.1, p. 18
book.statement: For a tuple $(U, C, E)$, $U$ relatively open in the partial quadrant $C$ of $E$, an sc-smooth map $r : U \to U$ with $r \circ r = r$ is an *sc-smooth retraction* on $U$. After Definition 2.3: for $x \in U_1$ the chain rule gives $Dr(r(x)) \circ Dr(x) = Dr(x)$, so for $x \in O_1$, $Dr(x)$ is a projection.

lean.statement: An *sc-smooth retraction* on $C$ is a set $U \subseteq E_0$ relatively open in the partial quadrant $C$ and a map $r : E_0 \to E_0$ (only its values on $U$ matter) with $r(U) \subseteq U$, $r$ sc-smooth on $U$ and $r(r(x)) = r(x)$ for $x \in U$. Its retract is $O = r(U)$; $O \subseteq U$, $O$ is the fixed-point set of $r$ in $U$, and for $x \in O_1$ the derivative satisfies $Dr(x) \circ Dr(x) = Dr(x)$.

diff: The retraction is a total map $E_0 \to E_0$ with $r(U) \subseteq U$ as a field; only its values on $U$ enter any statement.
The remark that $Dr(x)$ is a projection for $x \in O_1$ is `ScRetraction.scDeriv_comp_self`, by the chain rule applied to $r \circ r = r$.

items.title: Sc-smooth retracts

book.label: §2.1, Definition 2.3, p. 18
book.statement: A tuple $(O, C, E)$ is an *sc-smooth retract* if $O = r(U)$ for an sc-smooth retraction $r : U \to U$ on a relatively open subset $U$ of the partial quadrant $C$.

lean.statement: $(O, C, E)$ is an sc-smooth retract if $O$ is the retract $r(U)$ of some sc-smooth retraction on $C$. Every relatively open $U \subseteq C$ is a retract, with $r = \mathrm{id}$. A *local model* is a triple $(E, C, O)$ with $C$ a partial quadrant and $(O, C, E)$ a retract.

diff: As in the text. The local model packages the triple used by M-polyfold charts.

items.title: Proposition 2.4: the tangent of a retract does not depend on the retraction

book.label: §2.1, Proposition 2.4, p. 19
book.statement: If $r : U \to U$ and $r' : U' \to U'$ are sc-smooth retractions on relatively open subsets of $C$ with $r(U) = r'(U') = O$, then $Tr(TU) = Tr'(TU')$.

lean.statement: For sc-smooth retractions $r$ on $U$ and $r'$ on $U'$ (both relatively open in $C$) with the same retract, $Tr(TU) = Tr'(TU')$. More precisely, $r(U) \subseteq r'(U')$ already gives $r' \circ r = r$ on $U$ and $Tr(TU) \subseteq Tr'(TU')$. $TO = Tr(TU)$ is the fixed-point set of $Tr$ in $TU$.

diff: As in the text. The inclusion is proved under the weaker hypothesis $r(U) \subseteq r'(U')$ and applied twice.
The text's step \"$Tr'(x, h) = (x, h)$\" is the fixed-point description of $Tr(TU)$, proved separately (`ScRetraction.mem_tangent_iff`).

items.title: Definition 2.5: the tangent $TO$ of a retract

book.label: §2.1, Definition 2.5, p. 19
book.statement: The tangent of $(O, C, E)$ is $T(O, C, E) = (TO, TC, TE)$ with $TC = C^1 \oplus E$, $TE = E^1 \oplus E$ and $TO := Tr(TU)$ for any retraction $r$ onto $O$; explicitly $TO = \{(r(x), Dr(x)h) : x \in U_1, h \in E\}$. Definition 2.17: for $x \in O_1$, $T_xO = p^{-1}(x)$, the image of the projection $Dr(x)$.

lean.statement: $TO \subseteq E_1 \times E_0$ is $Tr(TU)$ for a chosen retraction onto $O$, and equals $Tr'(TU')$ for every other one; $TO = \{(r(x), Dr(x)h) : x \in U_1, h \in E_0\}$, and for $x \in O_1$, $(x, h) \in TO$ iff $h \in Dr(x)(E_0)$. The fibre $T_xO = \{h : (x, h) \in TO\}$ is the range of $Dr(x)$, a closed subspace of $E_0$.

diff: `retractTangent E C O` is defined for every set $O$ (empty when $O$ is not a retract), by a choice of retraction; Proposition 2.4 makes the choice irrelevant (`retractTangent_eq`).
That $TC$ is a partial quadrant in $TE$ and $TU$ relatively open in it is V2.8 (and V1.36).

items.title: Proposition 2.6: sc-smoothness on a retract is independent of the retraction

book.label: §2.1, Proposition 2.6, p. 20
book.statement: Let $f : O \to O'$ and $r : U \to U$, $s : V \to V$ two retractions onto $O$. (1) $f \circ r$ is sc-smooth iff $f \circ s$ is. (2) If so, $T(f \circ r) = T(f \circ s)$ on $TO$. (3) $T(f \circ r)$ maps $TO$ into $TO'$.

lean.statement: For retractions $r$, $s$ onto the same $O$: (1) if $f \circ r$ is sc-smooth on $U$ then $f \circ s$ is sc-smooth on $V$; (2) then $T(f \circ r) = T(f \circ s)$ on $Tr(TU)$; (3) if $f \circ r$ is sc-smooth and $f$ maps $O$ into the retract $O' = r'(U')$, then $T(f \circ r)$ maps $Tr(TU)$ into $Tr'(TU')$.

diff: (1) is stated in one direction; the other is the same theorem with $r$ and $s$ exchanged.
(3) assumes $f(O) \subseteq O'$, which the text's \"$f : O \to O'$\" contains.

items.title: Definition 2.7: sc-smooth maps between retracts and the tangent map

book.label: §2.1, Definition 2.7, pp. 20–21
book.statement: $f : O \to O'$ is *sc-smooth* if $f \circ r : U \to E'$ is sc-smooth for a retraction $r$ onto $O$; $Tf := T(f \circ r)|_{TO}$, which maps $TO$ into $TO'$ and does not depend on $r$. For $o \in O_1$, $Tf(o) : T_oO \to T_{f(o)}O'$ is the linearization.

lean.statement: $f : E_0 \to E'_0$ is sc-smooth between the retracts $(O, C, E)$ and $(O', C', E')$ if $f(O) \subseteq O'$ and $f \circ r$ is sc-smooth on $U$ for *every* retraction $r$ onto $O$; for an actual retract this is equivalent to the text's \"for one $r$\". $Tf$ is $T(f \circ r)$ for a chosen $r$; on $TO$ it equals $T(f \circ r)$ for every $r$ onto $O$, maps $TO$ into $TO'$, and $Tf(x, h) = (f(x), D(f \circ r)(x)h)$. Sc-smooth maps between retracts are continuous on $O$ and preserve the levels.

diff: The definition quantifies over all retractions onto $O$ and includes $f(O) \subseteq O'$; `isScSmoothRetractMap_iff_exists` recovers the text's form for a retract.
The linearization $Tf(o)$ is the second component of $Tf(o, \cdot)$; it is not given a separate name.

items.title: Theorem 2.8: the chain rule for retracts

book.label: §2.1, Theorem 2.8, p. 21
book.statement: If $f : O \to O'$ and $g : O' \to O''$ are sc-smooth maps between sc-smooth retracts, then $g \circ f$ is sc-smooth and $T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf$ (the text writes $(O'', C', E'')$ for $(O'', C'', E'')$).

lean.statement: Let $(O, C, E)$ and $(O', C', E')$ be retracts, $f$ sc-smooth $(O, C, E) \to (O', C', E')$ and $g$ sc-smooth $(O', C', E') \to (O'', C'', E'')$. Then $g \circ f$ is sc-smooth and $T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf$ on $TO$. The identity, a retraction $U \to O$ and the inclusion $O \to U$ are sc-smooth, and sc-smoothness depends only on $f|_O$.

diff: The source and middle sets are assumed to be retracts (the text's standing hypothesis); $O''$ need not be.

The text gives no proof (\"follows from Theorem 1.21\"); the proof writes $(g \circ f) \circ r = (g \circ r') \circ (f \circ r)$ on $U$, which uses $r' \circ f \circ r = f \circ r$, and applies Theorem 1.21.

items.title: The tangent functor on retracts

book.label: §2.1, after Theorem 2.8 and Definition 2.9, pp. 21–22
book.statement: $T$ is a functor $\mathcal R \to \mathcal R$: $(TO, TC, TE)$ is again a retract, $Tf : (TO, TC, TE) \to (TO', TC', TE')$, $Tf(x, h) = (f(x), Df(x)h)$, and $T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf$. If $r$ is a retraction, $Tr : TU \to TU$ is a (bundle) retraction.

lean.statement: $TC$ is a partial quadrant in $TE$ and $TU$ is relatively open in $TC$; $Tr : TU \to TU$ is an sc-smooth retraction with image $TO$, so $(TO, TC, TE)$ is an sc-smooth retract. If $f$ is sc-smooth between retracts, so is $Tf : (TO, TC, TE) \to (TO', TC', TE')$; $T(\mathrm{id}) = \mathrm{id}$ on $TO$, and the chain rule is V2.7. $T(O \cap W) = TO \cap (W_1 \times E_0)$ for $W$ open, and $Tf$ computed on $O \cap W$ is $Tf$ computed on $O$.

diff: The functor is stated as the two facts that make it one: $T$ sends retracts to retracts and sc-smooth maps to sc-smooth maps; functoriality is Theorem 2.8.
The bundle structure of $TO \to O^1$ (Definition 2.9's category $\mathcal{BR}$) is not formalized (G.5); the fibrewise linearity of $Tf$ is the linearity of the derivative.
The locality of $Tf$ under restriction to open subsets, used silently in Definitions 2.17–2.18, is proved here.

items.title: Proposition 2.10: open subsets and images of retractions are retracts

book.label: §2.2, Proposition 2.10, p. 23
book.statement: (1) An open subset $O'$ of a retract $O$ is a retract. (2) If $V \subseteq O$ is open and $s : V \to V$ is sc-smooth with $s \circ s = s$, then $s(V)$ is a retract.

lean.statement: (1) If $(O, C, E)$ is a retract and $W \subseteq E_0$ is open, $(O \cap W, C, E)$ is a retract, with the restriction of $r$ to $U \cap r^{-1}(W)$. (2) If $(V, C, E)$ is a retract and $s$ is sc-smooth $(V, C, E) \to (V, C, E)$ with $s \circ s = s$ on $V$, then $(s(V), C, E)$ is a retract, with the retraction $s \circ r$. Sc-smooth maps between retracts restrict to open subsets of the source, and sc-smoothness between retracts is a local property.

diff: \"An open subset $O'$ of $O$\" is written $O \cap W$ with $W$ open in $E_0$ (the subspace topology).
In (2), $V$ is a retract by (1) in the text; here it is assumed to be one, which is how (2) is applied.
The locality of sc-smoothness between retracts is not in the text; Definitions 2.13–2.14 need it (V2.12).

items.title: Definition 2.11: charts and their compatibility

book.label: §2.2, Definition 2.11, pp. 23–24
book.statement: A chart around $x$ in a space $X$ is $(V, \varphi, (O, C, E))$ with $V$ an open neighbourhood of $x$, $(O, C, E)$ an sc-smooth retract and $\varphi : V \to O$ a homeomorphism. Two charts are sc-smoothly compatible if $\psi \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi(V \cap V') \to \psi(V \cap V')$ and its inverse are sc-smooth (Definition 2.7); $\varphi(V \cap V')$ is a retract by Proposition 2.10(1).

lean.statement: A chart on $X$ is a local model $(O, C, E)$ and a partial equivalence $\varphi : X \rightharpoonup E_0$ with open source $V$, target $O$, continuous on $V$ with inverse continuous on $O$. The overlap $\varphi(V \cap V')$ is a retract; two charts are compatible if $\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is sc-smooth from $(\varphi(V \cap V'), C, E)$ to $(\psi(V \cap V'), C', E')$ and $\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}$ back. A chart is compatible with itself and with its restrictions; compatibility is local: two charts compatible with every chart of a family covering $V \cap V'$ are compatible.

diff: The chart is a partial equivalence $X \rightharpoonup E_0$; its inverse is a total function whose values off $O$ do not matter.
`MChart.compatible_of_locally` (chain rule plus locality) is not in the text; it makes the maximal atlas of V2.12 an atlas.

items.title: Definition 2.12: sc-smooth atlases and their equivalence

book.label: §2.2, Definition 2.12, p. 24
book.statement: An sc-smooth atlas is a set of pairwise compatible charts covering $X$; two atlases are equivalent if their union is an atlas.

lean.statement: An atlas is a set of pairwise compatible charts whose sources cover $X$. Two atlases are equivalent iff their union is an atlas iff every chart of one is compatible with every chart of the other; the relation is an equivalence relation.

diff: As in the text. Transitivity, which the “equivalence class” of Definition 2.13 presupposes without comment, is proved from the locality of compatibility (`MAtlas.Equiv.trans`; Findings, Chapter 2, item 41); the maximal atlas of V2.12 had made it unnecessary for the later notions. Updated in the third addendum of this page.

items.title: Definition 2.13: M-polyfolds

book.label: §2.2, Definition 2.13, p. 24
book.statement: An M-polyfold is a Hausdorff paracompact topological space with an equivalence class of sc-smooth atlases.

lean.statement: An M-polyfold structure on a Hausdorff paracompact space $X$ is an sc-smooth atlas. Its *charts* are all charts compatible with that atlas (the maximal atlas); any two of them are compatible, restrictions of charts are charts, every point lies in a chart, and equivalent atlases have the same charts. A nonempty retract $(O, C, E)$ is an M-polyfold with the single chart $\mathrm{id}$.

diff: An equivalence class of atlases is represented by one atlas; every later notion is defined through the maximal atlas `IsChart`, which depends only on the class (`isChart_congr`).
That charts compatible with an atlas are compatible with each other needs the locality of compatibility (V2.10); the text does not discuss it.

items.title: Definition 2.14: sc-smooth maps between M-polyfolds

book.label: §2.2, Definition 2.14, p. 24
book.statement: $f : X \to Y$ is sc-smooth if for charts $\varphi$ around $x$ and $\varphi'$ around $f(x)$ with $f(V) \subseteq V'$, $\varphi' \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1} : O \to O'$ is sc-smooth (Definition 2.7); \"the definition does not depend on the choice of charts\".

lean.statement: $f$ is sc-smooth on an open $U \subseteq X$ if it is continuous on $U$ and for all charts $\varphi$ of $X$, $\psi$ of $Y$ and every open $V \subseteq U \cap \operatorname{dom}\varphi$ with $f(V) \subseteq \operatorname{dom}\psi$, $\psi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is sc-smooth from $(\varphi(V), C, E)$ into $(O', C', E')$; sc-smooth means sc-smooth on $X$. It suffices to check one pair of charts around each point (the text's independence of charts). The identity is sc-smooth and compositions of sc-smooth maps are sc-smooth.

diff: Continuity of $f$ is a field: the text's charts with $f(V) \subseteq V'$ exist around every point only if $f$ is continuous.
The definition quantifies over all charts and all open $V$; `IsScSmoothOn.of_exists_charts` is the text's remark that one pair of charts per point suffices.
Maps on open subsets are included because germs and sub-M-polyfolds need them.

items.title: The filtration $X_m$ of an M-polyfold

book.label: §2.2, after Definition 2.14, p. 25
book.statement: $x$ is on level $m$ if $\varphi(x) \in O_m$ for a chart around $x$ (\"independent of the choice of a chart\"); $X_m$ is the set of such points, topologized by the basis of sets $\varphi^{-1}(W)$, $W$ open in $O_m$; $X = X_0 \supset X_1 \supset \cdots \supset X_\infty = \bigcap X_m$.

lean.statement: $X_m$ is the set of $x$ with $\varphi(x) \in \iota_m(E_m)$ for some chart $\varphi$ around $x$, and then for every chart around $x$. $X_0 = X$, $X_{m+1} \subseteq X_m$, $X_\infty = \bigcap_m X_m$. $X_m$ carries the topology generated by the sets $\{x \in V : \varphi(x) \in W\}$, $W$ open in $E_m$; with it the inclusion $X_m \to X$ is continuous, $X_m$ is Hausdorff, and $x \mapsto \varphi(x)$ embeds $V_m = V \cap X_m$ into $E_m$.

diff: The topology is the one *generated* by the text's family; that the family is a basis (closed under finite intersections) is not needed and not proved.
\"$\varphi : V_m \to O_m$ is a homeomorphism\" is `MPolyfold.isEmbedding_levelLift`.

items.title: Lemma 2.15: the inclusions $X_{m+1} \to X_m$ are continuous

book.label: §2.2, Lemma 2.15, p. 25
book.statement: The inclusion $i : X_{m+1} \to X_m$ is continuous for every $m \ge 0$.

lean.statement: For every $m$, the inclusion $X_{m+1} \to X_m$ is continuous for the topologies of V2.14.

diff: As in the text: the preimage of a generating set $\varphi^{-1}(W)$ is the generating set $\varphi^{-1}(\mathrm{incl}_m^{-1}(W))$.

items.title: The level $X^1$ is an M-polyfold

book.label: §2.2, after Definition 2.14, p. 25
book.statement: $(V_m, \varphi, (O_m, C_m, E_m))$ is a chart on $X_m$; any two such charts are sc-smoothly compatible, and they form an atlas on $X_m$.

lean.statement: For $m = 1$: a retraction $r$ on $U$ restricts to an sc-smooth retraction of $U^1 \subseteq C^1 \subseteq E^1$ with retract $O^1$, and an sc-smooth map between retracts induces an sc-smooth map $O^1 \to O'^1$. For every chart $\varphi$ of $X$, $(V_1, \varphi, (O^1, C^1, E^1))$ is a chart of $X_1$; any two are compatible; they form an atlas, and with it $X_1$ is an M-polyfold $X^1$ (its paracompactness is Theorem 2.16, V2.17).

diff: Only $X_1$ is made an M-polyfold; $X_m$ for $m \ge 2$ is reached as the iterate $(X^1)^1 \cdots$. Its points are those of $X_m$: $(X^1)_m = X_{m+1}$ as sets (`MPolyfold.mem_shift_levelSet_iff`, fourth addendum of this page); that its topology and charts are those of $X_m$ (V2.14) is not formalized (G.6).
The text's \"by Proposition 1.17\" is `IsScSmoothRetractMap.shift`, Proposition 1.17 for retracts.
`MPolyfold.shift` takes $X_1$ paracompact as an instance argument, which Theorem 2.16 now supplies (`MPolyfold.paracompactSpace_level`).

items.title: Theorem 2.16: $X$, $X_m$ and $X_\infty$ are metrizable

book.label: §2.2, Theorem 2.16, p. 25 (proof §2.6.2, pp. 56–58)
book.statement: For every $m \ge 0$ the space $X_m$ is metrizable, in particular paracompact; $X_\infty$ is metrizable. The proof uses Smirnov's theorem (2.55), Lemma 2.56 and Proposition 2.57.

lean.statement: For an M-polyfold $X$: $X$ is metrizable; every level $X_m$ (topology of V2.14) is metrizable and paracompact; $X_\infty$, with the initial topology of the inclusions $X_\infty \to X_m$, is metrizable. Every subset of $X$, in particular every sub-M-polyfold, is paracompact.

diff: No hypothesis is added. The text's route needs $X_m$ regular for Proposition 2.57 and does not check it; the formal proof avoids Lemma 2.56 and Proposition 2.57 altogether.
