Proof: a partition of unity of the paracompact Hausdorff $X$, subordinate to the chart domains and pulled back to $X_m$ along the continuous inclusion, gives an explicit metric (`metrizableSpace_of_pullback`); paracompactness follows by Stone's theorem.
The text never defines the topology of $X_\infty$; it is taken to be the initial topology of the inclusions, which is what the text's metric $\sum 2^{-m} d_m/(1 + d_m)$ induces.

items.title: Definition 2.17: tangent vectors in a chart

book.label: §2.2, Definition 2.17, pp. 25–26
book.statement: For $x \in O_1$, $T_xO = p^{-1}(x)$, the image of $Dr(x)$. Tuples $(x, V, \varphi, (O, C, E), h)$ with $x \in X_1$, $\varphi$ a chart around $x$ and $h \in T_{\varphi(x)}O$ are equivalent, $(x, \varphi, h) \sim (x', \psi, h')$, if $x = x'$ and $T(\varphi \circ \psi^{-1})(\psi(x))h' = h$.

lean.statement: A tangent tuple is $(x, \varphi, h)$ with $x \in X_1$, $\varphi$ a chart of the structure around $x$ and $(\varphi(x), h) \in TO$. Its transport to another chart $\psi$ around $x$ is $T(\psi \circ \varphi^{-1})(\varphi(x), h)$, computed on the overlap retract; transporting to $\varphi$ itself does nothing, transports land in $TO'$ over $\psi(x)$, and transporting to $\psi$ and then to $\chi$ is transporting to $\chi$. Two tuples are equivalent if their points agree and the transport of the first to the chart of the second is the second; this is an equivalence relation.

diff: The text does not check that the relation is an equivalence relation; it is, by the chain rule on the triple overlap and the locality of $Tf$ (`TangentPre.transport_transport`).
The relation is written with the transport in the direction $\varphi \to \psi$, $T(\psi \circ \varphi^{-1})(\varphi(x), h) = (\psi(x), h')$; it is the text's relation read from the other side.

items.title: Definition 2.18: the tangent space $TX$

book.label: §2.2, Definition 2.18, pp. 26–27
book.statement: $TX$ is the set of equivalence classes $[(x, \varphi, h)]$, $T_xX$ the classes over $x \in X_1$, a vector space; $TV$ is the set of classes over $V$ and $T\varphi : TV \to TO$, $[(x, \varphi, h)] \mapsto (\varphi(x), h)$, is linear on fibres. $TX$ is topologized by the sets $(T\varphi)^{-1}(W)$, $W$ open in $TO$.

lean.statement: $TX$ is the quotient of the tangent tuples by the equivalence of V2.18, with the projection $p : TX \to X_1$ and the fibres $T_xX = p^{-1}(x)$. For a chart $\varphi$, $TV = p^{-1}(V_1)$ and $T\varphi : TV \to TO$ sends a class to its transport to $\varphi$; $T\varphi[(x, \varphi, h)] = (\varphi(x), h)$, $T\varphi$ is injective on $TV$ with inverse $a \mapsto [(\varphi^{-1}(a), \varphi, a_2)]$, and $T\psi \circ (T\varphi)^{-1} = T(\psi \circ \varphi^{-1})$ on $T(\varphi(V \cap V'))$. The topology is generated by the sets $\{\alpha \in TV : T\varphi(\alpha) \in W\}$.

diff: The vector space structure of $T_xX$ and its Banach (resp. sc-Banach) structure are not formalized (G.7); $T_xX$ is a set, identified with $T_{\varphi(x)}O$ by $T\varphi$.
The topology is the one generated by the text's family; that it is a basis is not needed.

items.title: Proposition 2.19: $TX$ is Hausdorff and metrizable; $p$ is continuous

book.label: §2.2, Proposition 2.19, p. 27 (proof §2.6.3, pp. 58–60)
book.statement: (1) The family $\mathcal B$ is a basis of a Hausdorff topology on $TX$. (2) $p : TX \to X_1$ is continuous and open. (3) $TX$ is metrizable, hence paracompact.

lean.statement: (1) $TX$ is Hausdorff. (2) $p : TX \to X_1$ is continuous; so is $TX \to X$. (3) $TX$ is metrizable and paracompact. The sets $TV$ are open in $TX$.

diff: (1): Hausdorffness is an instance (`T2Space P.TangentSpace`); the basis property is not needed.
(2): openness of $p$ is not proved (it is not used); continuity is. The exposition's proof of openness (§8.3) is not formalized (G.8).
(3) is proved like Theorem 2.16, pulling a partition of unity of $X$ back along $TX \to X_1 \to X$; the text's argument via Proposition 2.57 is not used.

items.title: $TX$ is an M-polyfold and $p : TX \to X^1$ is sc-smooth

book.label: §2.2, after Proposition 2.19, p. 27
book.statement: $T\varphi : TV \to TO$ is a homeomorphism; $T\varphi' \circ (T\varphi)^{-1} = T(\varphi' \circ \varphi^{-1})$ (formula (5)) is sc-smooth; the charts $(TV, T\varphi, (TO, TC, TE))$ form an atlas, $TX$ is an M-polyfold, and $p : TX \to X_1$ is an sc-smooth M-polyfold bundle.

lean.statement: For a chart $\varphi$ of $X$, $(TV, T\varphi, (TO, TC, TE))$ is a chart of $TX$; $T\varphi(TV \cap TV') = T(\varphi(V \cap V'))$ and $T\varphi' \circ (T\varphi)^{-1} = T(\varphi' \circ \varphi^{-1})$ there (formula (5)); any two such charts are compatible, they form an atlas, and $TX$ is an M-polyfold. The projection $TO \to O^1$ is sc-smooth between retracts, and $p : TX \to X^1$ is sc-smooth.

diff: \"Sc-smooth M-polyfold bundle\" is read as: $p$ is sc-smooth; the fibrewise linear structure is not formalized (G.7).
`tangentPolyfold` and `tangentProj_isScSmooth` take the paracompactness of $TX$ and $X_1$ as instance arguments, supplied by V2.17 and V2.20.

items.title: The tangent map $Tf : TX \to TY$ and the chain rule

book.label: §2.2–§2.3, the tangent functor on M-polyfolds (used in Proposition 2.21(4), Definition 2.38)
book.statement: The text uses $Tf$ for sc-smooth maps between M-polyfolds (Proposition 2.21(4), Definition 2.38) without defining it; it defines $Tf$ between retracts and calls $T$ a functor.

lean.statement: For $f : X \to Y$ sc-smooth, $Tf[(x, \varphi, h)] := [(f(x), \psi, T(\psi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1})(\varphi(x), h)_2)]$ for a chart $\psi$ around $f(x)$ is well defined (independent of $\psi$ and of the representative); $p \circ Tf = f \circ p$, $Tf(T_xX) \subseteq T_{f(x)}Y$, in charts $T\psi \circ Tf = T(\psi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1}) \circ T\varphi$; $T(\mathrm{id}) = \mathrm{id}$, $T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf$, and $Tf$ is continuous and sc-smooth $TX \to TY$. chips: defined only implicitly in the text
diff: Not stated in the text; it is the tangent functor of §2.1 transported to M-polyfolds, and the text uses it from §2.3 on.
Only maps sc-smooth on all of $X$ are treated.

items.title: Definition 2.20: sub-M-polyfolds

book.label: §2.2, Definition 2.20, p. 28
book.statement: $A \subseteq X$ is a sub-M-polyfold if every $a \in A$ has an open neighbourhood $V$ and an sc-smooth retraction $r : V \to V$ with $r(V) = A \cap V$.

lean.statement: $A \subseteq X$ is a sub-M-polyfold if every $a \in A$ has an open $V \ni a$ and a map $r$ with $r(V) \subseteq V$, $r$ sc-smooth on $V$ (Definition 2.14), $r \circ r = r$ on $V$ and $r(V) = A \cap V$. $X$ is a sub-M-polyfold of itself.

diff: As in the text, with \"sc-smooth retraction $V \to V$\" read through Definition 2.14 on the open set $V$.

items.title: Proposition 2.21 (1), (2): the M-polyfold structure of a sub-M-polyfold

book.label: §2.2, Proposition 2.21 (1), (2), pp. 28–30
book.statement: A sub-M-polyfold $A$ has a natural M-polyfold structure for which (1) the inclusion $i : A \to X$ is sc-smooth and a homeomorphism onto its image; (2) for every sc-smooth retraction $r : V \to V$ with $r(V) = A \cap V$, $i^{-1} \circ r : V \to A$ is sc-smooth.

lean.statement: Let $A$ be a sub-M-polyfold with the subspace topology. For a chart $\varphi$ of $X$ and data $(V, r)$ at a point, $W = V \cap \operatorname{dom}\varphi \cap r^{-1}(V \cap \operatorname{dom}\varphi)$ is open with $r(W) \subseteq W$, $r(W) = W \cap A$; $\rho = \varphi \circ r \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is sc-smooth and idempotent on $\varphi(W)$, so $\varphi(W \cap A)$ is a retract and $(\varphi|_{W \cap A}, (\varphi(W \cap A), C, E))$ is a chart of $A$. Any two such charts are compatible; they form an atlas and make $A$ an M-polyfold. (1) $i$ is sc-smooth (a homeomorphism onto its image by the choice of topology). (2) For any data $(V, r)$, $i^{-1} \circ r$ is sc-smooth on $V$. $A$ is paracompact (V2.17); for closed $A$ this is elementary.

diff: The text does not say which topology $A$ carries; the subspace topology is taken, so (1)'s homeomorphism is by construction.
`subPolyfold` takes `[ParacompactSpace A]` as an instance argument; it is discharged by `MPolyfold.paracompactSpace_subtype` (V2.17), which the text uses implicitly through Theorem 2.16.
The compatibility argument $(\psi' \circ \psi^{-1}) \circ s'' = (\varphi' \circ \varphi^{-1}) \circ s''$ is `IsScSmoothRetractMap.mono_source`.

items.title: Proposition 2.21 (3), (4): the tangent space of a sub-M-polyfold, in a chart

book.label: §2.2, Proposition 2.21 (3), (4), p. 30
book.statement: (3) At a smooth $a \in A$, $T_aA$ has an sc-complement in $T_aX$. (4) For a retraction $s : W \to W$ onto $W \cap A$, the induced map $W \to A$ is sc-smooth and $Ts(a)T_aX = T_aA$. Proof in coordinates: $t = s \circ r$, $T_aA = Dt(a)E$, $T_aO = Ds(a)Dr(a)E \oplus (I - Ds(a))Dr(a)E$.

lean.statement: In a chart: let $O = r(U)$, $s$ sc-smooth $(O, C, E) \to (O, C, E)$ with $s \circ s = s$, $t = s \circ r$ (a retraction onto $s(O)$), and $a \in s(O)_1$ smooth. Then $T_aO = Dr(a)E$, $T_a s(O) = Dt(a)E \subseteq T_aO$, both $Dt(a)E$ and $(Dr(a) - Dt(a))E$ are sc-subspaces of $E$, and on every level their level parts are disjoint with sum the level part of $T_aO$ (an sc-splitting $T_aO = T_aA \oplus (Dr(a) - Dt(a))E$). items.title: Definition 2.22: the degeneracy index $d_X$

book.label: §2.3, Definition 2.22, p. 31
book.statement: For a chart $\varphi$ around $x$, $d(x, \varphi) = d_C(\varphi(x))$; $d_X(x)$ is the minimum of $d(x, \varphi)$ over all smooth charts around $x$.

lean.statement: $d(x, \varphi) = d_C(\varphi(x))$ for a chart $\varphi$ around $x$; $d_X(x)$ is the infimum of $d(x, \varphi)$ over the charts of the structure (the maximal atlas) around $x$. It is attained, and $d_X(x) \le d(x, \varphi)$ for every chart; $d(\cdot, \varphi)$ is upper semicontinuous on the source of $\varphi$.

items.title: Lemma 2.23: upper semicontinuity of $d_X$

book.statement: Every $x \in X$ has an open neighbourhood $U(x)$ with $d_X(y) \le d_X(x)$ for $y \in U(x)$.

items.title: Proposition 2.24: $d_X$ is invariant under sc-diffeomorphism germs

book.label: §2.3, Proposition 2.24, p. 31
book.statement: If $f : (U, x) \to (V, f(x))$ is a germ of sc-diffeomorphisms between M-polyfolds, then $d_X(x) = d_Y(f(x))$.

Then $d_X(x) = d_Y(f(x))$ for $x \in U$. For a chart $\psi$ of $Y$, $\psi \circ f$ on $U \cap f^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}\psi)$ is a chart of $X$, with $d(x, \psi \circ f) = d(f(x), \psi)$.

items.title: Remark 2.28: $T^R_xO \subseteq C_xO \subseteq T_xO$

lean.statement: $T^R_xO \subseteq C_xO$, and $C_xO \subseteq T_xO$ by definition. **The negative claim is false**: at every smooth point $x$ of every sc-smooth retract (no tameness), $T_xO$ and $T^R_xO$ are sc-subspaces of $E$ and $C_xO$ is a partial quadrant in the sc-Banach space $T_xO$ (with the sc-structure induced from $E$), of dimension $\operatorname{rank} M = \dim(T_xO/T^R_xO) \le d_C(x)$, $M$ the matrix of $Dr(x)$ on $E/E_x \cong \mathbb R^{I(x)}$. **The remark's negative claim does not hold in our reading (checked in Lean).** The remark asserts, without an example, that $C_xO$ is in general not a partial quadrant in $T_xO$; in our formalization it is one at every smooth point of every sc-smooth retract. $Dr(x)$ maps $C_x$ and $E_x$ into themselves, so $C_xO = Dr(x)(C_x)$, and modulo $T^R_xO$ it is the column cone of the nonnegative idempotent matrix $M$ of $Dr(x)$ on $E/E_x$; by Flor's theorem this cone is simplicial, and the sc-isomorphism $T_xO \cong \mathbb R^r \oplus T^R_xO$ of the proof of Theorem 2.31 carries $C_xO$ onto $[0, \infty)^r \oplus T^R_xO$. (c) A face $F$ of a tame retract $O$, with its sub-M-polyfold structure, is a tame M-polyfold and $d_F(x) + 1 = d_O(x)$ for $x \in F$.

diff: The text's model $(F, C \cap f_1, f_1)$ uses the sc-subspace $f_1$; here the extended face is modelled on $\mathbb R^k \oplus W$ through $\iota$, $\pi$, and the retraction is $\pi \circ r \circ \iota$ rather than $r|_{U^* \cap f_1}$ (they correspond under $\iota$). Tameness (2) of $r'$ is proved with the complement $(1 - Dr'(x))E'$, by Proposition 2.35 for $r$, not by intersecting with $f_1$.

$U^*$ is the union of the balls $B_e$ intersected with their preimages under $P_i$, because $P_i$ need not be norm-decreasing for the norm of $E_0$ (the exposition's \"$|P_1z - e|_0 \le |z - e|_0$\" is false in general).
\"$r(0, b_2, \dots, b_k, v)$ has the first coordinate vanishing\" is the local structure lemma (V2.45). $d_F = d_O - 1$ is stated as $d_F + 1 = d_O$; $F$ is paracompact because faces are closed.

items.title: Proposition 2.44: local faces and their intersections are tame

book.label: §2.4, Proposition 2.44, p. 46
book.statement: In a tame M-polyfold every point $x$ has $d_X(x)$ local faces containing $x$; they are tame M-polyfolds with $d_F(x) = d_X(x) - 1$. The intersection $F^\sigma$ of the local faces of $\sigma \subseteq \mathcal F_x$ is a tame M-polyfold of codimension $\#\sigma$ with $d_{F^\sigma}(x) = d_X(x) - \#\sigma$ (stated without proof).

lean.statement: Let $X$ be tame and $x \in X$. There is a chart $\varphi : V \to O$ of the structure around $x$, with a tame retraction onto $O$, such that the point $\varphi(x)$ lies in exactly $d_X(x)$ faces of the M-polyfold $O$, and every face $F$ of $O$ is a sub-M-polyfold of $O$ which, with its induced structure, is tame, with $d_F(\varphi(x)) + 1 = d_X(x)$ when $\varphi(x) \in F$. For every set $\sigma$ of face germs at $x$, i.e. $\sigma \subseteq I(\varphi(x))$, there are pairwise distinct faces $F_i \ni \varphi(x)$ of the retract ($i \in \sigma$, $F_i$ in the $i$-th coordinate hyperplane) and an open $B \ni \varphi(x)$ such that $A = \{y \in V : \varphi(y) \in B,\ \varphi(y) \in F_i\ \forall i \in \sigma\}$ (whose germ at $x$ is $F^\sigma_x$) is a sub-M-polyfold of $X$, tame with its induced structure, and $d_A(y) + \#\sigma = d_X(y)$ for all $y \in A$.

chips: face germs = faces of a tame chart
diff: "Local faces" are the faces of the M-polyfold $O$ of a tame chart, as in Proposition 2.42; the face germs at $x$ are the faces $F_i$, $i \in I(\varphi(x))$, and "$F^\sigma_x$ is the germ of a sub-M-polyfold" is witnessed by the set $A$ itself. Face germs are not defined as germs.

"Codimension $\#\sigma$" is the number of quadrant coordinates removed in the tame model $\pi_\sigma(\varphi(A)) \subseteq [0, \infty)^{n - \#\sigma} \oplus W$; $d_A + \#\sigma = d_X$ holds on all of $A$, not only at $x$.

The text gives no proof; the exposition argues by induction on $\#\sigma$. The formal proof removes all coordinates of $\sigma$ at once: Lemma 4.C for each $i \in \sigma$ makes $r \circ P_\sigma$ a retraction onto $O \cap B \cap f_\sigma$ near $\varphi(x)$ (`corner_retraction`), with the tame model $\pi_\sigma \circ r \circ \iota_\sigma$ (`corner_tameModel`), as in Proposition 2.43.

items.title: Theorem 2.45: interiors of faces and faces of face-structured M-polyfolds

book.label: §2.4, Theorem 2.45, p. 46
book.statement: The interior of a face $F$ in a tame M-polyfold is an sc-smooth sub-M-polyfold of $X$. If $X$ is face-structured, every face is a sub-M-polyfold, its induced structure is tame, and $i : F \to X$ satisfies $d_X(i(x)) = d_F(x) + 1$. Every point has a neighbourhood $U$ in which each $y$ lies in exactly $d_X(y)$ faces of $U$; if $X$ is face-structured, each $x$ lies in exactly $d_X(x)$ faces of $X$ (stated without proof).

lean.statement: Let $X$ be tame, $G$ the connected component of $\{d_X = 1\}$ through a point, $F = \overline G$. (a) $F \cap \{d_X = 1\} = G$ (the interior of the face), and $G$ is a sub-M-polyfold of $X$. (b) If $X$ is face-structured, every face $F$ agrees near each of its points, in a tame chart, with a face of the model retract; $F$ is a sub-M-polyfold of $X$, tame with its induced structure, and $d_X(x) = d_F(x) + 1$ for $x \in F$. A local criterion: $A$ is a sub-M-polyfold if near each point $\varphi(A)$ agrees on an open set with an sc-smooth retract contained in $O$. The face counts of the theorem are Proposition 2.42 and the definition of face-structured.

diff: \"The interior of a face\" is not defined in the text; it is read as $F \cap \{d_X = 1\}$, which equals $G$.

The text has no proof. In the face-structured case, \"each global face through $x$ contains exactly one local face\" is a counting argument: the map from $I(\varphi x)$ to the faces through $x$ is onto (Lemma 4.C) and, by face-structuredness, injective.

The retraction near a point is $\varphi^{-1} \circ s \circ \varphi$ on $\varphi^{-1}(B \cap s^{-1}(B))$, shrunk so that $s$ maps it into itself; the exposition's \"transport by $\varphi^{-1}$\" omits this.

items.title: Products of M-polyfolds (exposition Lemma 4.D)

book.label: §2.4, proof of Proposition 2.46, p. 47
book.statement: Used without statement in Proposition 2.46: $X \times Y$ is an M-polyfold (with the product charts) and $d_{X \times Y}(x, y) = d_X(x) + d_Y(y)$.

lean.statement: For partial quadrants $C \subseteq E$, $C' \subseteq E'$, $C \times C'$ is a partial quadrant of $E \oplus E'$ with the product presentation $E \oplus E' \cong \mathbb R^{n+n'} \oplus (W \oplus W')$ and $d_{C \times C'}(x, x') = d_C(x) + d_{C'}(x')$; products of sc-smooth retractions are sc-smooth retractions, of tame ones tame. For M-polyfolds $X$, $Y$: $X \times Y$ is paracompact, and the product charts form an atlas of an M-polyfold structure on $X \times Y$; $d_{X \times Y}(x, y) \le d_X(x) + d_Y(y)$, with equality, and $X \times Y$ tame, if $X$ and $Y$ are tame. The projections are sc-smooth and the pairing of sc-smooth maps is sc-smooth.

diff: Not stated in the text; this is the exposition's Lemma 4.D. The text's \"$d_{X \times Y} = d_X + d_Y$\" is proved for tame $X$, $Y$; in general only the inequality, from the product charts.
Paracompactness of $X \times Y$ comes from Theorem 2.16 ($X$, $Y$ metrizable).

items.title: Proposition 2.46: fibred products

book.label: §2.4, Proposition 2.46, pp. 46–47
book.statement: For a local sc-diffeomorphism $f : X \to Z$ and an sc-smooth $g : Y \to Z$, $X {}_f\times_g Y$ is a sub-M-polyfold of $X \times Y$; if $Y$ is tame, so is the fibred product, with $d(x, y) = d_Y(y)$; with both maps local sc-diffeomorphisms and both spaces tame, $d = \frac12 d_{X \times Y} = d_X(x) = d_Y(y)$.

lean.statement: Let $f : X \to Z$ be a local sc-diffeomorphism (each point has an open neighbourhood mapped sc-diffeomorphically onto an open set) and $g : Y \to Z$ sc-smooth. The fibred product $\{(x, y) : f(x) = g(y)\}$ is closed in $X \times Y$, hence paracompact, and a sub-M-polyfold of $X \times Y$; $d_{X {}_f\times_g Y}(x, y) = d_Y(y)$; if $Y$ is tame, the fibred product is tame. If $g$ is also a local sc-diffeomorphism, $d_{X {}_f\times_g Y}(x, y) = d_X(x) = d_Y(y)$, and if moreover $X$ and $Y$ are tame, $2\,d_{X {}_f\times_g Y}(x, y) = d_{X \times Y}(x, y)$.

diff: $d_{X {}_f\times_g Y} = d_Y \circ \pi_2$, and in the last statement $d = d_X = d_Y$, hold for arbitrary $X$, $Y$ (Proposition 2.24 along $\pi_2$, $\pi_1$); tameness is used only for $d_{X \times Y} = d_X + d_Y$ (V2.52), stated as $2d = d_{X \times Y}$.

The inverse of $\pi_2$ near $(x, y)$ is $y' \mapsto ((f|_U)^{-1}(g(y')), y')$; the exposition's factorization through $y' \mapsto (x, y')$ is not sc-smooth unless $x$ is a smooth point (Findings, Chapter 2, item 15).

The text's $\pi_2 : X {}_f\times_g Y \to X$ is read with target $Y$; paracompactness of the fibred product, which the text does not mention, comes from its being closed in the metrizable $X \times Y$.

items.title: Definition 2.47: $U \triangleleft F$, strong bundle maps and retractions

book.label: §2.5, Definition 2.47, p. 48
book.statement: $U \triangleleft F$ is $U \times F$ with the double filtration $U_m \oplus F_k$, $0 \le k \le m + 1$, and $(U \triangleleft F)[i]$ with levels $U_m \oplus F_{m+i}$. A strong bundle map $\Phi(u, h) = (\varphi(u), \Gamma(u, h))$, $\Gamma$ linear in $h$, preserves the double filtration and is sc-smooth $(U \triangleleft F)[i] \to (U' \triangleleft F')[i]$, $i = 0, 1$; a strong bundle retraction is one with $R \circ R = R$; $R(u, h) = (r(u), \Gamma(u, h))$ with $r$ an sc-smooth retraction.

lean.statement: $\Phi : E_0 \times F_0 \to E'_0 \times F'_0$ is a strong bundle map on $U \triangleleft F$ if it maps $U \times F$ into $U' \times F'$, its first component does not depend on $h$, its second is linear in $h$ for $u \in U$, it maps $U_m \oplus F_k$ into $U'_m \oplus F'_k$ for $k \le m + 1$, and it is sc-smooth on $U \times F_0$ for $E \oplus F$ and (through the lift of the fibre component to $F'_1$) on $U \times F_1$ for $E \oplus F^1$. A strong bundle retraction is one with $R \circ R = R$; its base $r(u) = R(u, 0)_1$ is an sc-smooth retraction on $U$, $\Gamma(u, \cdot)$ is a projection for $u \in O$, and $R$ is an sc-smooth retraction on $(U \triangleleft F)[0]$ and on $(U \triangleleft F)[1]$. $C \times F$ is a partial quadrant in $E \oplus F$ and $U \times F$ is relatively open in it.

diff: Sc-smoothness on $[1]$ is that of the induced map $U \oplus F_1 \to U' \oplus F'_1$; \"preserves the double filtration\" is read level by level.
Strong bundle isomorphisms are not defined separately (G.14); the remarks after the definition ($r$ a retraction, $\Gamma(u, \cdot)$ a projection) are the exposition's Lemma 5.A, proved here.

items.title: Definition 2.48: local strong bundle retracts and $K[i]$

book.label: §2.5, Definition 2.48 and the remarks after it, pp. 49–50
book.statement: A local strong bundle retract is $K = R(U \triangleleft F)$ for a strong bundle retraction, $p : K \to O$; $K_{m,k} = \{(u, h) \in O_m \oplus F_k : \Gamma(u, h) = h\}$, $K[i] = K_{0,i}$ with the filtration $K_{m,m+i}$; the projections $p : K[i] \to O$ are sc-smooth.

lean.statement: $K \subseteq E_0 \times F_0$ is a local strong bundle retract over $C$ if $K = R(U \times F_0)$ for a strong bundle retraction on some relatively open $U \subseteq C$; then $K = \{(u, h) : u \in O, \Gamma(u, h) = h\}$. Its double filtration $K_{m,k}$ and $K[1] = \{(u, h) \in E_0 \times F_1 : (u, h) \in K\}$ are defined level by level. $K$ is an sc-smooth retract in $(C \times F, E \oplus F)$ and $K[1]$ one in $(C \times F, E \oplus F^1)$, $K[1]$ being the image of $R$ on $(U \triangleleft F)[1]$; $p : K[i] \to O$ and the inclusion $K[1] \to K[0]$ are sc-smooth.

diff: $K[1]$ is a subset of $(E \oplus F^1)_0 = E_0 \times F_1$. The text's \"$p$ is sc-smooth\" is proved, with \"sc-smooth bundle map\" read as sc-smooth.
That $K[1]$ is the image of $R$ on $(U \triangleleft F)[1]$ uses that $R$ preserves the double filtration at $(m, k) = (0, 1)$ (exposition Lemma 5.B).

items.title: Definition 2.49: sections of a local strong bundle retract

book.label: §2.5, Definition 2.49, p. 50
book.statement: A section of $p : K \to O$ is $f : O \to K$ with $p \circ f = 1_O$; sc-smooth if it is sc-smooth into $K[0]$, sc⁺-smooth if sc-smooth into $K[1]$ (the text writes $K(0)$, $K(1)$); $f(x) = (x, \mathbf f(x))$ with the principal part $\mathbf f$.

lean.statement: An sc-smooth section is $f$ with $f(x)_1 = x$ on $O$ and $f$ sc-smooth from $(O, C, E)$ to $(K, C \times F, E \oplus F)$; an sc⁺-section is $f : E_0 \to E_0 \times F_1$ with $f(x)_1 = x$ on $O$, sc-smooth into $(K[1], C \times F, E \oplus F^1)$. An sc⁺-section is an sc-smooth section.

diff: The principal part is not named separately; an sc⁺-section takes its fibre values in $F_1$ by type.
The category $\mathcal{SBR}$ and the forgetful functors are not formalized (G.14).

items.title: Definition 2.50: strong bundle charts, compatibility, atlases

book.label: §2.5, Definition 2.50, pp. 51–52
book.statement: For $P : Y \to X$ (Y paracompact Hausdorff, fibres Banachable), a strong bundle chart $(\Phi, P^{-1}(V), K, U \triangleleft F)$: $K = R(U \triangleleft F)$, $V$ open with a homeomorphism $\varphi : V \to O$, $\Phi : P^{-1}(V) \to K$ a homeomorphism covering $\varphi$, bounded linear on fibres. Charts are compatible if $(\Phi' \circ \Phi^{-1})[i]$ are sc-diffeomorphisms, $i = 0, 1$; atlases and their equivalence.

lean.statement: A strong bundle chart consists of a chart $\varphi$ *of the M-polyfold $X$*, an sc-Banach space $F$, a strong bundle retraction $R$ on a relatively open $U \subseteq C$ whose base retract is $O$, and a homeomorphism $\Phi : P^{-1}(V) \to K = R(U \times F_0)$ with $\Phi(y)_1 = \varphi(P(y))$, linear on each fibre $P^{-1}(x)$ (continuity on fibres follows). Two charts are compatible if $\Phi' \circ \Phi^{-1}$ and $\Phi \circ \Phi'^{-1}$ are sc-smooth between the overlap retracts on $[0]$ and, through the lift to $F_1$, on $[1]$, and map fibre components in $F_1$ to fibre components in $F'_1$. Atlases: pairwise compatible charts covering $Y$; equivalence: the union is an atlas. Equivalence of strong bundle atlases is an equivalence relation, and two atlases are equivalent iff every chart of one is compatible with every chart of the other; this rests on the locality of compatibility. A strong bundle chart restricts to every open $s \subseteq V$ (retraction domain $U \cap r^{-1}(W)$ for $\varphi(s) = O \cap W$, $K_s = \{(u, h) \in K \mid u \in \varphi(s)\}$, $\Phi$ unchanged), and restrictions of compatible charts are compatible.

diff: The base homeomorphism $\varphi$ is required to be a chart of $X$; the text asks only for a homeomorphism onto $O$, under which the strong bundle atlas would define its own structure on $X$.
\"Bounded linear on the fibres\" needs only linearity: continuity follows from $\Phi$ being a homeomorphism (`continuous_fiber`).
For $(\Phi' \circ \Phi^{-1})[1]$ to be defined, the transition must map fibre components in $F_1$ to $F'_1$; the text takes this for granted, the definition states it.

The “equivalence class of strong bundle atlases” of Definition 2.51 presupposes that the equivalence is transitive. It is: near a point of the overlap the transition $\Phi'' \circ \Phi^{-1}$ factors through a chart $\Phi'$ of the middle atlas, on $[0]$ and on $[1]$, and the $F_1$-condition passes through $\Phi'$; no continuity of $P$ is needed (Findings, Chapter 2, item 40). The restriction of a strong bundle chart to an open subset of the base, which the text uses silently (e.g. in Lemma 5.2, V5.4), is formalized; a restriction whose retraction domain lies inside a given open $W \ni 0$ of $E$ is not, since $U \cap W$ need not be invariant under $r$ (item 42). Updated in the third addendum of this page.

items.title: Definition 2.51: strong bundles; $Y[0]$, $Y[1]$, $P[0]$, $P[1]$ and $Y_{m,k}$

book.label: §2.5, Definition 2.51 and the remarks after it, p. 52
book.statement: A strong bundle over $X$ is $P : Y \to X$ (continuous surjection, $Y$ paracompact Hausdorff) with an equivalence class of strong bundle atlases. The charts induce a double filtration $Y_{m,k}$ and M-polyfolds $Y[i]$, $Y[i]_m = Y_{m,m+i}$; $P[i] : Y[i] \to X$ are sc-smooth.

lean.statement: A strong bundle is a continuous surjection $P : Y \to X$ ($Y$ Hausdorff paracompact) with Banachable fibres and a strong bundle atlas. The charts $\Phi$ form an sc-smooth atlas of $Y$, making it the M-polyfold $Y[0]$, and $P[0] : Y[0] \to X$ is sc-smooth. $Y_{m,k}$ ($k \le m + 1$) is defined by $\Phi(y) \in E_m \times F_k$ in all charts around $y$, and one chart suffices. $Y[1]$ is the set $Y_{0,1}$ with the topology generated by the charts $\Phi[1] : y \mapsto (\Phi(y)_1, \Phi(y)_2$ lifted to $F_1)$; these charts, onto the retracts $K[1]$, are pairwise compatible, their transition maps being the $[1]$-transitions, and make $Y[1]$ an M-polyfold; $P[1] : Y[1] \to X$ is sc-smooth. The charts of the strong bundle (`StrongBundle.IsChart`: compatible with the atlas) are those of the maximal atlas, which is equivalent to the given one: a chart is one iff it belongs to some atlas of the class, any two are compatible, restrictions of charts are charts, and equivalent atlases have the same charts.

chips: charts depend only on the class
diff: $Y[0]$ (the text's "the M-polyfold $Y$") and $Y[1]$ are constructed with the charts induced by the given atlas; the equivalence class of atlases is represented by one atlas, as for M-polyfolds. The notions defined through the charts compatible with the atlas therefore depend only on the class (`isChart_congr`, `isChart_iff_exists_equiv`; Findings, Chapter 2, item 43); those defined with the charts of the given atlas itself ($Y_{m,k}$, $Y[1]$ and its atlas, sc$^+$-sections) are not shown invariant. Updated in the third addendum of this page.

$Y[1]$ is the subset $Y_{0,1}$ with the topology generated by the sets $\Phi[1]^{-1}(W)$, as for $X_m$ in §2.2; its paracompactness, required of an M-polyfold and not mentioned in the text, follows from metrizability (V2.64).

Chart independence of $Y_{m,k}$: for $k \le m$ it follows from the $[0]$-transition; for $k = m + 1$, and for the set $Y_{0,1}$ itself, it uses the condition that the $[1]$-transition carries fibre components in $F_1$ to $F'_1$, made explicit in Definition 2.50 (V2.57).

items.title: Definition 2.52: sections of a strong bundle

book.label: §2.5, Definition 2.52, p. 53
book.statement: A section is $f : X \to Y$ with $P \circ f = 1_X$; sc-smooth if sc-smooth into $Y[0]$, sc⁺ if sc-smooth into $Y[1]$.

lean.statement: A section is $f$ with $P \circ f = \mathrm{id}$; it is sc-smooth if it is sc-smooth $X \to Y[0]$ (Definition 2.14); it is an sc⁺-section if in every strong bundle chart of the atlas its fibre values lie in $F_1$ and its representative $z \mapsto \Phi(f(\varphi^{-1}(z)))$, lifted to $E_0 \times F_1$, is sc-smooth from $O$ into $K[1]$. This holds iff $f$ is a section and $f = \iota \circ g$ for an sc-smooth $g : X \to Y[1]$, $\iota : Y[1] \to Y$ the inclusion.

chips: sc⁺ chart by chart = sc-smooth into $Y[1]$
diff: Sc⁺-sections are defined chart by chart through $\Phi[1]$; `isScPlusSection_iff` proves that this is the text's "sc-smooth as a map into $Y[1]$", the section being a map into the type $Y[1]$ followed by the inclusion.

items.title: Definition 2.53: the pull-back bundle

book.label: §2.5, Definition 2.53, p. 53
book.statement: For a strong bundle $P : Y \to X$ and an sc-smooth $f : Z \to X$, $f^*Y = \{(z, y) : P(y) = f(z)\}$, $P_f(z, y) = z$, $P'(z, y) = y$, and $P \circ P' = f \circ P_f$.

lean.statement: $f^*Y = \{(z, y) \in Z \times Y : P(y) = f(z)\}$ with $P_f$, $P'$ the projections; $P \circ P' = f \circ P_f$; $P_f$ is continuous, and $f^*Y$ is closed in $Z \times Y$ when $X$ is Hausdorff and $P$, $f$ are continuous.

diff: As in the text, for any maps $P$, $f$.

items.title: Proposition 2.54: the pull-back of a strong bundle is a strong bundle

book.label: §2.5, Proposition 2.54, p. 53
book.statement: $P_f : f^*Y \to Z$ carries a natural structure of a strong bundle over $Z$ (\"the easy proof is left to the reader\").

lean.statement: For a strong bundle $P : Y \to X$ and an sc-smooth $f : Z \to X$: $f^*Y$ is paracompact (it is metrizable, $Z$ and $Y[0]$ being metrizable by Theorem 2.16), $P_f$ is a continuous surjection, its fibres $P_f^{-1}(z) \cong P^{-1}(f(z))$ are Banachable, and the pulled-back charts $\Phi_f(z, y) = (\psi(z), \mathrm{pr}_F\Phi(y))$, with the strong bundle retractions $R_g(w, h) = (r_Z(w), \Gamma(g(r_Z(w)), h))$, $g = \varphi \circ f \circ \psi^{-1}$, form a strong bundle atlas; so $P_f$ is a strong bundle with this atlas. Locally: $R_g$ is a strong bundle retraction with image $\{(w, h) : w \in O_Z, (g(w), h) \in K\}$; the transition maps of pulled-back charts are $(w, h) \mapsto (\psi_2\psi_1^{-1}(w), \mathrm{pr}_F(\Phi_2\Phi_1^{-1})(g_1(w), h))$, sc-smooth on $[0]$ and $[1]$.

diff: \"Natural structure\" is the atlas of all pulled-back charts; any two are compatible, so it involves no choice.
The paracompactness of $f^*Y$, required by Definition 2.51 and not mentioned in the text, is proved from Theorem 2.16 for $Z$ and $Y[0]$.

“Natural” presumably also says that $P' : f^*Y \to Y$ is a strong bundle map (sc-smooth on $[0]$ and $[1]$); that is not formalized. In the charts $\Phi_f$, $\Phi$ it is $(w, h) \mapsto (g(w), h)$ on $K_g$ (Findings, Chapter 2, item 51; round-trip item V2.61). Recorded in the third addendum of this page.

items.title: Theorem 2.55: Smirnov's metrization theorem

book.label: §2.6.2, Theorem 2.55, p. 56
book.statement: A paracompact Hausdorff space in which every point has a metrizable open neighbourhood is metrizable (quoted from Smirnov).

lean.statement: A paracompact Hausdorff space in which every point has a metrizable open neighbourhood is metrizable. More generally: a space $Y$ with open metrizable $V_i$ and a locally finite family of continuous $\rho_i \ge 0$, $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i \subseteq V_i$, not all zero at any point, is metrizable, with the metric $\sum_i |\rho_i(x) - \rho_i(y)| + \min(\rho_i(x), \rho_i(y)) \min(d_i(x, y), 1)$; and if $\pi : Y \to X$ is continuous into a paracompact Hausdorff $X$ and every point of $X$ has an open $U$ with $\pi^{-1}(U)$ metrizable, $Y$ is metrizable. Metrizable spaces are paracompact (Stone, from Mathlib).

diff: Quoted in the text; proved here (Mathlib does not have it), in the stronger pull-back form that Theorem 2.16 and Proposition 2.19(3) use.

items.title: Restriction and locality of sc$^k$ maps

book.label: §2.1–§2.2, used in Propositions 2.4, 2.10 and Definitions 2.13–2.14
book.statement: Used without statement: an sc-smooth map restricted to a smaller relatively open set is sc-smooth (e.g. \"$r : U \to U \cap U'$ is sc-smooth\"), and sc-smoothness is a local property.

lean.statement: On sc-domains: an $\mathrm{sc}^k$ (sc-smooth) map on $U$ is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ (sc-smooth) on every smaller sc-domain $U'$, with the same tangent map on $TU'$; a map that is $\mathrm{sc}^1$, $\mathrm{sc}^k$ or sc-smooth on $U \cap W$ for an open $W$ around each point of $U$ is so on $U$; sc-smoothness depends only on the values on $U$.

diff: Not stated in the text. The restriction needs the uniqueness of derivatives on the smaller domain, because the tangent map is built from a chosen derivative; the locality glues the local derivatives into one family.

items.title: The space $Y[1]$ and the inclusion $Y[1] \to Y[0]$

book.label: §2.5, after Definition 2.51, p. 52
book.statement: Not stated: the text takes $Y[1]$ to be an M-polyfold on the set $Y_{0,1}$ without discussing its topology, its paracompactness or its inclusion into $Y[0]$.

lean.statement: $Y_{0,1}$ is the set of points whose fibre component lies in $F_1$ in one, equivalently every, chart of the atlas around them. With the topology generated by the charts $\Phi[1]$, the inclusion $Y[1] \to Y$ is continuous, so $Y[1]$ is Hausdorff; $Y[1]$ is metrizable, hence paracompact; and the inclusion $Y[1] \to Y[0]$ is sc-smooth (in the charts it is $(u, h) \mapsto (u, \iota h)$).

diff: Not stated in the text. Paracompactness is needed for $Y[1]$ to be an M-polyfold (Definition 2.13); it follows, as in Theorem 2.16, from the pull-back form of Smirnov's theorem over the paracompact base (V2.62).
The sc-smooth inclusion $Y[1] \to Y[0]$ is the global form of $K[1] \to K[0]$ (V2.55).

items.title: Definition 3.1: sc-germs of neighbourhoods

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.1, p. 62
book.statement: An sc-germ of neighbourhoods $\mathcal O(C, 0)$ around $0$ in a partial quadrant $C \subseteq E$ is a decreasing sequence $U_0 \supset U_1 \supset \cdots$ with $U_m$ a relatively open neighbourhood of $0$ in $C_m = C \cap E_m$; its tangent $T\mathcal O(C, 0)$ is $U_1 \oplus E_0 \supset U_2 \oplus E_1 \supset \cdots$. A relatively open $U \ni 0$ with $U_m = U \cap E_m$ is an example; \"the size of the sets $U_m$ does not matter\".

lean.statement: An `ScNbhdGerm E C` is a family of sets $U_m \subseteq E_m$, each of the form $O \cap C_m$ with $O$ open and $0 \in U_m$, nested along the inclusions $E_{m+1} \to E_m$. Its tangent germ has levels $U_{m+1} \times E_m$; `ofSet` is the text's example $U_m = U \cap E_m$. The theorems on germs ask $C$ to be *quadrant-like* (every $C_m$ convex with nonempty interior, $0 \in C$), which every partial quadrant is; then derivatives on $U_1$ are unique.

chips: a germ is a fixed sequence of sets
diff: A germ is a fixed sequence of sets, not a class \"up to shrinking\". The text's remark that the size of the $U_m$ does not matter is therefore not built in; where it matters (Theorems 3.30, 3.33–3.35) the formal statements say on which germ they hold (V3.27, V3.30–V3.32).

The re-indexed sequence $(U_{m+1})_m$ is a germ only when all levels coincide (a finite-dimensional parameter space); the text does not remark this, and the germ implicit function theorem uses it once per derivative.

items.title: Definition 3.2: sc$^k$-germs

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.2, pp. 62–63
book.statement: An sc$^0$-germ $f : \mathcal O(C, 0) \to F$ is a continuous $f : U_0 \to F$ with $f(U_m) \subseteq F_m$ and $f : U_m \to F_m$ continuous. It is sc$^1$ if for $x \in U_1$ there is a bounded $Df(x) : E_0 \to F_0$ with $|f(x + h) - f(x) - Df(x)h|_0 / |h|_1 \to 0$ ($h \in E_1$, $x + h \in U_1$) and $Tf(x, h) = (f(x), Df(x)h)$ is an sc$^0$-germ on $T\mathcal O(C, 0)$; sc$^k$ inductively, sc-smooth if sc$^k$ for all $k$.

lean.statement: `IsSc0Germ`, `IsSc1GermWith` (with a given derivative family), `IsSc1Germ`, `IsSckGerm`, `IsScSmoothGerm` are the notions of Definitions 1.12–1.15 with $U \cap E_m$ replaced by $U_m$. An sc$^k$ map on a relatively open $U \ni 0$ is an sc$^k$-germ on `ofSet U`.

diff: As in the text, with the derivative family chosen (as in Chapter 1); it is unique on $U_1$ for quadrant-like $C$ (`IsSc1GermWith.eq_of_uniqueDiffWithinAt`).

items.title: The calculus of germs

book.label: §3.1–§3.3, used without statement (proofs of Lemma 3.31, Theorems 3.33, 3.38)
book.statement: Not stated: the text restricts, composes and pairs germs and applies sc-operators to them as it does with maps on open sets.

lean.statement: (1) sc$^k$-germs depend only on the values on $U_0$ and restrict to smaller germs; (2) the chain rule: if $f$ is an sc$^k$-germ on $G$, $g$ an sc$^k$-germ on $G'$ and $f$ maps $U_m$ into $U'_m$ for every $m$, then $g \circ f$ is an sc$^k$-germ and $T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf$ on $TG$; (3) sc-operators are sc-smooth germs on every germ; (4) the pairing of two sc$^k$-germs is an sc$^k$-germ; (5) the germ $\{x \in G_0 : f(x) \in G'\}$ on which an sc$^0$-germ maps into a given germ.

diff: The chain rule needs the inner germ to map $U_m$ into the domain $U'_m$ of the outer one on every level (`ScNbhdGerm.MapsToGerm`); for maps on open sets this is $f(U) \subseteq V$. The shrinking of germs that the text performs with \"near $0$\" is `ScNbhdGerm.preimage`.

items.title: Propositions 1.16–1.18 for germs

book.label: §3.1, proof of Lemma 3.9 ("recalling Proposition 1.17"), Lemma 3.31, Corollary 3.34
book.statement: Not stated: Propositions 1.16–1.18 are stated in Chapter 1 for relatively open sets; the proofs of Lemma 3.9, Lemma 3.31 and Corollary 3.34 apply them to germs.

lean.statement: For an sc$^1$-germ $f$ with derivative family $D$: $Df(x)$, $x \in U_{m+1}$, restricts to bounded level operators $E_m \to F_m$, jointly continuous in $(x, h)$ (also in operator norm), and $f : U_{m+1} \to F_m$ is differentiable within $U_{m+1}$ with these derivatives (1.16); the shifted sequence $(U_{m+1})_m$ is a germ in $E^1$ and an sc$^k$-germ on $G$ is an sc$^k$-germ $G^1 \to F^1$ (1.17); an sc$^k$-germ is $C^k$ from $U_{m+k}$ to $F_m$ (1.18).

diff: The proofs are those of Chapter 1 with $U \cap E_m$ replaced by $U_m$. The text's \"recalling Proposition 1.17\" in Lemma 3.9 is Proposition 1.16 for germs.

items.title: Definition 3.3: sc-smooth section germs

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.3, p. 63
book.statement: An sc-smooth section germ $(f, x_0)$ of $P : Y \to X$ is a continuous section $f : V \to P^{-1}(V)$ near the smooth point $x_0$ such that in a strong bundle chart with $\varphi(x_0) = 0$ the principal part $\mathbf f$ of $\Phi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1} : O \to K$ has $\mathbf f \circ r : \mathcal O(C, 0) \to F$ an sc-smooth germ.

lean.statement: `StrongBundle.IsScSmoothSectionGerm f x₀`: $x_0$ smooth, and for some strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas (`StrongBundle.IsChart`) with $\varphi(x_0) = 0$, $\mathbf f \circ r$ is an sc-smooth germ on some sc-germ of neighbourhoods $G$ with $G_0 \subseteq U$, whose levels may shrink with $m$ (the text’s germ reading). An sc-smooth section is an sc-smooth section germ at every smooth point with a centred chart (with the germ $U \cap E_m$).

diff: \"A strong bundle chart\" is read as a chart compatible with the atlas, not a member of it: a chart of the atlas need not be centred at $x_0$, and the notion must not depend on the atlas within its class (Findings, Chapter 3, item 41). That it does not is proved: equivalent atlases have the same compatible charts (`isChart_congr`; V2.58, Findings, Chapter 2, item 43). Updated in the third addendum of this page.
Continuity of $f$ near $x_0$ is not a separate field: it follows near $x_0$ from the continuity of $\mathbf f \circ r$ on level $0$ of the germ.

**Germs.** Since the fourth addendum of this page the definition is in the text’s germ reading: $\mathbf f \circ r$ is an sc-smooth germ on some sc-germ of neighbourhoods inside $U$, whose levels may shrink with $m$, as for Definitions 3.4, 3.6 and 3.11 since phase 2. Before, it was required on the whole $U$ of the chart (levels $U \cap E_m$), which is stricter: a function $C^k$ on $(-1/k, 1/k)$ for every $k$ is an sc-smooth germ in the constant scale $\mathbb R$ and sc-smooth on no neighbourhood of $0$ (`exists_isScSmoothGerm_not_isScSmooth`). No theorem assumes the definition. Hence “hypotheses explicit” again (“narrower” from the third addendum until the fourth) (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 260; round-trip item V3.5).

items.title: The section algebra and the sum rule

book.label: §3.1, used in Theorems 3.12, 3.15 ("$f + s$ is an sc-smooth section")
book.statement: Not stated: the fibrewise sum of sections, principal parts in a chart, the sum rule of the sc-calculus, and the sc-smoothness of the local representatives of sc$^+$-sections in a chart that is not in the atlas.

lean.statement: The fibrewise sum $f + s$ is a section with principal part $\mathbf f + \mathbf s$ in every chart; $f(x) = 0$ iff $\mathbf f(\varphi(x)) = 0$; the fibres of $K$ are linear. Sums, differences and negatives of sc-smooth maps on relatively open subsets of partial quadrants are sc-smooth. In every strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas, $z \mapsto (z, \mathbf f(z))$ is sc-smooth $O \to K$ for an sc-smooth section and $z \mapsto (z, \mathbf s_1(z))$ is sc-smooth $O \to K[1]$ for an sc$^+$-section.

diff: For an sc$^+$-section in a chart outside the atlas the sc-smoothness of the representative is the change of chart $(\Phi \circ \Phi'^{-1})[1]$, i.e. the compatibility on $[1]$ of Definition 2.50; this is its first use (Findings, Chapter 3, item 41).
The sum rule is pairing followed by the sc-operator $F \oplus F \to F$.

items.title: Definition 3.4: fillers

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.4, p. 64
book.statement: For a tame strong local bundle $K = R(U \triangleleft F) \to O$, $R(u, h) = (r(u), \rho(u)h)$, $r(0) = 0$, an sc-smooth section germ $(f, 0)$ has a filling $(g, 0)$ (an sc-smooth section germ of $U \triangleleft F \to U$) if (1) $f = g$ on $O$ near $0$; (2) $g(y) = \rho(r(y))g(y)$ for $y \in U$ near $0$ forces $y \in O$; (3) the linearization of $y \mapsto [1 - \rho(r(y))]g(y)$ at $0$, restricted to $\ker Dr(0)$, is a topological isomorphism onto $\ker\rho(0)$.

lean.statement: `IsFillingGerm` for the principal parts $f, g : E_0 \to F_0$ (the text’s germ reading, also Definition 3.6, V3.9): $g$ is an sc-smooth germ on an sc-germ of neighbourhoods $G$ with $G_0 \subseteq U$; (1) and (2) near $0$; (3) the map $y \mapsto [1 - \rho(r(y))]g(y)$ (`fillDefect`) is an sc$^1$-germ on $G$ with a derivative family $Dk$, and $Dk(0)$ induces a continuous linear equivalence $\ker Dr(0) \simeq \ker\rho(0)$. Here $r(u) = (R(u, 0))_1$, $\rho(u)h = (R(u, h))_2$, with $R(u, h) = (r(u), \rho(u)h)$, $r \circ r = r$, $\rho(x)$ a projection for $x \in O$, and $\rho(u)$ a bounded operator. The whole-chart form `IsFillerOf` asks the map in (3) to be sc$^1$ on all of $U$ and says nothing about the regularity of $g$.

chips: sc¹ of the map in (3) required
diff: Condition (3) presupposes that $y \mapsto [1 - \rho(r(y))]g(y)$ is differentiable at $0$; it is required to be an sc$^1$-germ with a derivative family, which holds for every sc-smooth germ $g$ (`fillDefect_isScSmoothGerm`); the value of the family at $0$ is unique (Findings, Chapter 3, items 261, 272).
The sc-smoothness of $g$ is part of the filling, as in the text (“$(g, 0)$ an sc-smooth section germ”); tameness of the retraction is not used.

**Germs.** Since the switch to the text’s germ reading (phase 2) $g$ and the map in (3) are germs whose levels may shrink with $m$ (`IsFillingGerm`); the stricter whole-chart filler (`IsFillerOf`, with $g$ sc-smooth on all of $U$ added in `IsFilledVersion`) is kept for the `…WholeChart` notions. Hence “hypotheses explicit” again (“narrower” in the third addendum) (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 261, 330; round-trip items V3.7, V3.19). On the text’s domain of definition, tame strong local bundles, it is not broader: tameness is simply not used.

items.title: Proposition 3.5: the filler and the linearization

book.label: §3.1, the paragraph after Definition 3.4 and Proposition 3.5, pp. 64–65
book.statement: If $f$ has the filling $g$ and $f(0) = 0$, then in the splittings $E = Dr(0)E \oplus \ker Dr(0)$, $F = \rho(0)F \oplus \ker\rho(0)$, $Dg(0) = \begin{pmatrix} Tf(0) & * \\ 0 & C \end{pmatrix}$ with $C$ an isomorphism, and (1) $Tf(0) : Dr(0)E \to \rho(0)F$ is onto iff $Dg(0)$ is; (2) $Tf(0)$ is Fredholm iff $Dg(0)$ is, with equal index.

lean.statement: For a filler $g$ of $f$ with $g$ sc-smooth, $g(0) = 0$ and $f$ a section of $K \to O$: $D(\rho(r(\cdot))g)(0) = \rho(0)Dg(0)$, $(1 - \rho(0))Dg(0)Dr(0) = 0$, $D(f \circ r)(0) = Dg(0)Dr(0)$; and $Tf(0) := Dg(0)|_{Dr(0)E} : Dr(0)E \to \rho(0)F$ is onto iff $Dg(0)$ is, Fredholm iff $Dg(0)$ is, and $\mathrm{ind}\,Tf(0) = \mathrm{ind}\,Dg(0)$. The linear algebra holds for any idempotents $p, q$ and $L$ with $(1 - q)Lp = 0$ and $(1 - q)L : \ker p \to \ker q$ a topological isomorphism. In sc form: if $Dg(0)$ is an sc-Fredholm sc-operator, then $Dr(0)E$, $\rho(0)F$, $\ker Dr(0)$ and $\ker\rho(0)$ are sc-subspaces, $Tf(0) : Dr(0)E \to \rho(0)F$ is sc-Fredholm, of index $\mathrm{ind}\,Dg(0)$ on every level, and $(1 - \rho(0))Dg(0) : \ker Dr(0) \to \ker\rho(0)$ is an sc-isomorphism (condition (3) of the filler on every level). Conversely, for $Dg(0)$ an sc-operator: $Dg(0)$ is sc-Fredholm if and only if $Tf(0)$ is sc-Fredholm and condition (3) holds on every level. The same for a filling germ (V3.7), with $Dg(0)$ the value at $0$ of any derivative family of $g$ on any germ (`IsFillingGerm.proposition_3_5`, `IsFillingGerm.proposition_3_5_sc`, `IsFillingGerm.proposition_3_5_sc_iff`).

chips: sc form: filler (3) on level 0 suffices
sc converse needs (3) on every level
diff: The proof exhibits $\ker Tf(0) \simeq \ker Dg(0)$ and $\mathrm{coker}\,Tf(0) \simeq \mathrm{coker}\,Dg(0)$ directly instead of the text's factorization and additivity of the index, so the index equality holds as $\dim\ker - \dim\mathrm{coker}$ with no finiteness assumption; closedness of the ranges transfers through the continuous $y \mapsto y - LC^{-1}(1 - q)y$, which is where \"topological\" in (3) is used.
The text's \"by linearization at $y = 0$\" needs $(u, h) \mapsto \rho(u)h$ differentiable and $g(0) = 0$; the target \"$(1 - D\rho(0))F$\" is $(1 - \rho(0))F$ (Findings, Chapter 3, item 47).

Proposition 3.5 (2) is a level-$0$ statement. Its sc form in the direction Proposition 3.52 uses (“$Dg(0)$ sc-Fredholm ⟹ $Tf(0)$ sc-Fredholm”) needs condition (3) of the filler on level $0$ only, as the text states it: the higher levels of $Tf(0)$ come from the regularity of $Dg(0)$ (`IsScFredholm.restrict`), and condition (3) on every level then follows at the zero. The converse in sc form needs condition (3) on every level as a hypothesis; with level $0$ only it fails (an example on a weighted $\ell^2$ with the shift, Findings, Chapter 3, item 238, not formalized). Nothing in the text uses the converse (Findings, Chapter 3, items 234, 237, 238). Updated in the third addendum of this page.

For filling germs (the text’s reading of Definition 3.4) the proofs are the same, with the derivative family of the fill defect in place of the derivative on $U$ (Findings, Chapter 3, items 272, 289, 314). Updated after the switch of Definition 3.11 to the text’s germ reading (phase 2).

items.title: Definition 3.6: filled versions

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.6, p. 66
book.statement: $(f, x_0)$ has a filling if in a strong bundle chart with $\varphi(x_0) = 0$ the section germ $\Phi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1} : O \to K$ has a filling $g : U \to U \triangleleft F$ near $0$; $(g, 0)$ is a filled version.

lean.statement: `IsFillingGerm fb g` (V3.7): $g$ is an sc-smooth germ on an sc-germ of neighbourhoods $G$, $G_0 \subseteq U$, whose levels may shrink with $m$, and fills the principal part $\mathbf f$ near $0$; the centred chart is that of Definition 3.11 (V3.13). The whole-chart form `IsFilledVersion` ($g$ sc-smooth on all of $U$, filling in the sense of `IsFillerOf`) is a filling (`IsFilledVersion.isFillingGerm`), and a filling sc-smooth on all of $U$ is a filled version (`IsFillingGerm.isFilledVersion`).

chips: local data; the chart in Def. 3.11
diff: The text asks for a filling of the section germ in some strong bundle chart centred at $x_0$; the formal notion is the datum in a given chart, for the principal parts, and the centred chart is quantified in Definition 3.11 (V3.13).

**Germs.** Since the switch to the text’s germ reading (phase 2) the filling is a germ (`IsFillingGerm`). The earlier filled version, sc-smooth on all of $U$, is stricter (round-trip items V3.9, V3.43) and is kept as `IsFilledVersion`, exactly the fillings sc-smooth on $U$. Hence “restated” again (“narrower” in the third addendum) (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 260–262, 330).

items.title: Definition 3.7: basic germs

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.7, p. 66
book.statement: A basic germ is an sc-smooth germ $f : \mathcal O([0, \infty)^k \oplus \mathbb R^{n-k} \oplus W, 0) \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W$ with $f(0) = 0$ and $P_W \circ f(a, w) = w - B(a, w)$, $B(0, 0) = 0$, $|B(a, w) - B(a, w')|_m \le \varepsilon|w - w'|_m$ for $(a, w), (a, w')$ close enough to $(0, 0)$ on level $m$, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $m \ge 0$.

lean.statement: `IsBasicGerm C̃ G f B`: $f$ an sc-smooth germ on the germ $G$ around $0$ in $\widetilde C \oplus W$ with $f(0) = 0$, whose $W$-component is $w - B(a, w)$ on $U_0$, with $B$ an sc$^0$-contraction germ (V3.25: $B$ sc$^0$, $B(0, 0) = 0$, and the contraction estimate on balls whose points lie in $U_m$). $\widetilde C$ is a quadrant-like subset of a finite-dimensional $P$, $\mathbb R^N$ any finite-dimensional $Q$.

chips: points of the balls lie in $U_m$
diff: \"Close enough on level $m$\" presupposes that the points lie in the domain $U_m$; this is required. The theorems that use basic germs add \"$\widetilde C$ closed\" or \"a partial quadrant\" where needed.
Remark 3.8 (in [21] $f(0) = 0$ was not required) is a historical remark and makes no claim.

items.title: Lemma 3.9: the fibre derivative of $B$ is small

book.label: §3.1, Lemma 3.9, p. 67
book.statement: For $B$ as in Definition 3.7, every $\varepsilon > 0$ and $m \ge 0$: $|D_2B(a, w)\zeta|_m \le \varepsilon|\zeta|_m$ for $\zeta \in W_m$ if $(a, w) \in E_{m+1}$ is close enough to $(0, 0)$ in $E_m$; in particular $D_2B(0, 0) = 0$.

lean.statement: Four formal forms: (a) on level $m$, for an sc$^1$-germ $B$ in the working form of a contraction germ, $\|D_2B(a, w)\|_{L(W_m)} \le \tfrac12$ at points $(a, w) \in U_{m+1}$ with $a \in N(m+1)$, $w \in O(m+1)$, $\iota w \in O(m)$; (b) $D_2B(0, 0) = 0$ for an sc$^1$ sc$^0$-contraction germ; (c) on level $0$ with arbitrary $\varepsilon$: $|D_2B(x)\zeta|_0 \le \varepsilon|\zeta|_0$ for $x \in U_1$ small on level $1$. (d) **as stated**: for $B$ an sc$^1$ sc$^0$-contraction germ on a quadrant-like $\widetilde C$, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and every $m$ there is $r > 0$ with $|D_2B(x)\zeta|_m \le \varepsilon|\zeta|_m$ for $\zeta \in W_m$ at every $x \in U_{m+1}$ with $|x|_m < r$.

diff: Stronger in regularity: $B$ sc$^1$ suffices (Theorem 3.30 and Lemma 3.31 apply the lemma to sc$^1$ and sc$^k$ germs).

The general statement (every $\varepsilon$, every level $m$, points of $E_{m+1}$ small in $E_m$) is proved as stated, from the contraction estimate of Definition 3.28 applied at points small on level $0$; smallness on level $m + 1$ is not needed (Findings, Chapter 3, item 215). It is what Proposition 3.10 on level $m$ (V3.12) and Lemma 3.31 in the sense of Definition 3.28 (V3.28) use. The constant $\tfrac12$ on level $m$ in the working form, the value at $(0, 0)$ and the level-$0$ form are kept for the theorems that use them. Formerly narrower (the general statement not formalized). Updated in the third addendum of this page.

items.title: Proposition 3.10: the linearization of a basic germ plus an sc$^+$-germ

book.label: §3.1, Proposition 3.10, p. 68
book.statement: If $f = h + s$ with $h$ a basic germ and $s$ an sc$^+$-germ, $f(0) = 0$, then $Df(0) : \mathbb R^n \oplus W \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W$ is sc-Fredholm of index $n - N$; and for every $m$, $Df(a, w)$ on level $m$ is Fredholm of index $n - N$ for $(a, w) \in E_{m+1}$ small in $E_m$.

lean.statement: For a basic germ $h$, an $s$ sc$^1$ into $(\mathbb R^N \oplus W)^1$ and $f = h + s$ sc$^1$: $Df(0)$ is an sc-operator, sc-Fredholm of index $\dim P - \dim Q$; it is $T_0 + S$ with $T_0(\delta a, \delta w) = (0, \delta w)$ (sc-Fredholm of index $n - N$) and an sc$^+$-operator $S$ built level by level. For the data of Theorem 3.38 and $x \in U_1$ small on level $1$, $D(h + s)(x) : E_0 \to F_0$ is Fredholm of index $n - N$. **On every level** (the second statement): for every $m$ there is $\delta > 0$ such that at every $x \in U_{m+1}$ with $|x|_m < \delta$ the level-$m$ operator $Df(x)_m : \mathbb R^n \oplus W_m \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W_m$ is Fredholm of index $\dim P - \dim Q$, for $\widetilde C$ quadrant-like (partial quadrants are); $f(0) = 0$ is not used.

diff: First statement as in the text, with $s$ only sc$^1$ into $F^1$ and $f$ only sc$^1$. The verification that $Df(0) - T_0$ is sc$^+$ (finite-rank terms through $\mathbb R^n$ and $\mathbb R^N$ with smooth values because $Dh(0)$ is an sc-operator at the smooth point $0$) is not in the text (Findings, Chapter 3, item 46).

Second statement: on every level $m$, at the points of $U_{m+1}$ small in $E_m$, as in the text, by the text's proof: $Df(x)_m = T_0 + S(x) + K(x)$ with $\|S(x)\| \le \varepsilon$ by Lemma 3.9 on level $m$ (V3.11) and $K(x)$ compact (finite rank, and $\iota\,\mathrm{pr}_W Ds(x)$ through $W_{m+1} \to W_m$). The one identity the text uses silently, the $W$-component of $Df(x)_m$, is proved from the uniqueness of derivatives within $U_1$ (Findings, Chapter 3, item 230). With both statements as in the text under weaker hypotheses ($s$ and $f$ only sc$^1$, $f(0) = 0$ unused) the verdict is “stronger”; formerly narrower, the second statement on level $0$ only (G.21). Updated in the third addendum of this page.

items.title: Definition 3.11: sc-Fredholm germs

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.11, p. 69
book.statement: $(f, x_0)$ is an sc-Fredholm germ if it has a filled version $(g, 0)$ and a local sc$^+$-section $s$ with $s(0) = g(0)$ such that $g - s$ is conjugated to a basic germ: a strong bundle isomorphism $\Psi : U \triangleleft F \to U' \triangleleft F'$ covering an sc-diffeomorphism $\psi$ with $\Psi \circ (g - s) \circ \psi^{-1}$ a basic germ.

lean.statement: `StrongBundle.IsScFredholmGerm f x₀` (the text’s germ reading): in a strong bundle chart of $P$ centred at $x_0$, a filling $g$ (`IsFillingGerm`, an sc-smooth germ on a germ of neighbourhoods inside $U$, V3.9), a local sc$^+$-section $s$ (`IsScPlusGerm`: $s : E_0 \to F_1$ an sc-smooth germ into $F^1$ on a germ inside $U$) with $\iota s(0) = g(0)$, and `IsConjugateToBasicGerm` for $u \mapsto g(u) - \iota s(u)$: strong bundle maps $\Psi, \Psi'$ inverse to each other (`IsStrongBundleIso`), $\psi(0) = 0$, $U'$ relatively open in $\widetilde C \oplus W$ ($\widetilde C$ a partial quadrant of a finite-dimensional space), a basic germ $h$ on a germ inside $U'$, and $(\Psi(u, g(u) - s(u)))_2 = h(\psi(u))$ for $u \in U$ near $0$.

diff: The conjugation identity is required for $u \in U$ near $0$ (Theorem 3.15's identity $(g + \tilde t) - (\tilde t + t_0) = g - t_0$ holds on $U$ only). The text's $C' = T\psi(0)C$ (used in Theorem 3.54) is not part of the data; it is proved (V3.48).
The index statement after the definition is V3.46 (Proposition 3.52, in the chart).
The witnesses of the conjugation are also available as a structure, `ConjugationData`, so that the dimensions of the basic germ can be named (V3.46).

**Germs.** Since the switch to the text’s germ reading (phase 2) the filling and the sc$^+$-section are germs whose levels may shrink with $m$; $\Psi$ is a strong bundle isomorphism on all of $U$, which is no restriction (on a relatively open $U_0 \subseteq U$ it is the same after restricting the chart on level $0$). The project’s earlier notion, with $g$ and $s$ sc-smooth on the whole $U$, is `IsScFredholmGermWholeChart`: it implies the germ reading and is exactly the germ reading with $g$, $s$ sc-smooth on $U$ (`isScFredholmGerm_iff_germG_wholeChart`). Whether the two agree for sections sc-smooth on $X$ is open, and no theorem depends on it (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 261–264, 330). What remains is the formulation above and the untamed chart (formerly also the stricter germ side, third addendum).

The existential over charts is essential: a filling in a chart gives a topological isomorphism $\ker Dr(0) \cong \ker\rho(0)$ (`IsFillingGerm.nonempty_kerEquiv`), a condition on the chart, so a filling in one chart gives none in another unless these normal spaces match; a compatible tame chart of the trivial bundle carries no filling of any section (`TrivialBundle.not_isFillingGerm_evenBundleChart`) (Findings, Chapter 3, items 350–352). Added in the fourth addendum of this page.

items.title: Theorem 3.12: local compactness for sc-Fredholm germs

book.label: §3.1, Theorem 3.12, p. 70 ("an immediate consequence of Theorem 3.40")
book.statement: Let $f$ be an sc-smooth section of the tame strong bundle $P : Y \to X$ and $(f, x_0)$ an sc-Fredholm germ with $f(x_0) = 0$. There are nested open neighbourhoods $O(0) \supset O(1) \supset \cdots$ of $x_0$ in $X_0$ such that $\mathrm{cl}_{X_0}\{x \in O(i) \mid f(x) = 0\}$ is a compact subset of $X_i$.

lean.statement: For a section $f$ ($P \circ f = \mathrm{id}$) of any strong bundle with $(f, x_0)$ an sc-Fredholm germ and $f(x_0) = 0$: nested open $O(i) \ni x_0$ such that the closure in $X$ of $\{x \in O(i) \mid f(x) = 0\}$ is the image of a compact subset of $X_i$ (level topology) under the inclusion $X_i \to X$.

diff: Of \"$f$ an sc-smooth section of the tame strong bundle\" only $P \circ f = \mathrm{id}$ is used; regularity enters through the filling germ (germ reading, V3.13); tameness not at all.

\"Immediate consequence of Theorem 3.40\" hides: the correspondence of zeros through chart, filler and the fibre maps of $\Psi$; the push-forward $t$ of the sc$^+$-section is an sc$^+$-germ with $t(0) = 0$; shrinking so that $E_0$-closures stay inside the chart and the region of the identities; and the continuity of the inverse chart $O_i \to X_i$ for the level topology (Findings, Chapter 3, items 12, 44).

items.title: Corollary 3.13: convergence on every level

book.label: §3.1, Corollary 3.13, p. 70
book.statement: Under the hypotheses of Theorem 3.12, if $f(x_k) = 0$ and $x_k \to x$ in $X_0$, then for every $m$, $x_k \in X_m$ for $k$ large and $x_k \to x$ in $X_m$.

lean.statement: (a) If $f(x_k) = 0$ and $x_k \to x_0$ (the base point of the germ), then for every $m$ there are lifts $y_k \in X_m$ of the $x_k$, $k$ large, converging in $X_m$ to the lift of $x_0$. (b) For an sc-Fredholm section and any limit $x$ of zeros: $x$ is a zero and a smooth point, and the same conclusion holds at $x$.

chips: limit $x_0$, or any limit for sections
diff: As stated, the corollary concerns an arbitrary limit $x$ while the hypothesis is about the germ at $x_0$; it is proved for $x = x_0$, and for any limit when $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section, which provides the germ property at $x$ (Findings, Chapter 3, items 15, 45).
$X_m$ is not known to be first countable here, so convergence is proved by a cluster-point argument in the compact set of Theorem 3.12.

items.title: Definition 3.14: sc-Fredholm sections

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.14, p. 70
book.statement: A section $f$ of the tame strong bundle $P : Y \to X$ is sc-Fredholm if (1) it is sc-smooth; (2) regularizing: $x \in X_m$, $f(x) \in Y_{m,m+1}$ imply $x \in X_{m+1}$; (3) $(f, x)$ is an sc-Fredholm germ at every smooth point $x$.

lean.statement: `StrongBundle.IsScFredholmSection f`: (1)–(3) for a section of any strong bundle, clause (3) in the germ reading of V3.13. A zero of a regularizing section is a smooth point.

diff: As in the text; the bundle is not required to be tame, which plays no role in the definition (Findings, Chapter 3, item 40).

**Germs.** Clause (3) is the germ notion of V3.13, the text’s germ reading since the switch (phase 2); the earlier whole-chart notion, stricter, is `IsScFredholmSectionWholeChart` and implies this one (`IsScFredholmSectionWholeChart.isScFredholmSection`). Hence “as in the book” again (“restated” in the third addendum) (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 330).

items.title: Theorem 3.15: stability under sc$^+$-perturbations

book.label: §3.1, Theorem 3.15, p. 71 (proof pp. 72–73)
book.statement: If $P : Y \to X$ is a strong bundle over a tame M-polyfold, $f \in \mathrm{Fred}(P)$ and $s \in \Gamma^+(P)$, then $f + s \in \mathrm{Fred}(P)$.

lean.statement: For any strong bundle: if $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section and $s$ an sc$^+$-section, the fibrewise sum $f + s$ is an sc-Fredholm section: sc-smooth (sum rule in the charts), regularizing ($Y_{m,m+1}$ is closed under fibrewise subtraction and $s$ takes values in $Y_{m,m+1}$ over $X_m$), and an sc-Fredholm germ at every smooth point (filling germ $g + \tilde t$ on the germ of $g$, sc$^+$-germ $\tilde t + t_0$ on the germ of $t_0$, the same conjugation).

The text's \"$f + s$ is an sc-smooth section which is also regularizing\" is two proofs here (Findings, Chapter 3, item 42).

In the germ reading of Definition 3.11 (V3.13), with the text’s proof: $\tilde t = \hat s \circ r$ is sc-smooth on the whole $U$ because $s$ is a global sc$^+$-section, and a germ plus a whole-chart map is a germ on the same germ (Lemma 3.17 for germs, V3.19); the whole-chart form is `theorem_3_15_wholeChart` (Findings, Chapter 3, item 300). Updated after the switch of Definition 3.11 to the text’s germ reading (phase 2).

items.title: Lemma 3.16: the extension $\tilde s = s \circ r$

book.label: §3.1, Lemma 3.16, p. 72
book.statement: An sc$^+$-section $s : O \to K$ extends to the sc$^+$-section $\tilde s(u) = s(r(u))$ of $U \triangleleft F \to U$ with (1) $\tilde s = s$ on $O$; (2) $R(r(u), \tilde s(u)) = s(r(u))$.

lean.statement: For a section $s$ of $K \to O$ ($(x, s(x)) \in K$ on $O$): $s(r(x)) = s(x)$ on $O$, and $\rho(r(u))s(r(u)) = s(r(u))$, $R(r(u), s(r(u))) = (r(u), s(r(u)))$ for $u \in U$. That $s \circ r$ is sc-smooth into $F^1$ is proved inside Theorem 3.15.

items.title: Lemma 3.17: fillers are stable under sc$^+$-sections

book.label: §3.1, Lemma 3.17, p. 72
book.statement: If the sc-smooth section $f : O \to K$ has the filler $g$ and $s : O \to K$ is an sc$^+$-section, then $f + s$ has the filler $g + \tilde s$.

lean.statement: If $g$ is a filling of $\mathbf f$ (`IsFillingGerm`, V3.7) and $s$ is a section of $K \to O$, then $g + s \circ r$ is a filling of $\mathbf f + s$, with the same derivative family in (3): for $s$ sc-smooth on $U$ on the same germ (`IsFillingGerm.add_section`), and for $s$ an sc-smooth germ on $G \cap r^{-1}(G_s)$ (`IsFillingGerm.add_section_germ`); (3) because $[1 - \rho(r(y))](g + s \circ r)(y) = [1 - \rho(r(y))]g(y)$. Of $s$ only the sc-smoothness is used, not that it is sc$^+$.

**Germs.** Since the switch to the text’s germ reading (phase 2) the lemma is the text’s, for fillings that are germs, and proved in the project; the round-trip audit had found it true outside the project. The whole-chart `lemma_3_17` (fillers in the sense of `IsFillerOf`, the regularity left to Theorem 3.15) neither implies it nor follows from it (round-trip item V3.19; Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 273). Hence “stronger” (formerly “restated”).

items.title: Definition 3.21: good position

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.21, pp. 76–77
book.statement: A finite-dimensional sc-subspace $N \subseteq E$ is in good position to the partial quadrant $C$ if $N \cap C$ has nonempty interior in $N$ and $N$ has an sc-complement $P$ (a good complement) with: for some $\varepsilon > 0$, $|p|_0 \le \varepsilon|n|_0$ implies ($n \in C \iff n + p \in C$). A merely topological complement is allowed for non-smooth $N$.

lean.statement: `IsGoodComplement E C N P`: $E_0 = N \oplus P$ algebraically and the $\varepsilon$-condition; `IsInGoodPosition E C N`: $N \cap C$ has nonempty interior in $N$ and $N$ has a good complement. $N$ finite-dimensional is a separate instance argument. Definition 3.21 as written: `IsScGoodComplement` ($E = N \oplus P$ an sc-splitting, with the constant $\varepsilon$) and `IsInGoodPositionSc`; each implies the project's form. On a partial quadrant a smooth finite-dimensional $N$ in good position (algebraic complement) is in good position with an sc-complement, also inside any sc-subspace $T \supseteq N$; for smooth $N$ the text's good complements are the project's closed ones, and Definition 3.21 as written is the project's good position together with $N \subseteq E_\infty$.

As a *conclusion* the algebraic form is weaker than the text's: an algebraic good complement need not be closed (round-trip item V3.20: $C = E_0$ infinite-dimensional, $P$ the kernel of a discontinuous functional; not in the project). The text's definition is therefore formalized as well, and on a partial quadrant the two agree for smooth $N$: a closed good complement of a smooth $N$ is an sc-complement (the projection along $N$ acts on every level), and a closed good complement always exists there (Findings, Chapter 3, items 210, 211). The theorems that conclude good position are given in the sc form in V3.94, V3.95. Updated in the third addendum of this page.

items.title: Proposition 3.22: $N \cap C$ is a partial quadrant

book.label: §3.1, Proposition 3.22, p. 77 (proof §3.8.1, pp. 120–126)
book.statement: If the finite-dimensional sc-subspace $N$ is in good position to the partial quadrant $C$, then $N \cap C$ is a partial quadrant in $N$.

lean.statement: For $N$ finite-dimensional in good position to the partial quadrant $C$: $N \cap C$ is a partial quadrant in $N$ (constant sc-structure). The core: for continuous functionals $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_n$ jointly onto $\mathbb R^n$ with $C = \{\ell_i \ge 0\}$, a linear isomorphism $e : N \to \mathbb R^k \times N_0$ with $N \cap C = e^{-1}([0, \infty)^k \times N_0)$, $k = \dim N - \dim(N \cap W)$.

The proof keeps the text's case distinction but replaces Lemmas 3.62–3.64 (Krein–Milman for cones, extreme-ray counts, cited from [21]) and 3.66–3.68 by a segment argument and the surjectivity of $Q : N \to \mathbb R^\Sigma$ from Lemma 3.65; the case $N \cap C = N$ is treated separately (Findings, Chapter 3, item 18).

items.title: Definition 3.25: the $n$-dimensional tangent germ property

book.label: §3.2, Definition 3.25, p. 79
book.statement: $M \subseteq X$ (tame) has the $n$-dimensional tangent germ property if $M \subseteq X_\infty$ and every $x \in M$ has a chart $\varphi : (U, x) \to (O, 0)$ onto a tame retract $(O, C, E)$, an $n$-dimensional smooth $N \subseteq E$ in good position to $C$ with good complement $Y$, $E = N \oplus Y$, a relatively open $V \ni 0$ in $N \cap C$ and a continuous $\delta : V \to Y$ with (i) $\varphi(M \cap U) = \{v + \delta(v)\}$, (ii) $\delta : \mathcal O(N \cap C, 0) \to (Y, 0)$ an sc$^\infty$-germ, $\delta(0) = 0$, $D\delta(0) = 0$.

lean.statement: `MPolyfold.TangentGermChart M x n`: the data of (2), with $Y$ **closed**, and (ii) read as `IsScInftyGermAt`: for every $m$ and $k$ a relatively open $V_{m,k} \ni 0$ in $N \cap C$ with $\delta(V_{m,k}) \subseteq E_m$ and $\delta : V_{m,k} \to E_m$ of class $C^k$. `MPolyfold.HasTangentGermProperty M n`: $M \subseteq X_\infty$ and the data at every point. Both other readings of \"sc$^\infty$-germ\" (one fixed germ; sc-smooth on $V$) imply this one.

\"sc$^\infty$-germ\" is read with $k$-dependent neighbourhoods, the reading in which Theorem 3.43 (1) is proved (V3.38) and the weakest of the three (Findings, Chapter 3, item 80); Corollary 3.34 now also holds on one germ (V3.31, third addendum).

items.title: Proposition 3.26: invariance of the tangent germ property

book.label: §3.2, Proposition 3.26, p. 80
book.statement: For a pair $(X, M)$ with $X$ a tame M-polyfold, and an sc-diffeomorphism $\psi : X \to X'$ with $\psi(M) = M'$: $M'$ has the $n$-dimensional tangent germ property iff $M$ has it.

lean.statement: For an sc-diffeomorphism $\psi : X \to X'$ of M-polyfolds with inverse $\psi'$ (sc-smooth both ways on all of $X$, $X'$) and $\psi(M) = M'$: $M'$ has the $n$-dimensional tangent germ property iff $M$ has it. The data at $\psi(x)$ are the transported chart $\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}$ with the same $N$, $Y$, $V$, $\delta$; $\psi(M) \subseteq X'_\infty$ because sc-smooth maps preserve the levels.

diff: As in the text, for Definition 3.25 as formalized (V3.22, $Y$ closed); the tameness of $X$ is not used (the chart models are tame retracts as part of the data).
The text's first sentence, that $X' = \psi(X)$ is tame, is not needed here; that tameness is carried by sc-diffeomorphisms is V3.71.

items.title: Theorem 3.27: subsets with the tangent germ property are sub-M-polyfolds

book.label: §3.2, Theorem 3.27, p. 81 (proof pp. 81–84)
book.statement: If $X$ is a tame M-polyfold and $M \subseteq X$ has the $n$-dimensional tangent germ property, then (1) $M$ is a sub-M-polyfold whose induced structure is tame and sc-smoothly equivalent to a smooth manifold with boundary with corners; (2) with the data of Definition 3.25, $y \mapsto \pi \circ \varphi(y)$ is a smooth chart of $M$ around $x$.

lean.statement: Let $M \ne \emptyset$ have at every point data of Definition 3.25 satisfying `IsRegular`: (a) $\delta$ is sc-smooth on $V$ (set sense), (b) $\pi(O) \subseteq C$. Then $M$ is a sub-M-polyfold (retraction $s = \varphi^{-1} \circ t \circ \varphi$, $t(v + w) = v + \delta(v)$); its induced structure is tame and has an equivalent atlas of $n$-dimensional corner charts; every $y \mapsto \pi\varphi(y)$ is a chart of the induced structure, modelled on $(V, N \cap C, N)$; and $d_M(y) = d_{N \cap C}(\pi\varphi(y))$.

(b) \"$\Sigma = \{v + y \in C\}$ is relatively open in $C$\" is false for $C = [0, \infty)^3$, $N = \mathbb R(1, 1, 1)$, $Y = \{x + y - z = 0\}$ (item 83).

Tameness of $X$ is not used (only that the chart models are tame retracts). \"Manifold with boundary with corners\" (Chapter 4) is `IsManifoldWithCorners`: an equivalent atlas of charts on relatively open subsets of $n$-dimensional partial quadrants. The relation $d_{N \cap C}(v) = d_X(y)$ via Lemma 3.70 is proved in the model $\mathbb R^n \oplus W$ only (item 84).

For the solution set of an sc-Fredholm section both conditions are theorems: (a) by re-centring (V3.73, V3.74), (b) by the choice of the good complement (V3.75, V3.77); read off the statement of V3.74, (a) follows from (b) after shrinking the data for any set with the tangent germ property. With a dimension that may vary from point to point: V3.72.

items.title: Definition 3.28: sc$^0$-contraction germs and their working form

book.label: §3.3, Definition 3.28, p. 85
book.statement: An sc$^0$-germ $f : \mathcal O(\widetilde C \oplus W, 0) \to (W, 0)$ is an sc$^0$-contraction germ if $f(a, w) = w - B(a, w)$ and for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $m \ge 0$, $|B(a, w) - B(a, w')|_m \le \varepsilon|w - w'|_m$ for $(a, w), (a, w')$ on level $m$ sufficiently close to $(0, 0)$.

The working form `ContractionGerm`: the same data with explicit regions $N(m) \subseteq P$ open, $K(m) \subseteq O(m) \subseteq W_m$ ($K$ closed, $O$ open) on which $B_m(a, \cdot)$ is a $\tfrac12$-contraction ($O$) mapping $K$ into itself; every contraction germ has one.

items.title: Theorem 3.29: existence of the solution germ

book.label: §3.3, Theorem 3.29, p. 86
book.statement: An sc$^0$-contraction germ $f : \mathcal O(\widetilde C \oplus W, 0) \to (W, 0)$ admits a uniquely determined sc$^0$-solution germ $\delta : \mathcal O(\widetilde C, 0) \to (W, 0)$ with $f(a, \delta(a)) = 0$; proof by \"the parametrized version of Banach's fixed point theorem\".

The parametrized fixed point theorem: the fixed point of a family of $\tfrac12$-contractions of a closed set, continuous in the parameter pointwise, is continuous in the parameter.

items.title: Theorem 3.30: the solution germ is sc$^1$

book.label: §3.3, Theorem 3.30, p. 86 (cited from [21, Theorem 2.3], no proof)
book.statement: If the sc$^0$-contraction germ $f : \mathcal O(\widetilde C \oplus W, 0) \to (W, 0)$ is of class sc$^1$, its solution germ $\delta$ is of class sc$^1$.

items.title: Lemma 3.31: the contraction germ $f^{(1)}$

book.label: §3.3, Lemma 3.31, pp. 86–87
book.statement: If $f = w - B(a, w)$ is an sc$^0$-contraction germ of class sc$^k$, $k \ge 1$, with solution germ $\delta$ of class sc$^j$, then $f^{(1)}(v, b, u, w) = (u - B(v, u), w - DB(v, \delta(v))(b, w))$ is an sc$^0$-contraction germ of class sc$^{\min(k-1, j)}$ with solution germ $T\delta$ (\"from the uniqueness\").

items.title: Lemma 3.32: the iterated contraction germs
