items.title: The index of the linearization at a zero, in every chart

book.label: §3.6, Proposition 3.52, p. 110; Theorem 3.19, p. 74
book.statement: If $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section and $f(x) = 0$, then $Tf(x) : T_xX \to Y_x$ is an sc-Fredholm operator (Proposition 3.52); “the linearization $f'(x_0)$ is a sc-Fredholm operator” (Theorem 3.19).

lean.statement: `IsSurjLinOfIndex f y d`: in every strong bundle chart around $y$, at the level-$1$ point over $\varphi(y)$, $\mathrm{Lin}(z) : T_zO \to K_z$ is onto, Fredholm, $\mathrm{ind} = \dim\ker = d$. For an sc-smooth section and the chart of Definition 3.11 at a zero $x_0$ with conjugation data of $g - s$ to a basic germ $O(\widetilde C \oplus W, 0) \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W$, $\widetilde C \subseteq \mathbb R^n$: in every chart around $x_0$ the linearization is Fredholm of index $n - N$, onto if the germ is in good position; so `IsSurjLinOfIndex f x_0 (n − N)` at a zero in good position. For an sc-Fredholm section in good position, in the chart of Definition 3.53: $\mathrm{ind}\,Dg(0) = \mathrm{ind}\,Tf(x_0) = \dim\ker Tf(x_0) = n - N$ for every conjugation. In sc form: for an sc-Fredholm section, a zero $y$ and **any** strong bundle chart around $y$, at the level-$1$ point $z$ over $\varphi(y)$ (a smooth point), $T_zO = Dr(z)E$ and $K_z = \rho(z)F$ are sc-subspaces and $\mathrm{Lin}(z) : T_zO \to K_z$ is an sc-Fredholm operator, Fredholm on every level of the index $n - N$ of every conjugation of every germ datum at $y$; under `IsSurjLinOfIndex f y d` it is onto on every level, of index $d$ on every level. In the chart of Definition 3.53 at a zero in good position, $Dg(0)$ and $f'(x_0) = Tf(x_0)$ are sc-Fredholm and $Tf(x_0)$ is onto on every level.

chips: sc-Fredholm on every level, in charts
diff: Proved in sc form, in every chart: the level-$0$ conjugation between the linearizations in two charts (V3.78) is realised by bounded operators on the ambient spaces that preserve the levels at smooth points (derivatives of the sc-smooth transition maps, and the fibre part of the strong bundle transition, sc$^0$ on $Y[0]$), so the regularity of the linearization in the chart of the germ (V3.46) passes to every chart; then the criterion of V1.8. Tameness is not used. $T_xX$ itself carries no linear structure here (G.7), so the operator is read in charts. The passage to every chart is the chart independence at zeros, which the text does not state (Findings, Chapter 3, items 170, 236, 239). Added in the second addendum of this page with the level-$0$ Fredholm property only (G.22); updated in the third addendum.

**Germs.** The hypothesis is the text’s since the switch to the germ reading (phase 2): the germ data of the sc-Fredholm section are germs whose levels may shrink with $m$ (V3.13, V3.16), and Proposition 3.52 enters at the centre of the chart of the germ datum, where $\mathrm{Lin}(0) = Dg(0)$ on $T_0O$ for the filling germ (Findings, Chapter 3, items 284, 310, 314, 330). `theorem_3_19_linearization_sc` gives the conclusions in the chart at $x_0$, and `linAt_isScFredholm_of_isSurjLinOfIndex` with `IsGoodPositionGerm.exists_isSurjLinOfIndex` in every chart. Hence “stronger” (formerly “narrower”, for the hypothesis): the index on every level, and the surjectivity on every level at a zero in good position, in every chart, go beyond the text’s statement.

items.title: The dimension of the solution set is the Fredholm index

book.label: §3.1, Theorem 3.19, p. 74; §3.6, proof of Theorem 3.54, p. 115
book.statement: The solution set $S(f, U)$ has the structure of a smooth manifold “whose dimension agrees with the Fredholm index” (Theorem 3.19); with $d = \dim\ker f'(x)$ the solution set has the $d$-dimensional tangent germ property (proof of Theorem 3.54).

lean.statement: For an sc-smooth section and a zero $x_0$ in good position in a tame chart (V3.103): the data of Definition 3.25 at $x_0$ have a dimension $d$ with `IsSurjLinOfIndex f x_0 d`, also the regular data of Theorem 3.54 (2). For an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data: an open $U \ni x_0$ and $d$ with every zero $y \in U$ in good position in a tame chart, `IsSurjLinOfIndex f y d`, and $S(f, U)$ a tame $d$-dimensional manifold with boundary with corners (`theorem_3_23_index`; without boundary if $d_X \equiv 0$, `theorem_3_19_index`); under the hypotheses of Theorem 3.57, regular data at every zero whose dimension is the index at the zeros of their chart domain (`theorem_3_57_index`). For an sc-Fredholm section, at a zero $y$ with `IsSurjLinOfIndex f y d`, in every chart $\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ is moreover sc-Fredholm and onto on every level, of index $d$ on every level.

chips: at every zero, in every chart
diff: $d = \dim\ker D(h + t)(0) = n - N$ for the conjugation from which the chart of the tangent germ data is built, and $n - N$ is the index of $f'(x_0)$ for the same conjugation (Proposition 3.52); the proofs of Theorem 3.54 had to expose that conjugation (`_conj` forms). The index is stated at every zero near the point and in every chart; the text states no dimension in Theorems 3.23 and 3.57 (Findings, Chapter 3, item 170). Added in the second addendum of this page.

Updated after the repair of the tameness hypothesis: first proved with “the base retraction of every strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas is tame” (`htame`), which no strong bundle over a nonempty base satisfies (V3.104), so that form was vacuous; now with the hypotheses of V3.103 (Findings, Chapter 3, items 190–192).
That $d$ is the index on every level of $f'(y)$ as an sc-Fredholm operator, in every chart, is V3.96 (Findings, Chapter 3, item 239). Updated in the third addendum of this page.

items.title: The Fredholm index along the solution set and along paths (Definition 6.1, Proposition 6.2)

book.label: Definition 6.1, pp. 200–201; Proposition 6.2, p. 201
book.statement: Definition 6.1: at a smooth point $x$, $\mathrm{ind}(f, x)$ is the Fredholm index of $(f - s)'(x)$ for a local sc$^+$-section $s$ with $s(x) = f(x)$; it does not depend on $s$. Proposition 6.2: over a tame M-polyfold, if $x_0$, $x_1$ are smooth points connected by an sc-smooth path $\varphi : [0, 1] \to X$, then $\mathrm{ind}(f, x_0) = \mathrm{ind}(f, x_1)$. In Chapter 3 the statement along the solution set is implicit in Theorem 3.54 (1).

lean.statement:
For an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data (V3.103), $f(x_0) = 0$, $(f, x_0)$ in good position in a tame chart: an open $V_x 
i x_0$ and $d$ with `IsSurjLinOfIndex f y d` at every zero $y \in V_x$, so $\mathrm{ind}\,f'(y) = \dim\ker f'(y) = \mathrm{ind}\,f'(x_0)$. With Theorem 3.54: every zero in $V_x$ in good position in a tame chart, and regular data of dimension $d$ at $x_0$ with chart domain $V_x$. In sc form: at every zero $y \in V_x$, in **every** strong bundle chart around $y$, $\mathrm{Lin}(z) : T_zO 	o K_z$ is sc-Fredholm, onto on every level and of index $d$ on every level; at any zero of an sc-Fredholm section, in every chart, $\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ is sc-Fredholm with the same index on every level (`StrongBundle.linAt_isScFredholm`). **Without good position, with the text’s hypotheses**: if $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data and $f(x_0) = 0$, there are an open $V 
i x_0$ and $i \in \mathbb Z$ such that at every zero $y \in V$, in every strong bundle chart around $y$, $f'(y)$ is Fredholm of index $i$ (`IsLinOfIndex`; `index_locally_constant_tame`), and in sc form $\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ is sc-Fredholm of index $i$ on every level (`theorem_3_54_index_locally_constant_general_tame`); neither good position, nor surjectivity at $x_0$, nor bump functions are assumed (the first forms, for $X$ admitting sc-smooth bump functions (Definition 5.9): `index_locally_constant_of_admitsBumpFunctions`, `theorem_3_54_index_locally_constant_general`). **Definition 6.1** (`StrongBundle.IsIndexAtLocal f x i`, with the text’s locally defined section): there are an open $V 
i x$ and an sc$^+$-section $s$ of the restriction $P|V$ (`StrongBundle.restrictOpen`) with $(f|_V + s)(x) = 0$ and $(f|_V + s)'(x)$ Fredholm of index $i$ in every strong bundle chart of $P|V$; for an sc-Fredholm section the index is unique (`IsIndexAtLocal.unique`), at a zero it is the index of $f'(x)$, and it exists at every smooth point (`exists_isIndexAtLocal`). The reading with an sc$^+$-section on all of $X$ (`StrongBundle.IsIndexAt`; unique, `IsIndexAt.unique`; existing at every smooth point if $X$ admits bump functions, `exists_isIndexAt`) implies it, and is the same notion when $X$ admits sc-smooth bump functions (`isIndexAtLocal_iff_isIndexAt`). **Proposition 6.2** (`proposition_6_2_local`): if $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data, then for every sc-smooth path $\varphi : \mathbb R 	o X$ there is $i$ with $\mathrm{ind}(f, \varphi(t)) = i$ for all $t$, and any two values of the index at $\varphi(0)$ and $\varphi(1)$ agree (`proposition_6_2_local'`); if $X$ admits sc-smooth bump functions, the same holds for the global reading (`proposition_6_2`).

diff: **Proposition 6.2 is proved with the text’s hypotheses** (fifth addendum of this page; in the fourth, with bump functions), by the text’s device run on the restriction $P|V$ of $P$ to the domain $V$ of a strong bundle chart around $\varphi(t_0)$ (`StrongBundle.restrictOpen`), for each $t_0$: an sc$^+$-section $S$ of the pull-back to $\mathbb R \times V$ with $\tilde f + S = 0$ along the graph of the path near $t_0$ (the text’s $s(t, x) = R(x, f(\varphi(t)))$ in the chart, with no cut-off, since the chart covers $V$), the local constancy of the index of $\tilde f + S$ along its zero set (stabilizing sections $R(\cdot, e_i)$ in the product chart, again without cut-off, and the implicit function theorem), the index count $\mathrm{ind}(\tilde f + S)'(t, x) = \mathrm{ind}(f, x) + 1$ through the slice $S(t, \cdot)$ (`isIndexAt_of_pullback_isLinOfIndex`), and the connectedness of $\mathbb R$ (`proposition_6_2_local`). No bump functions are assumed (“we do not need a sc-smooth partition of unity”, p. 202); tame germ data are the project’s reading of the text’s tameness (V3.103), as in V3.94, where they are no narrowing. With bump functions the proposition holds for the global reading of Definition 6.1 as well (`proposition_6_2`, the form of the fourth addendum, whose section along the path is cut off by a bump; `exists_isScPlusSection_pullback_of_path`) (Findings, Chapter 3, items 340–349, 360–367).

**Why still “narrower”.** The path is $\varphi : \mathbb R \to X$, not $[0, 1] \to X$: $\mathbb R \times X$ is the product of Theorem 3.18 and has no boundary, and the text’s tame M-polyfold $[0, 1] \times X$ is not used. A path on $[0, 1]$ that extends sc-smoothly to $\mathbb R$ is covered; a path sc-smooth on $[0, 1]$ only, in the sense of M-polyfolds with boundary, is not, and the project has no M-polyfold $[0, 1]$. This is the one narrowing left: the bump functions are gone, Definition 6.1 has the text’s local sections, and the hypotheses on $f$ are the text’s in the project’s reading of tameness.

Definition 6.1 has no row of its own. It is `IsIndexAtLocal`: the text’s locally defined sc$^+$-section is a section of the restriction $P|V$ to an open $V \ni x$ — the restriction of a strong bundle to an open set, which the text uses without comment, is constructed (`StrongBundle.restrictOpen`, whose atlas consists of the charts of $P$ inside $V$) — and the text’s $f - s$, $s(x) = f(x)$, is written $f + s$, $(f + s)(x) = 0$. It is well defined, two local sections being compared on the intersection of their domains (`IsIndexAtLocal.unique`), and it exists at every smooth point without bump functions, through the section $-R(\cdot, f(x))$ on a chart domain (`exists_isIndexAtLocal`). The global reading `IsIndexAt` of the fourth addendum implies it, and when $X$ admits bump functions the two agree, the local section being cut off (`isIndexAtLocal_iff_isIndexAt`). The independence of $s$ is proved from the germ data and Theorem 3.15, without the text’s appeal to Proposition 1.10, for which the project has no lemma that the linearization of an sc$^+$-section is compact (Findings, Chapter 3, items 340, 364, 367).

Along the solution set the formal proof combines the good position of the nearby zeros (V3.94), the local constancy of the dimension (V3.85) and dimension = index at each zero (V3.97); the text’s proof of Proposition 6.2 uses the step of V3.82 for an extended section, which along solution sets is repaired by V3.93 (Findings, Chapter 3, items 171, 188). Added in the second addendum of this page.

Updated after the repair of the tameness hypothesis: first proved with “the base retraction of every strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas is tame” (`htame`), which no strong bundle over a nonempty base satisfies (V3.104), so that form was vacuous; now with the hypotheses of V3.103 (Findings, Chapter 3, items 190–192).

The sc form (the index of $f'(y)$ as an sc-Fredholm operator, on every level, in every chart) is proved as well; that $\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ is sc-Fredholm at every zero in every chart, with the level-$0$ index on every level, is `StrongBundle.linAt_isScFredholm` (V3.96), cited here since the fifth addendum. **The local constancy without good position holds with the text’s hypotheses** (tame germ data, no bump functions; `index_locally_constant_tame`, in sc form `theorem_3_54_index_locally_constant_general_tame`), by the text’s device for Proposition 6.2 on the restriction $P|V$ to a chart domain: finitely many sc$^+$-sections $R(\cdot, e_i)$, which on $P|V$ need no cut-off, put the parametrized section of Theorem 3.18 into general position at $(0, x_0)$, its index is constant along its solution set (the case above), at $(0, y)$ it is $k + \operatorname{ind} f'(y)$, and the index at a zero is the same for $P$ and $P|V$, through the germ datum (Findings, Chapter 3, items 240–242, 360–363). The first proof, for M-polyfolds admitting bump functions (Lemma 5.11 for the sections), is kept (`index_locally_constant_of_admitsBumpFunctions`). The candidate counterexample of items 188 and 243 is excluded under tame germ data by Theorem 3.54 (1). Without tame germ data the question is open: $\operatorname{ind} f'(y) = \operatorname{ind} f'(x_0)$ iff the block $C(z) = (1 - \rho(z))Dg(z)|_{\ker Dr(z)}$ of the filling has index $0$, which condition (3) of Definition 3.4 gives at $z = 0$ only (items 243, 343). Updated in the third, fourth and fifth addenda of this page.

items.title: $\ker f'(y) = T_yS$ in a chart

book.label: §3.1, Theorem 3.19, p. 74
book.statement: $U$ can be chosen such that for $y \in S(f, U)$ the linearization $f'(y)$ is surjective and $\ker f'(y) = T_yS(f, U)$ is the tangent space.

lean.statement: For an sc-smooth section and a zero $x_0$ in good position in a tame chart (V3.103): in a tame chart $c$ centred at $x_0$ (as in Definition 3.53), with the conjugating sc-diffeomorphism $\psi$, $K = \ker D(h + t)(0)$ and the solution graph $\sigma : V' \to E'$ ($C^1$, $\sigma(0) = 0$, $D\sigma(0) = 0$) with $\psi\varphi(\{y \in V_x \mid f(y) = 0\}) = \{v + \sigma(v)\}$, there is an open $V_{x,2} \ni x_0$ such that at every zero $y \in V_{x,2}$ with $\psi\varphi(y) = v + \sigma(v)$ and every level-$1$ point $z$ over $\varphi(y)$, $D\psi(z)$ maps $\ker\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ onto $N_v = \{n + D\sigma(v)n \mid n \in K\}$.

diff: In the chart of the tangent germ data, where $N_v$ is the tangent space of the solution set; $T_yS$ as a subspace of $T_yX$ needs the linear structure of $T_yX$ (Definition 2.38, Chapter 2 gap G.13) and is not formalized. The surjectivity of $f'(y)$ is V3.94 (Findings, Chapter 3, item 172). Added in the second addendum of this page.

Updated after the repair of the tameness hypothesis: first proved with “the base retraction of every strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas is tame” (`htame`), which no strong bundle over a nonempty base satisfies (V3.104), so that form was vacuous; now with the hypotheses of V3.103 (Findings, Chapter 3, items 190–192).

items.title: Good position is surjectivity at a zero with $d_X = 0$

book.label: §3.6, after Theorem 3.54, p. 111; Corollary 3.24, p. 79
book.statement: “In case $\partial X = \emptyset$, the requirement that $(f, x)$ is in good position just means that $f'(x)$ is surjective”; the kernel condition is “an empty condition if $d_X(x) = 0$” (Corollary 3.24).

lean.statement: `IsLinSurjAt f y`: in some strong bundle chart around $y$, at a level-$1$ point over $\varphi(y)$, $\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ maps onto the fibre $K_z$; at a zero it then does so in every chart (`IsLinSurjAt.linAt_surjective`). For an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data (V3.103) and a zero $y$ with $d_X(y) = 0$: $(f, y)$ is in good position in a tame chart iff `IsLinSurjAt f y`. On the way: a subspace of $T$ is in good position inside $T$ to any cone containing $T$; in the tame chart of the germ data at $y$, $d_C(\varphi(y)) = d_X(y) = 0$, so the partial quadrant at $\varphi(y)$ is the whole space, and the good position is read there (V3.107).

diff: Definition 3.53 is stated in the chart of Definition 3.11 with the chart's partial quadrant, which need not be the whole space where $d_X = 0$; in a tame chart $d_C = d_X$ (Proposition 2.36). In a non-tame chart $d_C(\varphi(y))$ can exceed $d_X(y)$ (Findings, Chapter 3, item 173). Added in the second addendum of this page.

Updated after the repair of the tameness hypothesis: first stated for “a strong bundle whose charts have tame base retractions” (`htame`), which cannot be met (V3.104), and with the surjectivity read in an arbitrary chart, which needed that chart tame; the surjectivity is now carried to the tame chart of the germ data (Findings, Chapter 3, items 190, 194).

items.title: Theorems 3.19 and 3.56 with “$f'(x)$ surjective”

book.label: §3.1, Theorem 3.19, p. 74; §3.6, Theorem 3.56, p. 115
book.statement: (3.19) $d_X \equiv 0$, $f(x_0) = 0$, $f'(x_0)$ surjective: the local solution set is a smooth manifold of dimension the Fredholm index. (3.56) $\partial X = \emptyset$ and $f'(x)$ surjective at every zero: $S$ is a sub-M-polyfold whose induced structure is equivalent to a smooth manifold without boundary.

lean.statement: For $d_X \equiv 0$ and an sc-Fredholm section: if $f$ has tame germ data (V3.103), $f(x_0) = 0$ and `IsLinSurjAt f x_0`, the conclusions of `theorem_3_19_index` (V3.97); if $f$ has tame germ data and `IsLinSurjAt f x` at every zero (`theorem_3_56_of_surjective`), or $(f, x)$ is in good position in a tame chart at every zero (`theorem_3_56_tame`), and $S \ne \emptyset$, $S$ is a sub-M-polyfold with tame induced structure, a manifold of locally constant dimension without boundary, with regular data at every zero whose dimension is the Fredholm index at the zeros of their chart domain.

diff: The text's hypotheses; the tameness of the induced structure and the index are added conclusions; $S \ne \emptyset$ for the formal charts (Findings, Chapter 3, item 173). Added in the second addendum of this page.

Updated after the repair of the tameness hypothesis: first proved with “the base retraction of every strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas is tame” (`htame`), which no strong bundle over a nonempty base satisfies (V3.104), so that form was vacuous; now with the hypotheses of V3.103 (Findings, Chapter 3, items 190–192).

items.title: The filler condition at the nearby zeros follows from good position

book.label: no counterpart in the text (Definition 3.4 (3), p. 64)
book.statement: Not in the text. Definition 3.4 (3) asks that $(1 - \rho(0))Dg(0)$ be an isomorphism $\ker Dr(0) \to \ker\rho(0)$, at $0$ only.

lean.statement: (a) For $Dg(z)$ the value at $z$ of a derivative family of a germ $g$ with $z$ in its germ, at a level-$1$ point $z$ over a point $z_0$ of the retract with $\ker Dg(z) \subseteq T_{z_0}O$: if $\rho(z_0)k \in Dg(z)(T_{z_0}O)$ for all $k$, then $(1 - \rho(z_0))Dg(z)$ is injective on $\ker Dr(z)$. (b) If moreover $Dg(z)$ is onto and $g$ fills $\mathbf f$ near $z_0$ with $\mathbf f(z_0) = 0$, the two conditions are equivalent. (c) For an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data (V3.103) and a zero $x_0$ in good position in a tame chart, `IsGoodPositionGermFilled f x_0` holds (in a tame chart).

diff: (c) uses Theorem 3.54 (1) with the text's hypotheses (V3.94) and the tangency of the kernel (V3.81): the added hypothesis of the first forms V3.68, V3.69, V3.82, V3.85 is satisfied whenever the text's hypotheses are (Findings, Chapter 3, item 174). Added in the second addendum of this page.

Updated after the repair of the tameness hypothesis: first proved with “the base retraction of every strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas is tame” (`htame`), which no strong bundle over a nonempty base satisfies (V3.104), so that form was vacuous; now with the hypotheses of V3.103 (Findings, Chapter 3, items 190–192).

items.title: Definitions 3.50, 3.51 and 3.53 in a tame chart

book.label: §3.6, Definitions 3.50, 3.51, p. 110; Definition 3.53, p. 111
book.statement: (3.50) For an sc-smooth section $f$ of the tame strong bundle $P : Y \to X$ and a smooth point $x$: $(f, x)$ is an sc-Fredholm germ if there is a strong bundle chart $\Phi : \Phi^{-1}(V) \to K$ around $x$ covering $\varphi : (V, x) \to (O, 0)$, “where $K \to O$ is a tame strong local bundle”, in which the local section has a filling $g$ near $0$ and a local sc$^+$-section $s$ with $s(0) = g(0)$ and $g - s$ conjugated near $0$ to a basic germ. (3.51) An sc-smooth section of the tame strong bundle is sc-Fredholm if it is regularizing and an sc-Fredholm germ at every smooth point. (3.53) Good position is defined for an sc-Fredholm germ of a tame strong bundle. A strong bundle retraction is tame when its base retraction $r$ is (p. 49).

lean.statement: `StrongBundle.IsTameChart`: a strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas whose base retraction $r : U \to U$ is tame (Definition 2.34). `IsScFredholmGermTame f x` (“tame germ data”): $x$ smooth and the data of Definition 3.11 in the text’s germ reading (V3.13) in a tame chart. `IsGoodPositionGermTame f x`: the same data with the germ in good position in that chart (V3.47). `IsScFredholmSectionTame f`: an sc-Fredholm section (V3.16) with tame germ data at every smooth point. Each implies the form without tameness; good position in a tame chart gives tame germ data; `IsGoodPositionGermFilled` (V3.82) is stated in a tame chart. A retraction agreeing on its domain with a tame one is tame, so a compatible chart whose base retraction is the identity of $U$ is tame.

chips: tame chart of the germ data
diff: These are the hypotheses of the implicit function theorems of §3.6 (V3.48, V3.68–V3.70, V3.80–V3.82, V3.84–V3.87, V3.94–V3.102). They were first proved with “tame strong bundle” read as: the base retraction of **every** strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas is tame. No strong bundle over a nonempty base satisfies that (V3.104), so those first statements were vacuous; the proofs used the tameness only for particular charts, and the repair changed the statements, not the arguments (Findings, Chapter 3, items 190–192, 198).

Whether germ data in some chart (V3.13) can be moved to some compatible tame chart when the atlas consists of tame charts (Definition 3.11 $\Rightarrow$ Definition 3.50) is open. It cannot be done by re-centring a chart of the tame atlas: whether a filling exists in a chart depends on the chart ($\ker Dr(0) \cong \ker\rho(0)$ is necessary, `IsFillingGerm.nonempty_kerEquiv`), and the trivial bundle with the one-chart tame atlas of `evenBundleChart` has sc-Fredholm sections with tame germ data in compatible charts but none in the atlas chart (`tame_atlas_no_germData_in_atlas_chart`). The text builds the tame chart into Definition 3.50, and so do the theorems (Findings, Chapter 3, items 199, 350–353). Updated in the fourth addendum of this page.

**Germs.** Since the switch to the text’s germ reading (phase 2) the three notions carry the germ data of the text (V3.13, V3.45); the earlier whole-chart forms are `IsScFredholmGermTameWholeChart`, `IsGoodPositionGermTameWholeChart`, `IsScFredholmSectionTameWholeChart`, and the non-vacuity witnesses satisfy both readings (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 304, 330). For Definition 3.53 the comparison is that of V3.47. Hence “hypotheses explicit” again (“restated” in the third addendum).

items.title: A non-tame retraction onto a product with a point: the earlier tameness hypothesis cannot be met

book.label: no counterpart in the text (Definitions 2.34, 2.50, pp. 39–40, 51–52)
book.statement: Not in the text. Definition 2.34 (1) asks a tame retraction to preserve the degeneracy index, $d_C(r(x)) = d_C(x)$; Definition 2.50 asks of compatible strong bundle charts only that their transition maps be sc-smooth.

lean.statement: For an sc-Banach space $W$, the constant retraction $c : (a, w) \mapsto (1, 0)$ of the partial quadrant $[0, \infty) \oplus W$ of $\mathbb R \oplus W$ (sc-smooth, with retract $\{(1, 0)\}$), and every sc-smooth retraction $r$ of a nonempty relatively open $U$ in a partial quadrant $C$: the product retraction $c \times r$, with retract $\{(1, 0)\} \times r(U)$, is not tame. At $((0, 0), u)$, $u \in r(U)$, the degeneracy index is $1 + d_C(u)$, at its image $((1, 0), u)$ it is $d_C(u)$.

diff: The retraction-level half of the argument that the hypothesis under which the theorems of §3.6 were first proved, “the base retraction of every compatible strong bundle chart is tame”, fails for every strong bundle over a nonempty base: from a compatible chart $(\varphi, U, R, \Phi)$, the chart $(1, \varphi)$ onto $\{1\} \times O$ with base retraction $(a, u) \mapsto (1, r(u))$ on $[0, \infty) \times U$ (the retraction above with $W = 0$) has the transition maps of the first composed with affine maps, hence is compatible with every chart the first one is. That chart and its compatibility are not formalized (sc-calculus for affine maps). So the earlier statements were vacuous, and they are replaced by those with the hypotheses of V3.103 (Findings, Chapter 3, items 190, 199). Added after the repair of the tameness hypothesis.

items.title: Theorem 3.15 for tame germ data

book.statement: If $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section of the tame strong bundle and $s$ an sc$^+$-section, then $f + s$ is an sc-Fredholm section.

items.title: Theorem 3.18 for tame germ data

book.label: §3.1, Theorem 3.18, p. 74
book.statement: Let $P : Y \to X$ be a tame strong bundle and $f$ an sc-Fredholm section. If $s_1, \dots, s_n \in \Gamma^+(P)$, then $(r, x) \mapsto f(x) + \sum_i r_is_i(x)$ is an sc-Fredholm section of the pull-back bundle $\pi^*(P) \to \mathbb R^n \times X$.

lean.statement: In the setting of V3.91: if $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data (V3.103) and $s_1, \dots, s_n$ are sc$^+$-sections, then $F(r, x) = f(x) + \sum_i r_is_i(x)$ is an sc-Fredholm section of $\pi^*P$ with tame germ data. On the way: the product chart $(r \mapsto r - r_0) \times c$ (V3.92), with base retraction $1 \times r$ on $\mathbb R^n \times U$, is tame when $r$ is ($\mathbb R^n$ carries the identity retraction, so $d(a, u) = d_C(u)$, and minimal subspaces and tangent spaces are products); so $\tilde f$ has germ data in the tame product charts, and V3.105 adds $\tilde s$.

chips: product of tame charts is tame

items.title: Good position in any chart of the germ data

book.label: §3.6, Definition 3.53, p. 111; proof of Theorem 3.54, p. 115
book.statement: Definition 3.53 defines good position through $f'(x) : T_xX \to Y_x$ and $C_xX$, presupposing that it does not depend on the chart; the proof of Theorem 3.54 concludes good position at the nearby zeros “proceeding as above”.

lean.statement: (a) In the setting of V3.79 (a zero $y$, a chart $c$ around $y$ not necessarily centred, an sc$^1$-germ $g$ agreeing with $\mathbf f$ on $O$ near $\varphi(y)$ with $z$ in its germ, $Dg(z)$ mapping $T_zO$ onto $K_z$, $\ker Dg(z) \cap T_zO$ in good position to $C_{\varphi(y)}$ inside $T_zO$): for **every** datum of Definition 3.11 at $y$ (a compatible chart $c'$ centred at $y$, a filling germ $g'$ with a derivative family $Dg'$), the germ is in good position in $c'$ at $Dg'(0)$; with only $\rho(z)k$ in the range for every smooth $k$, under the hypothesis that $Dg'(0)$ is Fredholm. (b) If $(f, y)$, $f(y) = 0$, is in good position in some chart and has tame germ data, it is in good position in that tame chart.

chips: every chart of the germ data
diff: V3.79 gives the good position in the chart that Definition 3.11 provides at $y$; (a) gives it in every chart carrying germ data, and (b) applies (a) at $z = 0$ in the chart of the given good position. This is how the good position of the nearby zeros (V3.94) and the good position from surjectivity (V3.100) are obtained in tame charts (Findings, Chapter 3, items 193, 194). In the germ reading (b) needs no Fredholm input: in the chart of the given good position, centred at $y$, (a) applies at $z = 0$, which lies in every germ, and $K_0$ is the whole target, so the form with all of $K_z$ in the range suffices. items.title: Definition 4.1: corner charts and corner structures

book.label: §4.1, Definition 4.1, p. 147
book.statement: An M-polyfold $X$ has a compatible smooth manifold structure with boundary with corners if it admits an atlas of sc-smoothly compatible charts $(V, \varphi, (U, C, \mathbb R^n))$, $\varphi : V \to U$ an sc-diffeomorphism from an open $V \subseteq X$ onto a relatively open subset $U$ of a partial quadrant $C$ in $\mathbb R^n$ (or in a finite-dimensional vector space).

lean.statement: A corner chart (`MChart.IsCornerChart`) is a chart whose model is $(U, C, V)$ with $V$ finite-dimensional, the constant sc-structure, $U$ relatively open in the partial quadrant $C$, and the identity retraction. `HasCornerStructure`: an atlas of corner charts equivalent to the atlas of $X$; equivalently every point lies in a corner chart that is a chart of $X$. The dimension may vary. Corner models are tame retracts and sc⁺-retracts; a corner structure makes $X$ tame.

diff: "Sc-smoothly compatible" and "$\varphi$ an sc-diffeomorphism" are read as compatibility with the atlas of $X$, as for tameness (Findings, Chapter 4, item 50).
The classical manifold structure is represented by the corner atlas; local constancy of the dimension is neither stated nor formalized.

items.title: Definition 4.1: the transition maps are $C^\infty$

lean.statement: For compatible corner charts $\chi$, $\chi'$ the overlap $\chi(V \cap V')$ is relatively open and the transition map $\chi' \circ \chi^{-1}$ is $C^\infty$ on it (derivatives within the set).

items.title: Finite-dimensional sc-Banach spaces have the constant structure

book.statement: A finite-dimensional Banach space $E$ has precisely one sc-structure, namely the constant structure $E_m = E$.

lean.statement: If $E_0$ is finite-dimensional, every level is finite-dimensional, every inclusion $E_m \to E_0$ is onto, $E$ is sc-isomorphic to $E_0$ with the constant structure through the inclusions, and every point is smooth.

items.title: Remark 4.3: $1_1^0$, $1_0^1$, and the constant structure

book.label: §4.1, Remark 4.3, p. 148
book.statement: If $X_0 = X_\infty$, $1_0^1 : X \to X^1$ has the inverse $1_1^0$, which is always sc-smooth; so if $1_0^1$ is sc-smooth it is an sc-diffeomorphism. It is possible that $X^1 \ne X$ as M-polyfolds although the underlying sets agree. A finite-dimensional space with the constant structure has $X = X^1$.

lean.statement: $1_1^0 : X^1 \to X$ is sc-smooth (in charts the sc-operator $\iota : E^1 \to E$). If $X = X_1$ as sets and $1_0^1$ is sc-smooth, it is an sc-diffeomorphism with inverse $1_1^0$. For a finite-dimensional $V$: $(\mathrm{const}\,V)^1 = \mathrm{const}\,V$, the lift is the identity, every retract is an sc⁺-retract. **The example** (`remark_4_3_example`): an M-polyfold with $X_0 = X_\infty$ for which $1_0^1 : X \to X^1$ is not sc-smooth, so $X^1 \ne X$ as M-polyfolds; it is a retract $O = O_\infty \subseteq \mathbb R \oplus X$ that is not an sc⁺-retract (`remark_4_3_retract_example`), the image of the retraction $(t, z) \mapsto (t, L(t)z)$ of moving rank-one projections on a weighted sequence space, sc-smooth by a criterion for parameter families of level operators with one level of loss (`IsLossFamily.isScSmooth`). $(X^1)_m = X_{m+1}$ as sets (`MPolyfold.mem_shift_levelSet_iff`).

diff: “It is possible that $X^1 \ne X$ as M-polyfolds although the sets agree” is proved by an example the text does not give (fourth addendum of this page; formerly gap G.31). By Proposition 4.8 an example is a retract $O = O_\infty$ that is not an sc⁺-retract; it cannot come from a retraction whose level maps are $C^1$ (an argument, not formalized), so its retraction loses a level in its first derivative, as the splicings of HWZ do, and its sc-smoothness rests on a criterion with loss proved for it, not on Proposition 1.19. In the example $X$ and $X^1$ even have different topologies on the same set (Findings, Chapter 4, items 140–146).

“$X^1 \ne X$” is read as “$1_0^1$ is not sc-smooth”, equivalently (by `remark_4_3_isScDiffeo`) “the identity is not an sc-diffeomorphism $X \to X^1$”. The sc-diffeomorphism clause needs only $X = X_1$, not $X_0 = X_\infty$. “$(X^1)_m = X_{m+1} = X_i$” misprints $X_0$; $(X^1)_m = X_{m+1}$ holds as sets, the topologies of the iterated levels being gap G.6 (Findings, Chapter 4, items 5, 125). Hence “stronger” (formerly “narrower”, for the missing example).

items.title: $\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$, the allowable sections, and the metric $\rho$

book.label: §5.3, p. 174
book.statement: $\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$: the $s \in \Gamma^+(P)$ with $\operatorname{supp}(s) \subseteq U$ and $N(s(x)) \le 1$ for all $x$, a metric space for $\rho(s, s') = \sup_xN(s(x) - s'(x))$, not complete.

lean.statement: `allowableSections N U`; `sectionDistAt`: $N(s(x) - s'(x))$ in the fibre $(Y_{0,1})_x$. `allowableDist`: $\rho(s, s') = \sup_xN(s(x) - s'(x))$, finite ($\rho \le 2$); for an auxiliary norm $N$ a metric on $\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$ (`allowableMetric`), with $\rho(s, s') \le \varepsilon$ iff $N(s(x) - s'(x)) \le \varepsilon$ for all $x$. Not complete for the trivial bundle $\mathbb R \times \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ with $N(x, v) = |v|$ and $U = \mathbb R$ (`TrivialBundle.not_completeSpace_allowableSections`); complete for $U = \emptyset$, for every bundle and auxiliary norm (`completeSpace_allowableSections_empty`), and over a point with fibre $\mathbb R^k$ (`TrivialBundle.completeSpace_allowableSections_point`).

diff: The text’s “$(\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P), \rho)$ is not complete” is false without a hypothesis: for $U = \emptyset$ the space is a point, and over a point with finite-dimensional fibre it is the closed unit ball of $\mathbb R^k$. It is read as “not complete in general” and proved by an example: the allowable sections $s_j(x) = (x, \sqrt{x^2 + 1/(j+1)^2}/(2\sqrt{1 + x^2}))$ form a $\rho$-Cauchy sequence whose pointwise limit has fibre part $|x|/(2\sqrt{1 + x^2})$, not differentiable at $0$, while the fibre part of an sc⁺-section of the trivial bundle is $C^1$. That non-completeness holds whenever $U$ contains a non-isolated point over which $Y_{0,1}$ is nonzero (the text’s setting) is expected by the same mechanism and not formalized (Findings, Chapter 5, items 150–153; gap G.42).

Only Definition 5.1 (1) is used for the metric axioms (symmetry and subadditivity of the fibre norms, $N$ vanishing only at $0_x$); the density statements of Theorems 5.13 and 5.18 are $\rho(s, s') \le \varepsilon$ (`allowableDist_le_iff`; V5.30, V5.39). Hence still “restated”; before the fourth addendum of this page $\rho$ was used pointwise only and the metric space was not formalized (Findings, Chapter 5, item 47).

items.title: Remark 5.12

book.label: §5.3, Remark 5.12, p. 174
book.statement: If $s$ is in the completion of $\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$, the solution set of $f + s = 0$ is still compact, provided $f$ has a compact solution set and $U$ is adapted to $N$.

As stated (`remark_5_12_completion`): with the points of the completion represented by sections $s$ with values in $Y_{0,1}$ that are uniform $N$-limits of allowable sections (`IsInAllowableCompletion`), for $f$ continuous and $U \supseteq f^{-1}(0)$ with $\operatorname{cl}\{x \in U \mid N(f(x)) \le 1\}$ compact, the solution set of $f + s$ is closed, hence compact; for $f$ sc-Fredholm with compact solution set, with the $U$ of Theorem 5.5 (`remark_5_12_of_isScFredholmSection`).

items.title: Transport along paths from local push-forwards

book.statement: For a path $\varphi$ and $t_0 \in [0, 1]$ one chooses an orientable neighbourhood $U(\varphi(t_0))$ and an open interval $I(t_0)$ on which orientations propagate; using the compactness of $[0, 1]$ and a finite covering, $o_0$ is transported to $o_1$; "by a covering argument" $\varphi_*$ depends only on $[\varphi]$, and the uniqueness of $\Gamma_f$ is called obvious.

items.title: Theorem 6.37: the functor $\Gamma_f$

book.label: §6.5, Theorem 6.37 and its proof, p. 228
book.statement: For a strong bundle over a tame $X$ and an sc-Fredholm $f$ there is a uniquely determined functor $\Gamma_f : PX \to \mathcal O_f$, $x \mapsto \mathrm{Or}^f_x$, $[\varphi] \mapsto \Gamma_f([\varphi]) : \mathrm{Or}^f_x \to \mathrm{Or}^f_y$, with property (∗): for every sc-smoothly contractible open $U(x)$ on which $f$ has the local propagation property, $\varphi_* = \Gamma_f([\varphi])$ for every sc-smooth path $\varphi$ in $U$.

items.title: Definition 6.40: orientations of sc-Fredholm sections

book.statement: An orientation of $f$ assigns to every smooth $y$ an orientation $o^f_y$ of $\mathrm{DET}(f, y)$ such that, for every smooth $x$ and every orientable neighbourhood $U(x)$, the restriction to $U_\infty$ is one of the two continuous orientations.

items.title: Theorem 6.41: the natural orientation of the solution set

book.label: §6.5, Theorem 6.41 and its proof, p. 229; the paragraph after it, pp. 229–230
book.statement: Over a tame $X$, for a proper sc-Fredholm section $f$ with $(f, x)$ in general position to $\partial X$ at every zero and an orientation $o^f$ of $f$, the solution set $S = f^{-1}(0)$ is a smooth compact manifold with boundary with corners with a natural orientation. Proof: $T_xS = \ker f'(x)$ is oriented by $o^f_x$ since $f'(x)$ is onto, and the local prolongation of this orientation on $S$ is the Fredholm one. For $f$ not generic, a small perturbation $s$ supported near the zero set orients $S_{f+s}$.

items.title: Definition 7.1: groupoids, $\mathrm{mor}(x, y)$ and the orbit space $|X|$

book.label: §7.1, Definition 7.1 and the paragraph after it, pp. 225–226
book.statement:
A *groupoid* $X = (X, \mathbf X)$ is a small category consisting of the set $X$ of objects, denoted by $x$, and the set $\mathbf X$ of morphisms (arrows), which are assumed to be invertible, and the following five structure maps $(s, t, m, u, \iota)$. (1) The source and target maps $s, t : \mathbf X \to X$ assign to every morphism $\varphi : x \to y$ in $\mathbf X$ its source $s(\varphi) = x$ and its target $t(\varphi) = y$. (2) The associative multiplication (composition) map $m : \mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X \to \mathbf X$, $m(\varphi, \psi) = \varphi \circ \psi$, is defined on the fibered product $\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X = \{(\varphi, \psi) \in \mathbf X \times \mathbf X \mid s(\varphi) = t(\psi)\}$, so that if $\psi : x \to z$ and $\varphi : z \to y$, then $\varphi \circ \psi : x \to y$. (3) For every object $x \in X$ there exists the unit morphism $1_x : x \to x$ in $\mathbf X$, a 2-sided unit for the composition: $\varphi \circ 1_x = \varphi$ and $1_x \circ \psi = \psi$ for all $\varphi, \psi \in \mathbf X$ satisfying $s(\varphi) = x = t(\psi)$; these define the unit map $u : X \to \mathbf X$, $u(x) = 1_x$. (4) For every morphism $\varphi : x \to y$ there exists the inverse morphism $\varphi^{-1} : y \to x$, a 2-sided inverse: $\varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} = 1_y$ and $\varphi^{-1} \circ \varphi = 1_x$; these define the inverse map $\iota : \mathbf X \to \mathbf X$, $\iota(\varphi) = \varphi^{-1}$.

After the definition: $\mathrm{mor}(x, y) \subset \mathbf X$ is the set of all morphisms $\varphi$ with $s(\varphi) = x$ and $t(\varphi) = y$. The *orbit space* $|X| = X/\sim$ is the quotient of the set of objects by the equivalence relation $x \sim y$ if and only if there exists a morphism $\varphi : x \to y$; the class of $x$ is $|x| := \{y \in X \mid y \sim x\}$, and $\pi : X \to |X|$, $\pi(x) = |x|$, is the quotient map.

lean.statement: `GroupoidStr Obj Mor`: types of objects and morphisms with the maps `src`, `tgt`, `comp`, `unit`, `inv` and the laws `src_comp`, `tgt_comp`, `comp_assoc` on composable pairs $s(\varphi) = t(\psi)$, `src_unit`, `tgt_unit`, `comp_unit` ($\varphi \circ 1_{s(\varphi)} = \varphi$), `unit_comp` ($1_{t(\varphi)} \circ \varphi = \varphi$), `src_inv`, `tgt_inv`, `comp_inv` ($\varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} = 1_{t(\varphi)}$), `inv_comp` ($\varphi^{-1} \circ \varphi = 1_{s(\varphi)}$) (fields of the structure). `mor x y` and `morOn A` (the morphisms with source and target in $A$) are sets of morphisms; `Isomorphic x y` is the existence of $\varphi : x \to y$, `orbitSetoid` the equivalence relation, `OrbitSpace` $= |X|$ its quotient and `π` the projection, with $\pi(x) = \pi(y) \iff x \sim y$ (`π_eq_π_iff`). `saturation A` $= \pi^{-1}(\pi(A))$, `IsSaturated A`, equivalent to: $s(\varphi) \in A \Rightarrow t(\varphi) \in A$ (`isSaturated_iff`). `Ob`, `instGroupoid`: the same data as a Mathlib `CategoryTheory.Groupoid`, whose isomorphism relation is `orbitSetoid` (`orbitSetoid_eq`).

Not in the definition: the saturation $\pi^{-1}(\pi(A))$, used from Definition 7.10 on, and the bridge to Mathlib's `CategoryTheory.Groupoid`, so that "full" and "faithful" (p. 232, Proposition 7.6) are Mathlib's `Functor.Full`, `Functor.Faithful`.

items.title: Definition 7.2: the isotropy group $G_x$

book.label: §7.1, Definition 7.2, p. 226
book.statement: For fixed $x \in X$ we denote by $G_x$ the isotropy group (stabilizer group) of $x$, defined by $G_x = \{\varphi \in \mathbf X \mid \varphi : x \to x\}$.

items.title: Definition 7.3: ep-groupoids

book.label: §7.1, Definition 7.3, pp. 226–227
book.statement: An *ep-groupoid* $X = (X, \mathbf X)$ consists of a groupoid equipped with M-polyfold structures on the object set $X$ and the morphism set $\mathbf X$ having the following properties. (1) (étale) The source and target maps $s, t : \mathbf X \to X$ are local sc-diffeomorphisms. (2) The unit map $u$ and the inverse map $\iota$ are sc-smooth. (3) (Properness) Every point $x \in X$ possesses an open neighborhood $V(x)$ of $x$ in $X$ such that the map $t : s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_X(V(x))) \to X$ is proper. Since $s$ is a local sc-diffeomorphism, the fibered product $\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X$ is in a natural way an M-polyfold in view of Lemma 2.8 in [38], and we require (4) the multiplication map $m : \mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X \to \mathbf X$ is sc-smooth. In particular, all the structure maps $(s, t, m, u, \iota)$ are sc-smooth maps.

lean.statement: `EpGroupoid Obj Mor` extends `GroupoidStr` by M-polyfold structures `PObj`, `PMor` on the Hausdorff paracompact spaces $X$, $\mathbf X$ and the conditions (1) `isLocalScDiffeo_src`, `isLocalScDiffeo_tgt`; (2) `isScSmoothMap_unit`, `isScSmoothMap_inv`; (3) `exists_isProperMap`: every $x$ has an open $V \ni x$ such that $t : s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}\,V) \to X$ is a proper map (Mathlib's `IsProperMap` of the restriction); (4) `isScSmoothComp`, i.e. `IsScSmoothComp`: $m$ is sc-smooth on $\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X$ with the sub-M-polyfold structure of Part I (`MPolyfold.isSubMPolyfold_fibredProduct`). (4) is equivalent to the sheet form `IsScSmoothCompSheet`: for every sheet $\sigma$ of $s$ over $V$, $\psi \mapsto m(\sigma(t(\psi)), \psi)$ is sc-smooth on $t^{-1}(V)$ (`isScSmoothComp_iff_sheet`, `EpGroupoid.isScSmoothCompSheet`); $s$ and $t$ are sc-smooth (`isScSmoothMap_src`, `isScSmoothMap_tgt`).

(3) is existential per point. The universal form "for every open $V \ni x$" does not hold for the pair groupoid of $\mathbb Z$, while every smaller open neighbourhood of a good one works (V7.4, V7.59) (Findings, Chapter 7, items 3, 103).

"Lemma 2.8 in [38]" cites the paper *A General Fredholm Theory III*, an external reference, not a misprint; its statement in the book is Part I's Proposition 2.15 (the preprint's Proposition 2.46), which the formalization uses. The proofs use the equivalent sheet form of (4) (Findings, Chapter 7, item 4).

items.title: Properness and its sequential form

book.label: §7.1, Definition 7.3 (3), p. 227; used on pp. 230–254
book.statement: Definition 7.3 (3) asks that $t : s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_X(V(x))) \to X$ be proper. The proofs use this in the form: if $s(\varphi_k) \in \mathrm{cl}_X(V(x))$ and $t(\varphi_k)$ converges in $X$, then, "after perhaps taking a subsequence", $(\varphi_k)$ converges in $\mathbf X$ (Proposition 7.3, p. 230; Lemma 7.1, p. 230; Proposition 7.7, p. 238; Proposition 7.11, p. 248; Lemma 7.8, p. 254), or through the compactness of preimages of compact sets (Proposition 7.13, p. 251). items.title: Definition 7.4: the local sc-diffeomorphism $\hat\varphi$ and the tangent $T\varphi$

book.label: §7.1, Definition 7.4 and the paragraph before it, p. 227
book.statement: Since $s, t : \mathbf X \to X$ are local sc-diffeomorphisms, every morphism $\varphi : x \to y$ of an ep-groupoid has an extension to a local sc-diffeomorphism $\hat\varphi$ satisfying $\hat\varphi(x) = y$, defined as follows: there exist open neighborhoods $\mathbf U(\varphi) \subset \mathbf X$ and $U(x), U(y) \subset X$ such that $s : \mathbf U(\varphi) \to U(x)$ and $t : \mathbf U(\varphi) \to U(y)$ are sc-diffeomorphisms, and $\hat\varphi = t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\varphi))^{-1} : U(x) \to U(y)$. In the case that $\varphi$ is smooth, i.e. $\varphi \in \mathbf X_\infty$, there is an associated sc-isomorphism $T\varphi : T_{s(\varphi)}X \to T_{t(\varphi)}X$ defined by $T\varphi := T\hat\varphi(x)$; more generally $T\hat\varphi : TU(s(\varphi)) \to TU(t(\varphi))$. $T\varphi$ can be defined for $\varphi$ on level at least $1$ and gives a bounded linear isomorphism on level $0$; only in the case that $\varphi$ is smooth is $T\varphi$ an sc-operator. Definition 7.4: associated to a smooth morphism $\varphi$ we have the so-called associated local sc-diffeomorphism $\hat\varphi$, as well as its tangent $T\varphi$.

lean.statement: `Sheet`: an open set `carrier` $= \mathbf U(\varphi)$ of morphisms with sc-diffeomorphisms $s : \mathbf U \to U(x)$ (`srcSet`) and $t : \mathbf U \to U(y)$ (`tgtSet`) and their inverses; every morphism lies in one (`exists_sheet`, `sheetAt`, `mem_sheetAt`). `Sheet.hat` $= t \circ (s|\mathbf U)^{-1}$ is an sc-diffeomorphism $U(x) \to U(y)$ with inverse $s \circ (t|\mathbf U)^{-1}$ (`Sheet.isScDiffeoOn_hat`); for a morphism, `hat φ` is that of `sheetAt φ`, an sc-diffeomorphism (`isScDiffeoOn_hat`) with $\hat\varphi(s(\varphi)) = t(\varphi)$ (`hat_src`). `tangentMor φ` defines $T\varphi$ on the tangent space of $X$ through a tangent vector of $\mathbf X$ at $\varphi$; no property of it is proved.

items.title: The levels of an ep-groupoid and the filtration of $|X|$

book.label: §7.1, pp. 227–228
book.statement: The M-polyfolds $X$ and $\mathbf X$ are equipped with the filtrations $X = X_0 \supset X_1 \supset X_2 \supset \dots \supset X_\infty = \bigcap_{k \ge 0} X_k$ and similarly for $\mathbf X$; $X_\infty$ is dense in every $X_k$. For $x$ in the M-polyfold $X$, $ml(x) \in \mathbb N \cup \{\infty\}$ is the largest non-negative integer $m$, or $\infty$, such that $x \in X_m$. Since the source and target maps are local sc-diffeomorphisms and therefore preserve the levels, $ml(x) = ml(y) = ml(\varphi)$ for every morphism $\varphi : x \to y$; consequently the filtration of $X$ induces the filtration $|X| = |X_0| \supset |X_1| \supset \dots \supset |X_\infty| = \bigcap_{k \ge 0}|X_k|$ of the orbit space. The degeneracy indices $d_X : X \to \mathbb N$ and $d_{\mathbf X} : \mathbf X \to \mathbb N$ are invariant under local sc-diffeomorphisms (Proposition 2.7), so $d_X(s(\varphi)) = d_{\mathbf X}(\varphi) = d_X(t(\varphi))$ for every morphism $\varphi$; in particular $d_X(x) = d_X(x')$ if $x \sim x'$.

lean.statement: `mem_levelSet_src_iff`, `mem_levelSet_tgt_iff`: $s(\varphi) \in X_m \iff \varphi \in \mathbf X_m \iff t(\varphi) \in X_m$. `MPolyfold.maxLevel` is $ml$, preserved by local sc-diffeomorphisms (`MPolyfold.IsLocalScDiffeo.maxLevel_eq`), as is the degeneracy index (`MPolyfold.IsLocalScDiffeo.degIndex_eq`), so $d_{\mathbf X}(\varphi) = d_X(s(\varphi)) = d_X(t(\varphi))$ (`degIndex_src`, `degIndex_tgt`). `orbitLevel k` $= \pi(X_k) = |X_k|$.

items.title: Definition 7.6: tame ep-groupoids; $\mathbf X$ is then tame

book.label: §7.1, Definition 7.6 and the paragraph after it, p. 228
book.statement: The ep-groupoid $(X, \mathbf X)$ is called *tame* if the object space $X$ is a tame M-polyfold as introduced in Definition 2.19. In a tame ep-groupoid not only $X$ is a tame M-polyfold but also $\mathbf X$ is a tame M-polyfold. This follows from the facts that $\mathbf X$ is locally sc-diffeomorphic by $s$ to $X$ and the tameness condition is invariant under local sc-diffeomorphisms.

items.title: The translation groupoid $G_x \ltimes U(x)$ is an ep-groupoid

book.label: §7.1, pp. 231–232
book.statement: The translation groupoid $G_x \ltimes U(x) := (U(x), G_x \times U(x))$ associated with $x$ and $U(x)$; abbreviate $U = U(x)$ and $G = G_x$. The object set of $G \ltimes U = (U, G \times U)$ consists of the points in $U$, the morphism set of the pairs $(g, y) \in G \times U$, with source and target maps $s, t : G \times U \to U$, $s(g, y) = y$ and $t(g, y) = \Phi(g)(y)$. The composition of the morphisms $(g, y)$ and $(h, z) \in G \times U$ satisfying $y = s(g, y) = t(h, z) = \Phi(h)(y)$ is defined by $(g, y) \circ (h, z) = (g \circ h, z) \in G \times U$. Using the proof of Theorem 7.1 one verifies that the category $G \ltimes U$ is an ep-groupoid.

lean.statement: `GroupoidStr.translation K U`: the action groupoid of a group acting on a type, $s(g, y) = y$, $t(g, y) = g \cdot y$, $(g, y) \circ (h, z) = (gh, z)$, $1_y = (1, y)$, $(g, y)^{-1} = (g^{-1}, g \cdot y)$; `NaturalRep.translationGroupoid` is it for $G_x$ acting on $U$. `translationEpGroupoid`: with `objPolyfold` and `morPolyfold` it is an ep-groupoid: $s$ and $t$ are local sc-diffeomorphisms (`translation_isLocalScDiffeo_src`, `translation_isLocalScDiffeo_tgt`; $t$ through the shear homeomorphism $(g, y) \mapsto (g, g \ast y)$, `shearHomeomorph`), (4) holds in sheet form (`translation_isScSmoothCompSheet`), and $t : s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}\,V) \to U$ is proper for **every** $V \subseteq U$ (`translation_isProperMap`).

items.title: The functor $\Gamma : G_x \ltimes U(x) \to X$ is fully faithful

book.label: §7.1, p. 232
book.statement: The natural functor $\Gamma : G \ltimes U = (U, G \times U) \to (X, \mathbf X)$ maps, on object level, $y \in U$ to $y \in X$ and, on the morphism level, the morphism $(g, y) \in G \times U$ into the unique morphism $\Gamma(g, y) \in \mathbf X$. By property (3) of Theorem 7.1 the functor $\Gamma$ is full and faithful (fully faithful): for two objects $y$ and $z$ in $G \ltimes U$ it induces a surjection (full) and an injection (faithful) $\mathrm{mor}_{G \ltimes U}(y, z) \to \mathrm{mor}_X(y, z)$. The image of the functor $\Gamma$ is the full subcategory $(U(x), \mathbf U(x))$ of $(X, \mathbf X)$; hence $\Gamma$ identifies the translation groupoid $G_x \ltimes U(x)$ with the category $(U(x), \mathbf U(x))$.

lean.statement: For $y \in U$: $\Gamma(g, h \ast y) \circ \Gamma(h, y) = \Gamma(gh, y)$ (`Γ_mul`), $\Gamma(1, y) = 1_y$ (`Γ_one`), $\Gamma(g^{-1}, g \ast y) = \Gamma(g, y)^{-1}$ (`Γ_inv`). `NaturalRep.functor`: $\Gamma$ as a functor $G_x \ltimes U \to X$, full and faithful in Mathlib's sense (`full`, `faithful`), and an ep-functor (`epFunctor`). `GroupoidStr.fullSub A`: the full subcategory on $A$; the image of $\Gamma$ on morphisms is that of $U$ (`iUnion_image_Γ`, V7.19).

diff: $\Gamma$ is a functor because $U$ is connected (V7.17); it is full and faithful by (3), and an ep-functor (Findings, Chapter 7, item 22).

items.title: The map $\hat\Phi : G_x \to \mathrm{Diff}_{sc}(\mathbf U(x))$

book.label: §7.1, pp. 232–233
book.statement: For $\varphi \in \mathbf U(x)$ there is a unique $h \in G_x$ with $\varphi \in \mathbf U(h)$, and $\varphi = \Gamma(h, s(\varphi))$, $t(\varphi) = \Phi(h)(s(\varphi))$. With $g \ast z := \Phi(g)(z)$, the map $\hat\Phi : G_x \to \mathrm{Diff}_{sc}(\mathbf U(x))$ is defined by $\hat\Phi(g)(\varphi) = \Gamma(g \circ h \circ g^{-1}, g \ast (s(\varphi))) \in \mathbf U(g \circ h \circ g^{-1})$ if $\varphi \in \mathbf U(h)$. Then $\hat\Phi$ is a group homomorphism satisfying $\hat\Phi(g)(\mathbf U(h)) = \mathbf U(g \circ h \circ g^{-1})$ for all $g, h \in G_x$, and $s(\hat\Phi(g)(\varphi)) = \Phi(g)(s(\varphi))$ and $t(\hat\Phi(g)(\varphi)) = \Phi(g)(t(\varphi))$. To sum up: one can choose a small connected neighborhood $U(x)$ such that $\mathbf U(x)$ is the disjoint union of the connected open subsets $\mathbf U(g)$, $g \in G_x$, and for $g, h \in G_x$ the sc-diffeomorphism $\hat\Phi(g) : \mathbf U(x) \to \mathbf U(x)$ induces the commutative diagrams of sc-diffeomorphisms $s \circ \hat\Phi(g)|\mathbf U(h) = \Phi(g) \circ s$ and $t \circ \hat\Phi(g)|\mathbf U(h) = \Phi(g) \circ t$, with $\hat\Phi(g)|\mathbf U(h) : \mathbf U(h) \to \mathbf U(g \circ h \circ g^{-1})$ and $s, t : \mathbf U(h), \mathbf U(g \circ h \circ g^{-1}) \to U(x)$.

lean.statement: `Φhat g φ` is the text's formula: $\hat\Phi(g)(\Gamma(h, y)) = \Gamma(g h g^{-1}, g \ast y)$ (`Φhat_Γ`); it maps $\mathbf U(h)$ into, and onto, $\mathbf U(ghg^{-1})$ (`Φhat_mem_image`, `image_Φhat`, `index_Φhat`); `src_Φhat`, `tgt_Φhat`: the two diagrams; `Φ_conj`: $(ghg^{-1}) \ast (g \ast y) = g \ast (h \ast y)$; `Φhat_one`, `Φhat_mul`: a homomorphism; `isScDiffeoOn_Φhat`: $\hat\Phi(g)$ is an sc-diffeomorphism of $\mathbf U(x)$ with inverse $\hat\Phi(g^{-1})$.

items.title: Proposition 7.5: natural representations of finitely many isomorphic objects

book.label: §7.1, Proposition 7.5, pp. 233–234 (proof pp. 234–236)
book.statement: Let $(X, \mathbf X)$ be an ep-groupoid and $Y = \{y_1, \dots, y_k\}$ a finite set of distinct objects in $X$ which are mutually isomorphic. Denote by $\mathbf Y = (Y, \mathbf Y)$ the full subcategory associated with $Y$, whose morphism set is $\mathbf Y$. Then, given a neighborhood $V$ of $Y$ in $X$, there exists a functor $f$, which associates with the objects $y$ in $Y$ mutually disjoint connected open neighborhoods $U(y)$ contained in $V$, and with a morphism $\psi : y \to y'$ in $\mathbf Y$ an sc-diffeomorphism $f(\psi) : U(y) \to U(y')$. The set of morphisms $\mathbf U = \{\varphi \in \mathbf X \mid s(\varphi) \text{ and } t(\varphi) \in \bigcup_{y \in Y}U(y)\}$ decomposes into the union of connected components $\mathbf U(\psi)$, $\psi \in \mathbf Y$, and the following holds true. (1) The isotropy group $G_y$ for $y \in Y$ acts via the natural action on $U(y)$. (2) For $\psi \in \mathbf Y$ the maps $s : \mathbf U(\psi) \to U(y)$ and $t : \mathbf U(\psi) \to U(y)$ are sc-diffeomorphisms. (3) If $\psi : y \to y'$ and $z \in U(y)$, then $f(\psi)(z) = t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\psi))^{-1}(z)$.

lean.statement: `NaturalRepFinite Y V` (the datum of Definition 7.8, V7.26): sets $U(y)$, $y \in Y$, open, connected, containing $y$, contained in $V$ and pairwise disjoint; maps $f(\psi)$, for $\psi$ between points of $Y$, that are sc-diffeomorphisms $U(s(\psi)) \to U(t(\psi))$ with inverse $f(\psi^{-1})$, with $f(\varphi \circ \psi) = f(\varphi) f(\psi)$ and $f(1_y) = \mathrm{id}$; open connected pairwise disjoint sets $\mathbf U(\psi) \ni \psi$ whose union is the set of morphisms between points of $\bigcup_y U(y)$; (1) at each $y$ a natural representation on $U(y)$ whose action is $g \mapsto f(g)$; (2) $s : \mathbf U(\psi) \to U(s(\psi))$ and $t : \mathbf U(\psi) \to U(t(\psi))$ sc-diffeomorphisms; (3) $f(\psi) = t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\psi))^{-1}$ on $U(s(\psi))$ (fields of the structure). `proposition_7_5`: for a finite set $Y$ of mutually isomorphic objects and an open $V \supseteq Y$ such a datum exists; `proposition_7_5_of_mem_nhdsSet`: for every neighbourhood $V$ of the set $Y$. The construction: `NatRepFinite.transportRep` (a natural representation transported along a sheet), `NatRepFinite.Star`, `NatRepFinite.exists_star`; `NatRepFinite.emptyNaturalRepFinite` for $Y = \emptyset$.

items.title: Proposition 7.6: $|U(x)|$ and $G_x\backslash U(x)$

book.label: §7.1, Proposition 7.6, p. 236 (proof pp. 236–237)
book.statement: Let $X$ be an ep-groupoid and $z \in |X|$. We fix $x \in X$ satisfying $z = |x|$, denote the isotropy group of $x$ by $G_x$ and take an open neighborhood $U(x)$ of $x$ on which we have the natural $G_x$-action $\Phi$, which we abbreviate as $g \ast y := \Phi(g)(y)$ for $g \in G_x$ and $y \in U(x)$. Then the map $\tau : G_x\backslash U(x) \to |U(x)| = \pi(U(x))$, $G_x \ast y \mapsto |y|$, is a homeomorphism. In other words, the obvious functor $G_x \ltimes U(x) \to X$, which on the object level is the inclusion map and on the morphism level the map $(g, y) \mapsto \Gamma(g, y)$, is a fully faithful functor, which on the orbit spaces defines a homeomorphism between the orbit spaces $|U(x)|_{G_x \ltimes U(x)} = G_x\backslash U(x)$ and $|U(x)| = \pi(U(x))$.

lean.statement: `π_eq_π_iff_exists_smul`: for $y, z \in U$, $|y| = |z|$ iff $z = g \ast y$ for some $g \in G_x$. `orbitQuotientMap`: $\tau : G_x\backslash U \to |X|$, an open embedding (`isOpenEmbedding_orbitQuotientMap`) with range $\pi(U)$ (`range_orbitQuotientMap`). `proposition_7_6`: the homeomorphism $G_x\backslash U \cong \pi(U)$; `proposition_7_6_fullyFaithful`: the functor $G_x \ltimes U \to X$ is fully faithful; `proposition_7_6_orbitMap`: it induces a homeomorphism of the orbit space of $G_x \ltimes U$ onto $\pi(U)$, through `translationOrbitHomeomorph`, the homeomorphism of that orbit space with $G_x\backslash U$.

items.title: Definition 7.9: local uniformizers

book.label: §7.1, Definition 7.9 and the two sentences after it, p. 237
book.statement: Let $X$ be an ep-groupoid and $x$ an object in $X$. A local uniformizer around $x$ is a fully faithful embedding $\Psi_x : G_x \ltimes U(x) \to X$, where $U(x)$ is an open neighborhood of $x$ equipped with the natural $G_x$-action, such that $\Psi_x$ induces a homeomorphism between $|U(x)|_{G_x \ltimes U(x)}$ and the open neighborhood $|U(x)| = \pi(U(x))$ of $\pi(x)$ in $|X|$. There exists a local uniformizer around every object $x$, as Proposition 7.6 shows; a local uniformizer is injective on objects as well as on morphisms.

lean.statement: `LocalUniformizer x`: a natural representation `rep` at $x$ and a functor `Ψ` from its translation groupoid to $X$ that is the inclusion on objects, full and faithful, and whose map of orbit spaces is an embedding with range $\pi(U(x))$ (fields `obj_eq`, `full`, `faithful`, `isEmbedding_orbitMap`, `range_orbitMap`). `NaturalRep.toLocalUniformizer`: every natural representation gives one; `exists_localUniformizer`: one exists inside every open $V \ni x$; `LocalUniformizer.injective_obj`, `LocalUniformizer.injective_mor`: injective on objects and on morphisms; for those built from natural representations, $\Psi_x$ is an open embedding on objects and on morphisms (`NaturalRep.isOpenEmbedding_functor_obj`, `NaturalRep.isOpenEmbedding_functor_mor`).

items.title: Definition 7.10: ep-subgroupoids

book.label: §7.1, Definition 7.10, p. 237
book.statement: Let $X$ be an ep-groupoid. An ep-subgroupoid $A$ of $X$ consists of the full subcategory associated with a subset $A$ of $X$ which has the following properties. (1) $A$ is a sub-M-polyfold of the object space $X$. (2) $A$ is saturated, i.e. $\pi^{-1}(\pi(A)) = A$.

lean.statement: `IsEpSubgroupoid A`: $A$ is a sub-M-polyfold of $X$ and saturated (fields `isSubMPolyfold`, `isSaturated`). Witnesses: $X$ itself (`isEpSubgroupoid_univ`), open saturated sets (`isEpSubgroupoid_of_isOpen`), saturations of open sets (`isEpSubgroupoid_saturation`), and every sub-M-polyfold for the trivial ep-groupoid (`isEpSubgroupoid_trivial`).

items.title: The facts (1)–(4) on the sub-M-polyfold $A$

book.label: §7.1, after Definition 7.10, pp. 237–238
book.statement: From the definition it follows, as proved in Proposition 2.6, that the object set $A$ has an induced M-polyfold structure for which the following holds. (1) The inclusion map $i : A \to X$ is sc-smooth and a homeomorphism onto its image. (2) For every $a \in A$ and every sc-smooth retraction $r : V \to V$ of an open neighborhood $V$ of $a$ in $X$ satisfying $r(V) = A \cap V$, the map $i^{-1} \circ r : V \to A$ is sc-smooth. (3) At a smooth point $a \in A$ the tangent space $T_aA$ has an sc-complement in $T_aX$. (4) If $W \subset X$ is open and equipped with an sc-smooth retraction $r : W \to W$ satisfying $r(W) = A \cap W$, then the induced map $r : W \to A$ is sc-smooth (see (2)); moreover, at a smooth point $a \in A$ the tangent space $T_aA$ is equal to $(Tr)(a)T_aX$.

The tangent facts (3) and (4) are not restated.

items.title: The morphisms $\mathbf A$ of a saturated sub-M-polyfold

book.label: §7.1, p. 238
book.statement: The set of morphisms $\mathbf A = \{\varphi \in \mathbf X \mid s(\varphi) \text{ and } t(\varphi) \in A\}$ has in a natural way the structure of an M-polyfold. For $\varphi \in \mathbf A$ and $a = s(\varphi)$ choose open neighborhoods $\mathbf U(\varphi) \subset \mathbf X$ and $U(a) \subset X$ such that $s : \mathbf U(\varphi) \to U(a)$ is an sc-diffeomorphism and (shrinking) an sc-smooth retraction $r : U(a) \to U(a)$ with $r(U(a)) = U(a) \cap A$; then $\mathbf r : \mathbf U(\varphi) \to \mathbf U(\varphi)$, $\mathbf r(\psi) = (s|\mathbf U(\varphi))^{-1} \circ r \circ s(\psi)$, is an sc-smooth retraction, and since $A$ is saturated, $\mathbf r(\mathbf U(\varphi)) = \mathbf U(\varphi) \cap \mathbf A$. This shows that $\mathbf A$ is a sub-M-polyfold of $\mathbf X$, and the properties listed for $A$ also hold for $\mathbf A$.

items.title: Proposition 7.7: the full subcategory of a saturated sub-M-polyfold

book.label: §7.1, Proposition 7.7 and the argument before it, pp. 238–239
book.statement: Let $X$ be an ep-groupoid and $A$ a saturated subset of the object space $X$ such that $A$ is also a sub-M-polyfold. items.title: Definition 7.11: effective ep-groupoids and regular objects

book.label: §7.2, Definition 7.11 and the sentences after it, p. 239
book.statement: An ep-groupoid $X$ is said to be effective provided for every $x \in X$ and $g \in G_x \setminus \{1_x\}$, given an open neighborhood $\mathbf U(g) \subset \mathbf X$, there exists a morphism $\psi \in \mathbf U(g)$ satisfying $s(\psi) \ne t(\psi)$. An object $x \in X$ is said to be regular provided $G_x = \{1_x\}$. If $\varphi \in \mathbf X$ and $s(\varphi)$ is a regular object, the same has to be true for $t(\varphi)$. The regular part $X_{reg}$ of an ep-groupoid is the subset $X_{reg} = \{x \in X \mid G_x = \{1_x\}\}$ of the object space $X$.

items.title: The subgroup $T_x$ of the elements acting trivially

book.label: §7.2, before Definition 7.12, p. 241
book.statement: Every point $x$ of the object set possesses a suitable open neighborhood $U(x)$, which can be chosen arbitrarily small, on which $G_x$ acts by the homomorphism $\Phi : G_x \to \mathrm{Diff}_{sc}(U(x))$. We say that $g \in G_x$ acts trivially if there exists an open neighborhood $U(x)$ equipped with the $G_x$-action $\Phi : G_x \to \mathrm{Diff}_{sc}(U(x))$ such that $g$ belongs to the kernel of $\Phi$, i.e., $\Phi(g) = 1$. Clearly $1_x$ always acts trivially, but there might be other elements $g \in G_x$ acting trivially. Since $G_x$ is finite, we can choose $U(x)$ so small that the kernel of $\Phi$ is equal to the subgroup of $G_x$ acting trivially on $U(x)$. We denote by $T_x \subset G_x$ the subgroup of $G_x$ acting trivially on $U(x)$, which, as the kernel of a group homomorphism, is a normal subgroup of $G_x$.

lean.statement: `ActsTrivially g`: some natural representation at $x$ has $\Phi(g) = \mathrm{id}$ on $U$; `trivialSet x` $= T_x$, containing $1$ (`one_mem_trivialSet`). For a fixed natural representation, $g \in T_x$ iff $\Phi(g)$ fixes a neighbourhood of $x$ (`NaturalRep.actsTrivially_iff`); intrinsically, $g \in T_x$ iff $s = t$ near $g$ in $\mathbf X$ (`mem_trivialSet_iff_eventually`, `mem_trivialSet_of_section`). `exists_mem_nhds_trivialSet_iff`: there is a neighbourhood $N$ of $x$ with $\ker\Phi = T_x$ for every natural representation inside $N$; `exists_naturalRep_trivialSet_iff`, `exists_naturalRep_kerΦ_eq`: such a natural representation exists inside every open $V \ni x$. `trivialSubgroup`: $T_x$ as a subgroup, normal (`trivialSubgroup_normal`), trivial for all $x$ iff $X$ is effective (`isEffective_iff_trivialSubgroup_eq_bot`). For $\varphi : x \to y$, $\varphi T_x \varphi^{-1} = T_y$ (`isotropyConj_mem_trivialSet`, `map_isotropyConj_trivialSubgroup`); if $g \in \ker\Phi$, then $\Gamma(g, y) \in T_y$ for $y \in U$ (`NaturalRep.mem_trivialSet_of_val_eq_Γ`).

items.title: Definition 7.12: the non-effective part $\mathbf X^T$ and the reduced morphisms $\mathbf X^R$

book.label: §7.2, Definition 7.12, p. 241
book.statement: The non-effective part $\mathbf X^T \subset \mathbf X$ is the subset of morphisms defined as $\mathbf X^T = \{\varphi \in T_x \subset G_x \mid x \in X\}$. The subset $\mathbf X^R$ of reduced morphisms of $\mathbf X$ is defined as follows. Two morphisms $\varphi$ and $\varphi' \in \mathbf X$ are called equivalent, $\varphi \sim \varphi'$, if the following two conditions are satisfied. (1) $s(\varphi) = s(\varphi') = x$. items.title: Theorem 7.3: continuous partitions of unity

items.title: Theorem 7.5: the natural representation, proved in Appendix 7.5.1

book.label: §7.5.1, Theorem 7.5 and its proof, pp. 253–254
book.statement: Given an ep-groupoid $X$, an object $x_0 \in X$, and an open neighborhood $V \subset X$ of $x_0$. Then there exist an open neighborhood $U \subset V$ of $x_0$, a group homomorphism $\Phi : G_{x_0} \to \mathrm{Diff}_{sc}(U)$, $g \mapsto \Phi(g) = t_g \circ s_g^{-1}$, and an sc-smooth map $\Gamma : G_{x_0} \times U \to \mathbf X$ having the following properties: $\Gamma(g, x_0) = g$; $s(\Gamma(g, y)) = y$ and $t(\Gamma(g, y)) = \Phi(g)(y)$ for all $y \in U$ and $g \in G_{x_0}$; if $h : y \to z$ is a morphism connecting two objects $y, z \in U$, then there exists a unique $g \in G_{x_0}$ such that $\Gamma(g, y) = h$. In particular, every morphism between points in $U$ belongs to the image of the map $\Gamma$. The homomorphism $\Phi$ is called a natural representation of the stabilizer group $G_{x_0}$. (In the proof, for every $g \in G_{x_0}$ one chooses contractible open neighborhoods $N^t_g$, $N^s_g$ on which $t$ and $s$ are sc-diffeomorphisms onto some open neighborhood $U_0$ of $x_0$, the sets $N^t_g \cup N^s_g$ disjoint; $N_g := N^t_g \cap N^s_g$, $s_g := s|N_g$, $t_g := t|N_g$, and $\Gamma(g, y) = s_g^{-1}(y)$.)

items.title: The proof of Theorem 7.4

book.label: §7.5.2, proof of Theorem 7.4, pp. 255–256
book.statement: Consider the open covering $(|U_\lambda|)_{\lambda \in \Lambda}$ of $|X|$. For every $x \in X$ take an open neighborhood $V(x)$ with: (1) there exists an open neighborhood $W(x)$ equipped with the natural $G_x$-action such that $V(x) \subset \mathrm{cl}_X(V(x)) \subset W(x)$ and $V(x)$ is invariant; (2) $t : s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_X(V(x))) \to X$ is proper; (3) there exists a $\lambda$ with $V(x) \subset U_\lambda$; (4) $(\pi^{-1}(|V(x)|) \setminus V(x)) \cap W(x) = \emptyset$. Take a locally finite refinement $(V'_i)_{i \in I}$ of $(|V(x)|)_{x \in X}$, with $V'_i \subset |V(x_i)|$, open $V''_i$ with $V''_i \subset \mathrm{cl}_{|X|}(V''_i) \subset V'_i$ and $|X| = \bigcup_i V''_i$; $U''_i = V(x_i) \cap \pi^{-1}(V''_i)$ is invariant under the $G_{x_i}$-action, with saturation $U_i = \pi^{-1}(V''_i)$. Take a continuous partition of unity $(\beta_i)$ subordinate to $(V''_i)$; $(\beta_i \circ \pi)|V(x_i)$ has support in $U''_i \subset V(x_i)$. Using the sc-smooth partitions of unity of $X$, approximate $(\beta_i \circ \pi)|V(x_i)$ by Lemma 7.10 by an sc-smooth $f_i$ supported in $V(x_i)$ with $f_i \ge (\beta_i \circ \pi)|V(x_i)$; average using the $G_{x_i}$-action, extend to the saturation of $V(x_i)$ and then by $0$ outside, which gives a function $h_i$ compatible with morphisms. The sum $h$ of all $h_i$ is locally finite and always bigger than $0$, and $(h_i/h)$ is the desired partition of unity for the ep-groupoid $X$.

lean.statement: `exists_invariant_nhds_of_isOpen`: inside every open $W \ni x$ there are a natural representation and an open invariant $V \ni x$ with $\mathrm{cl}\,V \subseteq U \subseteq W$ and $\mathrm{cl}\,V$ proper ((1)–(3)); (4) follows: an object of $U$ isomorphic to one of $V$ lies in $V$ (`mem_of_π_mem_image_of_invariant`, `saturation_diff_inter_eq_empty`). `orbitExtension`: the extension of an invariant function on $U$ to the saturation and by $0$, sc-smooth when its support is proper and inside $U$ (`isScSmoothMap_orbitExtension`). `exists_isScSmoothMap_orbit_urysohn`: for disjoint closed $s, t \subseteq |X|$ there is a continuous $F : |X| \to [0, 1]$, $0$ on $s$ and $1$ on $t$, with $F \circ \pi$ sc-smooth. `admitsScPartitionsOfUnity_of_approx`: Part I's normalization through Mathlib's bump coverings. `theorem_7_4` assembles these.

"The sum of all $h_i$ is locally finite" needs $\mathrm{supp}\,f_i \subseteq \pi^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}\,V'_i)$, the support bound of V7.66; the sc-smoothness of $h_i$ uses that saturations of proper sets are closed (V7.61).

The normalization $(h_i/h)$ and the return from the index set of the refinement to $\Lambda$, which the text leaves implicit, are replaced by Mathlib's bump coverings, as in Part I's Theorem 5.12 (the preprint's Theorem 5.37), with the text's construction as the Urysohn input.

items.title: Corollary 7.3: sc-Hilbert atlases

book.label: §7.5.2, Corollary 7.3, p. 256
book.statement: Let $X$ be an ep-groupoid with paracompact orbit space $|X|$. We assume that the object M-polyfold admits an atlas consisting of charts whose local models $(O, C, E)$ have the property that the $E_0$ are Hilbert spaces. Then every open covering of $X$ by saturated open subsets $(U_\lambda)_{\lambda \in \Lambda}$ possesses a subordinate sc-smooth partition of unity of the ep-groupoid $X$. This example, with the shift map of the 2010 paper, is the project's planned step H2.

notFormalized.title: Definition 1.14: $Df$ need not be norm continuous
notFormalized.label: §1.1, after Definition 1.14, p. 11
notFormalized.book: "In general, the map $U_1 \to \mathcal L(E_0, F_0)$, defined by $x \mapsto Df(x)$, will not(!) be continuous, if the space of bounded linear operators is equipped with the operator norm."
notFormalized.instead: **Formalized since the first edition of this page** (third addendum; V1.13, V1.34), by an example (the text gives none). $X$ is the sc-Banach space of sequences whose level $m$ consists of the $x$ with $(k+1)^m x_k \to 0$, normed by $|x|_m = \sup_k (k+1)^m|x_k|$: every level is a copy of $c_0$, the inclusion $X_{m+1} \to X_m$ is $\mathrm{diag}(1/(k+1))$, compact, and the finitely supported sequences are smooth points dense in every level. On $E = \mathbb R \oplus X$ the map $f(t, x)_k = \cos(kt)x_k$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with $Df(t, x)(\tau, \xi)_k = -k\sin(kt)x_k\tau + \cos(kt)\xi_k$ (the factor $k$ is absorbed by one level). $(\pi/(n+1), 0) \to 0$ in $E_1$, but $\|Df(\pi/(n+1), 0) - Df(0, 0)\| \ge 2$ (test on the unit vector $e_{n+1}$); since the derivative is unique on $E_1$, no derivative family of $f$ is continuous for the operator norm. Not formalized: that $f$ is sc-smooth (it is), and the shift map of the exposition (§6), which needs Example 1.2 (G.1).

notFormalized.title: Proposition 2.2: classical smooth retractions have submanifold images
