notFormalized.title: Definition 2.9: sc-smooth bundle retractions and bundle maps
notFormalized.label: §2.1, Definition 2.9, p. 22
notFormalized.book: A trivial sc-bundle $U \oplus F \to U$; an sc-smooth $R(u, v) = (r(u), \rho(u, v))$, $\rho$ linear in $v$, $R \circ R = R$, is an sc-smooth bundle retraction with bundle retract $B = R(U \oplus F) \to O$; bundle maps $\Phi(u, v) = (a(u), \phi(u, v))$ with \"$p' \circ \Phi = p$\" (read $a \circ p$); the category $\mathcal{BR}$ and the functor $T : \mathcal R \to \mathcal{BR}$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized as a definition.** The tangent retraction $Tr$ (V2.8) and the strong bundle retractions of §2.5 (V2.54) are the instances the theory uses; both are formalized as sc-smooth retractions of the stated form, with linearity in the fibre where it is needed. The categories $\mathcal R$, $\mathcal{BR}$, $\mathcal{SBR}$ and their functors are not formalized.

notFormalized.title: $X_m$ as an M-polyfold for $m \ge 2$
notFormalized.label: §2.2, after Definition 2.14, p. 25
notFormalized.book: For every $m$, the charts $(V_m, \varphi, (O_m, C_m, E_m))$ form an atlas on $X_m$.
notFormalized.instead: **Proved for $m = 1$** (V2.16). For $m \ge 2$ the structure is the iterate $(X^1)^1 \cdots$, whose underlying space is the level of a level. Since the fourth addendum its points are known to be those of $X_m$: $(X^1)_m = X_{m+1}$ and $(X^1)_\infty = X_\infty$ as sets, and an sc-smooth map $X \to Z$ induces an sc-smooth map $X^1 \to Z^1$; that the topology of $(X^1)_m$ is that of $X_{m+1}$ (V2.14), and so that the iterate is $X_m$ with its charts, is not formalized (Findings, Chapter 5, items 142, 146). Theorem 2.16 is proved for every $X_m$ directly (V2.17).

notFormalized.title: Definition 2.18: the linear structure of $T_xX$; Proposition 2.21 (3) in $T_aX$
notFormalized.label: §2.2, Definition 2.18 and Proposition 2.21 (3), (4), pp. 26–30
notFormalized.book: $T_xX$ is a vector space with $\lambda[(x, \varphi, h_1)] + \mu[(x, \varphi, h_2)] = [(x, \varphi, \lambda h_1 + \mu h_2)]$, a Banach space through $T\varphi$, an sc-Banach space at smooth $x$; Proposition 2.21 (3): $T_aA$ has an sc-complement in $T_aX$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** $T_xX$ is a set identified with $T_{\varphi(x)}O$ by $T\varphi$ (V2.19); the vector space, Banach and sc-structures on it are not defined. Proposition 2.21 (3), (4) are proved in a chart (V2.25), which is how the text proves them; their transport to $T_aX$ is not.

notFormalized.title: Proposition 2.19 (2): $p : TX \to X_1$ is open
notFormalized.label: §2.2, Proposition 2.19 (2), p. 27
notFormalized.book: The projection $p : TX \to X_1$ is an open map.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** (not used). Continuity of $p$ is V2.20. The exposition's §8.3 proves openness with the $\mathrm{sc}^0$ property of $Tr$.

notFormalized.title: Remark 2.28: $C_xO$ need not be a partial quadrant
notFormalized.label: §2.3, Remark 2.28, p. 33
notFormalized.book: Naively one might expect $C_xO$ to be a partial quadrant in $T_xO$; \"however, this is in general not the case\".
notFormalized.instead: **Settled since the first edition of this page, in the negative** (third addendum; V2.33): the claim is false. At every smooth point of every sc-smooth retract, tame or not, $C_xO$ is a partial quadrant in $T_xO$ (with the sc-structure induced from $E$), of dimension $\dim(T_xO/T^R_xO) \le d_C(x)$; the proof reduces it to Flor's theorem on nonnegative idempotent matrices, proved in the needed case. For a non-tame retract only the equality of that dimension with $d_C(x)$ can fail (Theorem 2.31). The text gives no example, and none exists (Findings, Chapter 2, item 50).

notFormalized.title: Lemma 2.29: $T^R_xO$ and $C_xO$ through sc-smooth paths; $T_xO = C_xO - C_xO$
notFormalized.label: §2.3, Lemma 2.29, pp. 33–35
notFormalized.book: For a retract and a smooth $x \in O$: (1) $T^R_xO$ is the closure of the derivatives $\dot\alpha(0)$ of sc-smooth paths $\alpha : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to O$ through $x$; (2) $C_xO$ the closure of the one-sided derivatives of sc-smooth paths $\alpha : [0, \varepsilon) \to O$; (3) $T_xO = C_xO - C_xO$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized in the path formulation.** Sc-smooth paths would need the constant sc-structure on an interval as a retract and the density of smooth points of $T^R_xO$ and $C_xO$ (the exposition's Lemma 3.A on all levels). The sign arguments that the proof consists of are formalized (V2.34), and Proposition 2.30 is proved from them, not from the lemma. (3) is not formalized.

notFormalized.title: Theorem 2.31, second statement: equality makes $C_xO$ a partial quadrant
notFormalized.label: §2.3, Theorem 2.31, p. 35 (second statement)
notFormalized.book: If $\dim(T_xO/T^R_xO) = d_O(x)$, then $C_xO$ is a partial quadrant in $T_xO$.
notFormalized.instead: **Formalized since the first edition of this page** (third addendum; V2.33, V2.37), without the hypothesis: $C_xO$ is a partial quadrant in $T_xO$ at every smooth point of every sc-smooth retract, whatever $\dim(T_xO/T^R_xO)$ is, and the quadrant has dimension $\dim(T_xO/T^R_xO)$, which is $d_O(x)$ under the hypothesis. The sc-Banach structure of $T_xO$ and $T^R_xO$ as an sc-subspace, which the exposition supplied on paper, are proved without tameness; the smooth lifts come from the columns given by Flor's theorem (V2.33).

notFormalized.title: The extended faces of a partial quadrant, intrinsically
notFormalized.label: §2.4, p. 39
notFormalized.book: $\{e \in C : d_C(e) = 1\}$ has exactly $k$ connected components $A_i$; each lies in a smallest subspace $f_i$ (an extended face), with a half-space $H_{f_i} \supset C$; $\mathcal F(e) = \{f : e \in f\}$ and $d_C(e) = \#\mathcal F(e)$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized as stated.** The formalization works with a presentation $T$ of $C$ and takes the coordinate hyperplanes $f_i = \{\lambda_i = 0\}$ as the extended faces (`coordHyper`); that a connected piece of $\{d_C = 1\}$ lies in one $f_i$ is `subset_coordHyper_of_isPreconnected` (V2.45). That $E_x$ does not depend on the presentation is proved (`minimalSubspaceWith_eq`, V2.39); the count of components, the minimality of $f_i$ and the intrinsic description of the extended faces are not formalized.

notFormalized.title: Definition 2.38: $T^R_xX$ and $C_xX$ of an M-polyfold
notFormalized.label: §2.4, Definition 2.38, p. 42
notFormalized.book: For a smooth $x \in X$, $T^R_xX$ and $C_xX$ are the preimages of $T^R_oO$ and $C_oO$ under $T\psi(x)$ for any chart $\psi$; well defined by Proposition 2.30. For tame $X$, $C_xX$ is a partial quadrant and $d_X(x) = \dim(T_xX/T^R_xX) = d_{C_xX}(0_x)$.
notFormalized.instead: **Only the local form is formalized**: $T^R_xO$ and $C_xO$ in a chart (V2.32) and their invariance under chart changes (V2.35). The global objects in $T_xX$ are not defined, since $T_xX$ carries no linear structure here (G.7); in a tame chart, $d_X(x) = \dim(T_xO/T^R_xO)$ is V2.42. In a tame chart at a smooth point, $C_oO$ is a partial quadrant in $T_oO$ (V2.42); its transport to $T_xX$ and $d_{C_xX}(0_x) = d_X(x)$ are not formalized.

notFormalized.title: Definition 2.47: strong bundle isomorphisms; the category $\mathcal{SBR}$
notFormalized.label: §2.5, Definition 2.47 and after Definition 2.49, pp. 48–51
notFormalized.book: A strong bundle isomorphism is an invertible strong bundle map with strong bundle inverse. The category $\mathcal{SBR}$ of local strong bundle retracts and the functors $\mathrm{forget}[i] : \mathcal{SBR} \to \mathcal{BR}$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** Strong bundle maps and retractions are V2.54; the transition maps of strong bundle charts are required to be sc-smooth on $[0]$ and $[1]$ in both directions (V2.57), which is the isomorphism property in the form it is used.

notFormalized.title: Lemma 2.56 and Proposition 2.57: closed locally finite refinements
notFormalized.label: §2.6.2, Lemma 2.56 and Proposition 2.57, p. 56
notFormalized.book: Lemma 2.56 (Michael): a regular Hausdorff space is paracompact iff every open cover has a closed locally finite refinement. Proposition 2.57: a regular space with a locally finite cover by closed paracompact subspaces is paracompact.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized, because not needed.** The proofs of Theorem 2.16 and Proposition 2.19(3) avoid them (V2.17, V2.20, V2.62). The text applies Proposition 2.57 to $X_m$ and $TX$ without checking that they are regular.

notFormalized.title: Theorem 3.18: parameterized perturbations
notFormalized.label: §3.1, Theorem 3.18, p. 74
notFormalized.book: For a tame strong bundle and an sc-Fredholm section $f$, $s_1, \dots, s_n \in \Gamma^+(P)$: $(r, x) \mapsto f(x) + \sum r_is_i(x)$ is an sc-Fredholm section of $\pi^*(P) \to \mathbb R^n \times X$.
notFormalized.instead: **Formalized since the first edition of this page** (V3.91, V3.92): $(r, x) \mapsto f(x) + \sum r_is_i(x)$ is an sc-Fredholm section of $\pi^*P$ for any strong bundle (tameness not used), by the text's route: $\tilde f$ is sc-Fredholm in the product chart through the translation charts of $\mathbb R^n$ and the $\mathbb R^n$-extension of the basic germ, $\tilde s$ is sc$^+$, and Theorem 3.15. The linearization at $(0, x)$ after Theorem 3.19 is V3.92; the form for germ data in tame charts is V3.106.

notFormalized.title: Theorem 3.19: implicit function theorem, interior case
notFormalized.label: §3.1, Theorem 3.19, p. 74
notFormalized.book: For $d_X \equiv 0$, $f$ sc-Fredholm, $f(x_0) = 0$: $f'(x_0)$ is sc-Fredholm; if it is onto, the solution set near $x_0$ is a smooth manifold of dimension the index, with $f'(y)$ onto and $\ker f'(y) = T_yS$.
notFormalized.instead: **Formalized since the first edition of this page.** First (V3.68) under the filler condition at the nearby zeros, which was the added hypothesis of Theorem 3.54 (1) (V3.82) and is now a theorem (V3.102); with the text's hypotheses (V3.95): for $d_X \equiv 0$, an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data and $(f, x_0)$ in good position in a tame chart (V3.103), an open $U \ni x_0$ in which every zero is a smooth point in good position in a tame chart and $S(f, U)$ is a sub-M-polyfold equivalent to a $d$-dimensional manifold without boundary; with the hypothesis “$f'(x_0)$ surjective” (V3.101); the dimension is the Fredholm index (V3.97), $\ker f'(y) = T_yS$ in the chart (V3.99), and the first clause, “$f'(x_0)$ is sc-Fredholm”, is Proposition 3.52 in sc form, in the chart at $x_0$ and in every chart, with $f'(x_0)$ onto on every level (V3.46, V3.96; third addendum).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 3.23 and Corollary 3.24: implicit function theorem, boundary case
notFormalized.label: §3.1, Theorem 3.23 and Corollary 3.24, pp. 77–78
notFormalized.book: At a zero with surjective linearization whose kernel is in good position to $C_xX$, the local solution set consists of smooth points and is a tame sub-M-polyfold with a unique structure of a manifold with boundary with corners; globally if this holds at every zero.
notFormalized.instead: **Formalized since the first edition of this page.** Theorem 3.23 (V3.69): the local solution set consists of smooth points and is a tame sub-M-polyfold equivalent to a $d$-dimensional manifold with boundary with corners, when $x$ and the zeros near it are in good position in tame charts (V3.103; or under the filler condition at the nearby zeros, V3.82), and since the second addendum with the text's hypotheses (V3.95), with the dimension as the Fredholm index (V3.97). Corollary 3.24 (V3.70) with the text's hypotheses: good position in a tame chart at every zero gives a sub-M-polyfold with tame induced structure, a manifold with boundary with corners of locally constant dimension.

notFormalized.title: Remark 3.36: the quantitative solution germ
notFormalized.label: §3.3, Remark 3.36, p. 89
notFormalized.book: Decreasing sequences $(\varepsilon_i)$, $(\tau_i)$ with: $\delta$ on $\{|a|_0 \le \varepsilon_0\}$ a continuous solution, unique for $|w|_0 \le \tau_0$; $\delta(a) \in W_i$, $|\delta(a)|_i \le \tau_i$ for $|a|_0 \le \varepsilon_i$; $\delta : \{|a|_0 \le \varepsilon_i\} \to W_i$ of class $C^i$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized in quantitative form.** Its content is Theorem 3.29 (existence, uniqueness in $O(0)$, $\delta_i(a) \in K(i)$; V3.26) and Corollary 3.34 with $m = k = i$ (V3.31), with $\varepsilon_i$ below the radius of $N(2i + 2^i - 1)$.

notFormalized.title: Corollary 3.39: composition with a given conjugation
notFormalized.label: §3.4, Corollary 3.39, p. 93
notFormalized.book: If $g$ is equivalent by a strong bundle isomorphism $\Phi$ to a basic germ and $s$ is an sc$^+$-germ, there is $\Psi$ with $((\Psi \circ \Phi)_*(g + s))^1$ basic.
notFormalized.instead: **Formalized since the first edition of this page** (V3.76): for $g$ sc-smooth and conjugated to a basic germ and $s$ sc-smooth into $F^1$ with $s(0) = 0$, $(g + s)^1$ is conjugated to a basic germ on the shifted structures, by the composite of the index raise of the given conjugation and the linear coordinate change of Theorem 3.38.

notFormalized.title: Proposition 3.10, second statement, on levels $m \ge 1$
notFormalized.label: §3.1, Proposition 3.10, p. 68
notFormalized.book: $Df(a, w) : \mathbb R^n \oplus W_m \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W_m$ is Fredholm of index $n - N$ for $(a, w) \in E_{m+1}$ small in $E_m$, for every $m$.
notFormalized.instead: **Formalized since the first edition of this page** (third addendum; V3.12): for every $m$ there is $\delta > 0$ such that $Df(x)_m : \mathbb R^n \oplus W_m \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W_m$ is Fredholm of index $n - N$ at every $x \in U_{m+1}$ with $|x|_m < \delta$, by the text's proof on level $m$; the input it needed, Lemma 3.9 on level $m$ with arbitrary $\varepsilon$, is proved as stated (V3.11).

notFormalized.title: Proposition 3.52 as an sc-Fredholm operator on $T_xX$
notFormalized.label: §3.6, Proposition 3.52, p. 110
notFormalized.book: $Tf(x) : T_xX \to Y_x$ is an sc-Fredholm operator.
notFormalized.instead: **Formalized since the first edition of this page** (third addendum; V3.46, V3.96), in charts. In the chart of Definition 3.11 centred at the zero, $T_0O = Dr(0)E$ and $K_0 = \rho(0)F$ are sc-subspaces and $Tf(x_0) = Dg(0)|_{T_0O} : T_0O \to K_0$ is sc-Fredholm, of index $n - N$ on every level for every conjugating basic germ; in **every** strong bundle chart around a zero $y$, at the point $z$ over $y$, $\mathrm{Lin}(z) : T_zO \to K_z$ is sc-Fredholm, the levels being transported between charts at smooth points. No tameness is used. $T_xX$ and $Y_x$ themselves carry no linear structure here (G.7), so “an sc-Fredholm operator on $T_xX$” is read in charts.

notFormalized.title: Theorem 3.54 (1) with the text's hypotheses: surjectivity of $f'(y)$ at the nearby zeros
notFormalized.label: §3.6, Theorem 3.54 (1), pp. 111–114
notFormalized.book: (1) At every zero $y$ near $x$ the germ $(f, y)$ is in good position, “from Corollary 3.41 and Lemma 3.55”; (2) the solution set near $x$ is a sub-M-polyfold with the structure of a manifold with boundary with corners.
notFormalized.instead: **Formalized since the first edition of this page** (V3.93, V3.94): with the text's hypotheses (tame germ data, good position in a tame chart, V3.103), every zero $y$ near $x_0$ is in good position in a tame chart, in particular $f'(y)$ is onto. The text's argument does not give the surjectivity (it gives that of the filled linearization only; the same step is in the book's arXiv version); it is proved by an implicit function theorem at the nearby zero for $g + \mu\rho(r(\cdot))\lambda$, with Theorem 3.30 at the centre for a contraction germ whose regions in $a$ do not depend on $\lambda$ (Findings, Chapter 3, items 180–189). The first form under the filler condition at the nearby zeros (V3.82) is kept; that condition follows from good position (V3.102). (2) is proved from (1) (V3.85, V3.94); the index is locally constant along the solution set (V3.98).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 3.58: the basic germ criterion
notFormalized.label: §3.7, Theorem 3.58, pp. 116–120
notFormalized.book: Under (1) $Df(x)$ sc-Fredholm of constant index at smooth points, (2) a splitting $E = B \oplus X$ with a compactness condition, (3) a uniform estimate on $D_2f$: $f - f(0)$ is conjugated near $0$ to a basic germ.
notFormalized.instead: **Formalized since the first edition of this page**, in the coordinates of the text's proof ($E = \mathbb R^n \oplus X$, $F = \mathbb R^N \oplus Y$; V3.89, with the second half of the proof V3.88): under (1)–(3), $f - f(0)$ is conjugated near $0$ to a basic germ. The reduction of a general sc-splitting to these coordinates is not formalized.

notFormalized.title: Lemmas 3.62–3.64: extreme rays
notFormalized.label: §3.8.1, Lemmas 3.62–3.64, pp. 121–122
notFormalized.book: A closed convex cone in finite dimensions is the closed convex hull of its extreme rays (3.62); a cone with interior is a quadrant iff it has $\dim N$ extreme rays (3.63, from [21]); a generator $a$ of an extreme ray of $N \cap C$ has $\dim N - 1 \le \#\sigma_a$ (3.64).
notFormalized.instead: **Superseded, not formalized**: the proof of Proposition 3.22 (V3.21) avoids extreme rays (a segment argument and Lemma 3.65; Findings, Chapter 3, item 18).

notFormalized.title: Lemmas 3.66–3.68: the complement $\widetilde N$
notFormalized.label: §3.8.1, Lemmas 3.66–3.68, pp. 123–125
notFormalized.book: $\widetilde N$ is in good position with good complement $(N \cap W) \oplus N^\perp$ (3.66); $C \cap \widetilde N$ is a closed convex cone whose extreme rays satisfy $\dim\widetilde N - 1 = \#\sigma_a = d_C(a)$ (3.67); either $\widetilde N \cap (\mathbb R^{\Sigma^c} \oplus W) = \{0\}$ or $\widetilde N \subseteq \mathbb R^{\Sigma^c} \oplus W$ with $\dim\widetilde N = 1$, $\Sigma = \emptyset$ (3.68).
notFormalized.instead: **Superseded, not formalized as stated**: the normal form of Proposition 3.22 (V3.21) treats the three cases $N \cap C = N$, $\Sigma = \emptyset$, $\Sigma \ne \emptyset$ directly; the content of Lemma 3.68's second case is `quadrantNormalForm_of_vanIdx_empty`.

notFormalized.title: Definition 3.71: class $C^k$ on partial quadrants
notFormalized.label: §3.8.4, Definition 3.71, p. 135
notFormalized.book: $f : U \to \mathbb R^m$ on a relatively open subset of a partial quadrant is $C^1$ if it has one-sided derivatives depending continuously on $x$; $C^k$ if $f$ and $Tf$ are $C^{k-1}$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized separately**: the theorems of §§3.8.4–3.8.5 use Mathlib's $C^k$ within the set (`ContDiffOn`), which on relatively open subsets of partial quadrants agrees with sc$^1$ = $C^1$ (`isSc1_iff_contDiffOn_of_isRelOpenInQuadrant`, Chapter 1, V1.35).

notFormalized.title: Lemma 3.76: iterated tangent maps
notFormalized.label: §3.8.4, Lemma 3.76, p. 139
notFormalized.book: Under the assumptions of Proposition 3.73 the iterated tangent maps $T^kf : T^kU \to T^kV$ are smooth homeomorphisms.
notFormalized.instead: **Superseded, not formalized**: the regularity of $f^{-1}$ is proved by bootstrapping $Dg = [Df]^{-1} \circ g$ (V3.59, V3.62; Findings, Chapter 3, item 28).

notFormalized.title: Lemma 3.70 and Lemma 3.55 in a general presentation of $C$; Theorem 3.27 and $d_X$
notFormalized.label: §3.8.1, §3.8.3, Lemmas 3.70, 3.55; §3.2, proof of Theorem 3.27
notFormalized.book: Lemma 3.55 is stated for any partial quadrant $C \subseteq E$; the proof of Theorem 3.27 uses Lemma 3.70 to get $d_{N \cap C}(v) = d_X(y)$.
notFormalized.instead: **Lemma 3.70 is formalized in the model $\mathbb R^n \oplus W$**; Lemma 3.55 in the model, in coordinates for functionals cutting out $C$, and, since the first edition of this page, for any presentation of $C$ and $\sigma$ on a relatively open domain (V3.80). The transport of Lemma 3.70 to a general presentation, and hence $d_M = d_X$ on $M$ in Theorem 3.27, is not done (Findings, Chapter 3, item 84).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 3.19: the dimension is the index; $\ker f'(y) = T_yS$; good position for $d_X \equiv 0$
notFormalized.label: §3.1, Theorem 3.19, p. 74
notFormalized.book: The solution set near $x_0$ is a manifold whose dimension agrees with the Fredholm index of $f'(x_0)$; at its points $\ker f'(y) = T_yS(f, U)$; and for $d_X(x) = 0$ good position is the surjectivity of $f'(x)$.
notFormalized.instead: **Formalized since the first edition of this page** (second addendum). The dimension: the dimension $d$ of the solution set near a zero in good position is $\dim\ker f'(y) = \mathrm{ind}\,f'(y)$ at every zero $y$ near it, in every chart (V3.97, with V3.96), also in Theorems 3.23, 3.57, and the index is locally constant along the solution set (V3.98). The kernel: $D\psi$ maps $\ker f'(y)$, read in the chart at $x_0$, onto the tangent space of the solution graph (V3.99); $T_yS$ as a subspace of $T_yX$ is not formalized (Chapter 2 gap G.13). Good position in a tame chart at $d_X(y) = 0$ is surjectivity, for tame germ data (V3.100), so Theorems 3.19 and 3.56 hold with “$f'(x)$ surjective” (V3.101).

notFormalized.title: Remark 4.3: “$X^1 \ne X$ is possible”
notFormalized.label: §4.1, Remark 4.3, p. 148
notFormalized.book: If $X_0 = X_\infty$, then $X_m = X_0$ as sets for all $m$; "however, it is possible that $X^1 \ne X$ as sc-smooth spaces despite the fact that $(X^1)_m = X_{m+1} = X_i$ as sets".
notFormalized.instead: **Formalized since the first edition of this page** (fourth addendum; V4.6), by an example the text does not give. On the weighted sequence space $X$ of V1.13 ($|x|_m = \sup_k(k+1)^m|x_k|$), $L(t)$ is the projection onto $\cos\theta\,e_{n_k} + \sin\theta\,e_{n_{k+1}}$ ($n_k = 2^k$), the angle $\theta$ turning from $0$ to $\pi/2$ with flat ends while $t$ runs through $[1/(k+2), 1/(k+1)]$, and $L(t) = 0$ for $t \le 0$. The retraction $r(t, z) = (t, L(t)z)$ of $\mathbb R \oplus X$ is sc-smooth by a criterion for parameter families of level operators with one level of loss; its retract $O$ consists of smooth points, and the lift $O \to E_1$ is discontinuous at $0$, so $O$ is not an sc⁺-retract (Proposition 4.8), and the M-polyfold $O$ with its single chart has $X_0 = X_\infty$ and $1_0^1$ not sc-smooth. Why an example needs a retraction that loses a level (one with $C^1$ level maps gives none) is an argument, not formalized (Findings, Chapter 4, items 140–146).

notFormalized.title: Lemma 4.10: the section $u \mapsto (1 - p)(u - t(u))$ is sc-Fredholm
notFormalized.label: §4.1, Lemma 4.10, pp. 151–153
notFormalized.book: The section $u \mapsto (u, \mathbf f(u))$, $\mathbf f(u) = (1 - p)(u - t(u))$, of the local strong bundle $U \triangleleft Y \to U$ is sc-Fredholm.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized, because no longer used**: Proposition 4.9, its only use, is proved directly (V4.20–V4.25). It would need $U \triangleleft Y$ as a strong bundle, $Y$ and $Y \cap F$ as sc-subspaces, the sc-isomorphism $E \cong (T_0O \oplus B) \oplus W$ with $B \subseteq Y_\infty$, and at each smooth point the re-centred strong bundle chart (V4.18), filler and conjugation. The text's proof has a sign slip in $D\mathbf f(u)$, calls $D\mathbf f(u)$ an sc⁺-operator, writes $L(T_0O)$ for $L(Y)$, and omits the interior points of $(T_0O \oplus B) \cap C$ (Findings, item 57).

notFormalized.title: Remark 4.14: the local form near $\{d_X = 0\}$
notFormalized.label: §4.2, Remark 4.14, p. 157
notFormalized.book: Near points $a \in A$ with $d_X(a) = 0$ the submanifold $A$ is a smooth finite-dimensional manifold in the classical sense.
notFormalized.instead: **Formalized only globally**: if $d_X = 0$ on all of $A$, $A$ has a corner structure, without tameness of $X$ (V4.32). The local statement, for the open piece $A \cap \{d_X = 0\}$ of an arbitrary $A$, is not formalized (Findings, item 61).

notFormalized.title: The open question after Proposition 4.15
notFormalized.label: §4.2, Open Question, p. 159
notFormalized.book: Is a sub-M-polyfold with $A = A_\infty$ and $\dim T_aA$ finite and locally constant a smooth finite-dimensional submanifold? Is the "T" $\{(x, 0) : |x| < 1\} \cup \{(0, y) : 0 \le y < 1\}$ homeomorphic to a retract $O = O_\infty$? Impossible for sc⁺-retracts.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** (a question, not a statement). The last sentence, for a retract without boundary, is V4.32 with $A = O$: an sc⁺-retract in $(O, E, E)$ is a manifold; that the "T" is not a topological manifold is not formalized (Findings, item 65).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 4.22 (1): local faces of the chart as global local faces
notFormalized.label: §4.2, Theorem 4.22 (1), p. 162
notFormalized.book: There are precisely $d = d_X(x)$ local faces $F_1, \dots, F_d$ contained in $U$.
notFormalized.instead: **Formalized for the chart model only** (V4.50): $d_X(x) = n$, all coordinates vanish at the centre, and $\psi(x)$ lies in exactly $d_X(x)$ faces of the M-polyfold $O$. The identification of these faces with (germs of) global faces of $X$ (Theorem 2.45 in the face-structured case) is not formalized (Findings, items 86, 90). The text's local faces are faces of the neighbourhood $U$ itself (closures in $U$ of the components of $U \cap \{d_X = 1\}$), so (4) is affected as well; the missing step is a local face theorem for small neighbourhoods, believed true for tame $X$ (Findings, Chapter 4, item 130; third addendum).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 4.23: chart independence of stratified regularity
notFormalized.label: §4.3, proof of Theorem 4.23, p. 166
notFormalized.book: Regular values of the maps $p_\sigma : A \cap F_\sigma^\circ \to \mathbb R^m$, intrinsic to $A$ and its strata.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** Stratified regularity is defined in some product chart (V4.53); its independence of the chart is true by the transport argument of V4.39 (the transition maps of product charts are $\mathrm{id} \times \tau$ up to translation) but not formalized. Theorem 4.23 is unaffected: it produces $\Sigma$ (Findings, items 102, 108).

notFormalized.title: Definition 4.25: sc-differential forms and the directed system
notFormalized.label: §4.4, Definition 4.25, p. 167
notFormalized.book: An sc-differential $k$-form is an sc-smooth $\omega : \oplus^kTX \to \mathbb R$, linear in each argument and skew-symmetric; pull-back along $X^{i+1} \to X^i$ gives a directed system with limit $\Omega^*_\infty(X)$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** It needs $\oplus^kTX$ as an M-polyfold, a linear $T_xX$ (gap G.7) and the M-polyfolds $X^i$ for $i \ge 2$ (gap G.6). The text writes $\Omega^*_\infty$ for both the limit and the sum (Findings, item 124).

notFormalized.title: Proposition 4.26: the Lie bracket of sc-smooth vector fields
notFormalized.label: §4.4, Proposition 4.26, p. 167
notFormalized.book: For sc-smooth vector fields $A$, $B$ on $X$ the usual formula defines an sc-smooth vector field $[A, B]$ on $X^1$, a section of $T(X^1) \to X^2$ (quoted from another paper).
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** (no proof in the text; needs the tangent bundle of $X^1$ over $X^2$, gap G.6).

notFormalized.title: The exterior derivative, Definition 4.27 and the relative complex
notFormalized.label: §4.4, pp. 167–168, Definition 4.27
notFormalized.book: $d : \Omega^k(X^{i+1}) \to \Omega^{k+1}(X^i)$ by the usual formula, $d^2 = 0$; $H^*_{sc}(X) = \ker d/\operatorname{im} d$; the relative complex $\Omega^*_\infty(X) \oplus \Omega^{*-1}_\infty(\partial X)$ with $d(\omega, \tau) = (d\omega, j^*\omega - d\tau)$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** The direction of $d$ should presumably be $\Omega^k(X^i) \to \Omega^{k+1}(X^{i+1})$ (the bracket lives one level up); $d \circ d = 0$ and $dj^* = j^*d$ are asserted without proof; forms on $\partial X$, a union of faces, are not defined (Findings, items 120–122).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 4.28: Stokes' theorem
notFormalized.label: §4.4, Theorem 4.28, p. 168
notFormalized.book: For an oriented compact tame smooth $n$-dimensional submanifold $N$ whose boundary is a union of faces $F$, and an sc-differential $(n - 1)$-form $\omega$, $\int_N d\omega = \sum_F\int_F\omega$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** (no proof in the text; integration on manifolds with corners of varying dimension is not in Mathlib). The formula writes $\int_M$ for $\int_N$ (Findings, item 123).

notFormalized.title: Corollary 5.8 beyond the chart level
notFormalized.label: §5.2, Corollary 5.8, p. 173
notFormalized.book: $f^i$ is an sc-Fredholm section of $P^i : Y^i \to X^i$ with compact solution set ("it is a priori clear that $f^i$ is sc-Fredholm").
notFormalized.instead: **Formalized since the first edition of this page, for each fixed $i$** (fourth addendum; V5.13, V5.14). The shifted strong bundle $P^1 : Y^1 \to X^1$ is built (total space $Y_{1,1}$, the index raises of the strong bundle charts as atlas), and $f^1$ is an sc-Fredholm section of it with compact solution set, with condition (3) of the filling on level $1$ proved for the data of Definition 3.11 (by Lemma 3.17 and Proposition 3.52 in sc form; it does not follow from level $0$ alone); $f^2$ on $P^2 = (P^1)^1$ by iteration, and so every fixed $i$. Not formalized: one statement for a family $P^i$ indexed by $i$, the identification of $(X^1)^1$ with $X_2$ as topological spaces (the sets agree; gap G.6), and the tame form of the conclusion (the tameness of the index raises of tame charts) (Findings, Chapter 5, items 140–146).

notFormalized.title: The metric $\rho$ on $\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$
notFormalized.label: §5.3, p. 174
notFormalized.book: $\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$ "becomes a metric space with respect to the uniform distance $\rho(s, s') = \sup_xN(s(x) - s'(x))$. The metric space $(\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P), \rho)$ is not complete."
notFormalized.instead: **Formalized since the first edition of this page, with a correction** (fourth addendum; V5.21). $\rho$ is a metric on $\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$ for every auxiliary norm ($\rho \le 2$); the density statements $N(s(x) - s'(x)) \le \varepsilon$ of V5.30, V5.39 are $\rho(s, s') \le \varepsilon$. “Not complete” is proved for the trivial bundle $\mathbb R \times \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ ($N(x, v) = |v|$, $U = \mathbb R$) and is false without a hypothesis: the space is complete for $U = \emptyset$ and over a point with finite-dimensional fibre. Not formalized: a general sufficient condition for non-completeness, and the identification of the metric completion with the sections of Remark 5.12 (V5.22) (Findings, Chapter 5, items 150–153).

notFormalized.title: Remark 5.14
notFormalized.label: §5.3, Remark 5.14, p. 175
notFormalized.book: In [21] the fibres were separable sc-Hilbert spaces and auxiliary norms had more properties involving weak convergence; neither is needed here, "due to an improved treatment of the compactness".
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** (a comment on [21]). The formalization indeed assumes neither: the fibres are arbitrary and Definition 5.1 is as stated (V5.3, V5.10).

notFormalized.title: Remark 5.16
notFormalized.label: §5.3, Remark 5.16, pp. 176–177
notFormalized.book: For transversal $f_0$, $f_1$ joined by a sc-Fredholm arc $(t, x) \mapsto f_t(x)$ with compact solution set, a perturbation $s$ vanishing near $t = 0, 1$ makes the arc transversal, and its solution set is a compact cobordism; "the reader will be able to carry out this construction in more detail".
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** (a sketch, left to the reader; it needs the boundary case of Theorem 5.19 on $[0, 1] \times X$).

notFormalized.title: A dense form of Theorem 5.19
notFormalized.label: §5.3, Theorem 5.19, p. 180
notFormalized.book: "There exists an arbitrarily small section $s \in \Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$ satisfying $s(x) = 0$ near $\partial X$" with the properties of the theorem.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized in the dense form.** The generic form gives $s_\lambda = \sum\lambda_it_i$ for $\lambda$ off a null set of a small ball, so arbitrarily small as $\lambda \to 0$ (V5.40); density around a given allowable $s'$, as in Theorems 5.13 and 5.18, is not stated (Findings, Chapter 5, item 89).

notFormalized.title: Finding 88: the parametrized section at the boundary zeros
notFormalized.label: §5.3, proof of Theorem 5.19, p. 180
notFormalized.book: "Then we consider as before the section $(\lambda, x) \mapsto f(x) + \sum\lambda_is_i(x)$, and, for a generic value of $\lambda$ ... the associated section $s_\lambda$ has the desired properties."
notFormalized.instead: **Checked on paper only.** At a zero $(0, x)$, $x \in \partial X$, where all $s_i$ vanish, $\ker F'(0, x) = \mathbb R^m \times \ker f'(x)$ is in good position to $\mathbb R^m \times C_x$ only if $\ker f'(x) + E_x \supseteq T_xX$, a general position condition that good position does not imply ($\mathbb R(1, 1)$ in $[0, \infty)^2$). So "as before" cannot apply Theorem 3.54 to $F$ there; the formal proof avoids these points (V5.40) (Findings, Chapter 5, item 88).

notFormalized.title: Remark 5.21
notFormalized.label: §5.3, Remark 5.21, p. 181
notFormalized.book: Instead of $(f|X_i, P|Y_i) = (f_i, P_i)$ one should require that the problems are isomorphic and make this part of the data.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** Definition 5.20 takes the restrictions to $t^{-1}(0)$, $t^{-1}(1)$ as the end problems (V5.41) (Findings, Chapter 5, item 100).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 5.22: Morse-type structure
notFormalized.label: §5.3, Theorem 5.22, p. 181 (proof pp. 181–186)
notFormalized.book: For a generalized compact homotopy with end problems in general position and $\partial X = X_0 \sqcup X_1$, an arbitrarily small $s_0 \in \Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$ vanishing near $\partial X$ makes $(f + s_0, x)$ in general position at every zero and $t : S_{f+s_0} \to [0, 1]$ a function with only Morse-type critical points.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** It needs finite-dimensional Morse theory on manifolds with boundary, the cotangent bundle of the solution set, a parametric Sard theorem and a trivialization $\Phi_\lambda : S \to S_\lambda$ of the family (not "the classical standard implicit function theorem"); its proof also needs $dt(x) \ne 0$ at the critical points of $t|S$, which the statement does not assume (V5.42). Lemmas 5.23, 5.24 are V5.42–V5.44 (Findings, Chapter 5, items 101, 103).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 5.27: cobordism between good position perturbations
notFormalized.label: §5.3, Theorem 5.27, p. 188
notFormalized.book: For a proper homotopy $f_t$ and perturbations $s_0$, $s_1$ putting $f + s_i$ in good position, there is $s(x, t)$ with $s(\cdot, i) = s_i$ such that $f + s$ is in good position at all smooth points; its solution set is a compact manifold with corners meeting $\{i\} \times X$ in $S_0$, $S_1$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized**: "the proof is left to the reader" (Findings, Chapter 5, item 104).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 5.32: Bonic–Frampton
notFormalized.label: §5.4.2, Theorem 5.32, p. 193
notFormalized.book: On $L^p$, $\|\cdot\|^p$ is $C^\infty$ for $p$ an even integer, $C^{p-1}$ for $p$ odd, and $C^{[p]}$ for $p$ not an integer.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** (cited from [9], Theorem 1; deep Banach space geometry, not used on the main line; the statement misses "$p$" in (1), (2)) (Findings, Chapter 5, items 117, 120).

notFormalized.title: The $L^p$ and Sobolev remark
notFormalized.label: §5.4.2, pp. 193–194
notFormalized.book: The usual norms of $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ have the differentiability of $\|\cdot\|_{L^p}$; $\beta(\|x\|^p)$ is a bump function of $L^p$; $W^{1,4}(\Omega)$ with $E_m = W^{1+m,4}(\Omega)$ admits sc-smooth bump functions, while for $W^{1,3/2}(\Omega)$ the straightforward one is only sc¹ — "does there exist a sc-smooth bump function on $E$?"
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** It needs Sobolev spaces with their sc-structures (gap G.1) and Theorem 5.32 (Findings, Chapter 5, item 118).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 5.40: Toruńczyk
notFormalized.label: §5.4.2, Theorem 5.40, p. 198
notFormalized.book: A Banach space $E$ admits a $C^k$-partition of unity iff there are a set $\Gamma$ and a coordinate-wise $C^k$ homeomorphic embedding of $E$ into $c_0(\Gamma)$.
notFormalized.instead: **Stated, not proved** (`TorunczykStatement`, V5.59), and not used (cited from [9], Theorem 30) (Findings, Chapter 5, item 117).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 5.43: Godefroy–Troyanski–Whitfield–Zizler
notFormalized.label: §5.4.2, Theorem 5.43, p. 198
notFormalized.book: If the WCG space $E$ admits a $C^k$-bump function, then it also admits $C^k$-partitions of unity.
notFormalized.instead: **Stated, not proved** (`GodefroyTroyanskiWhitfieldZizlerStatement`, V5.62; cited from [12] and [9], Theorem 31); it is an explicit hypothesis of Corollary 5.44 (V5.63) (Findings, Chapter 5, items 116, 117).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 6.43: the invariant $\Psi_{(f,o)}$
notFormalized.label: §6.6, Theorem 6.43, p. 231 (proof pp. 231–233)
notFormalized.book: Over a tame $X$ with sc-smooth bump functions, a proper oriented sc-Fredholm section $(f, o)$ defines a linear map $\Psi_{(f,o)} : H^*_{dR}(X, \partial X) \to \mathbb R$ with (1) $\Psi_{(f,o)}([\omega, \tau]) = \int_{S_{f+s}}\omega - \int_{\partial S_{f+s}}\tau$ for every $s$ admissible for $(N, U)$, and (2) $\Psi_{(f_0,o_0)} = \Psi_{(f_1,o_1)}$ for a proper oriented homotopy. For $\partial X = \emptyset$, $\Psi_{(f,o)}([\omega]) = \int_{S_{f+s}}\omega$ on $H^n_{dR}(X)$, $n$ the index (p. 233).
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** (decision D1). It needs the sc-differential forms and their cohomology of §4.4 (gaps G.37–G.40), integration over oriented compact manifolds with boundary with corners and Stokes' theorem, which Mathlib does not have; its proof also uses the homotopy of Remark 5.16 (gap G.44). What the theorem rests on is formalized: the perturbations of Theorem 5.18 (V5.38, V5.39) and the tangent orientations of Theorem 6.41 (V6.61) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 100).

notFormalized.title: §6.6: the sections admissible for $(N, U)$
notFormalized.label: §6.6, p. 230
notFormalized.book: For a proper oriented $(f, o)$ over a tame $X$ with bump functions and an auxiliary norm $N$, Theorem 5.18 gives an open $U \supseteq S$ such that every sc⁺-section supported in $U$ with $N(s(x)) \le 1$ has a compact $S_{f+s}$; the distinguished ones, with $(f + s, x)$ in general position at every zero, have oriented solution sets and are called admissible for $(N, U)$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** as a notion; it is used only in Theorem 6.43 (gap G.54). The facts recalled are formalized: Theorem 5.18 (V5.38, V5.39) and the tangent orientations of the solution set (V6.61); the orientation of $S_{f+s}$ for a perturbed $f$ is gap G.69 (Findings, Chapter 6, item 101).

notFormalized.title: The facts on paths recalled on p. 201
notFormalized.label: §6.1, before Proposition 6.2, p. 201
notFormalized.book: An M-polyfold is locally path connected, and any two smooth points in the same path component can be joined by an sc⁺-smooth path $\varphi : [0, 1] \to X$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** beyond a chart: inside the domain of a chart, nearby smooth points are joined by sc-smooth paths (`exists_nhds_scPath`, V6.49), and "in the same path component" (Definitions 6.27, 6.38) is read as "joined by an sc-smooth path" (V6.58) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 42).

notFormalized.title: The alternative determinant $\lambda(\ker T) \otimes \lambda(\operatorname{coker}(T)^*)$
notFormalized.label: §6.3, after Definition 6.7, p. 208
notFormalized.book: Some authors use $\det(T) = \lambda(\ker T) \otimes \lambda(\operatorname{coker}(T)^*)$; the two definitions are naturally isomorphic, given a convention identifying $\lambda^*(A)$ and $\lambda(A^*)$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized**, and not used: the chapter's formal statements use Definition 6.7 (V6.8); the convention $\iota$ of Definition 6.3 is V6.3 (Findings, Chapter 6, item 10).

notFormalized.title: The identification (95) and the maps $V \otimes \lambda(\mathbb R^n) \to V$
notFormalized.label: §6.3, after Proposition 6.15, p. 213
notFormalized.book: Dual to (94), $\mathbb R \to \lambda(\mathbb R^n)$ maps $1$ to the wedge of the standard basis, with inverse (95) $c_1 \wedge \dots \wedge c_n \mapsto \det([c_1, \dots, c_n])$; this gives identifications $V \otimes \lambda(\mathbb R^n) \to V$ and $V \otimes \lambda^*(\mathbb R^n) \to V$ for every finite-dimensional $V$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized**, and not used: the formal statements use (94) only (V6.17, V6.18) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 10).

notFormalized.title: Lemma 6.19 in general
notFormalized.label: §6.4, Lemma 6.19, p. 216
notFormalized.book: For finite-dimensional topological vector bundles $E$, $F$ over $X$, the bundles $\lambda(E)$, $\lambda^*(F)$, $E \oplus F$ and $E \otimes F$ have the structure of topological vector bundles in a natural way (a standard lemma, cited from [29]).
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** in general: Mathlib has no exterior powers or tensor products of vector bundles. The lemma is applied only to trivial bundles, and Proposition 6.20 is proved with explicit frames (V6.22) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 22).

notFormalized.title: $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ is not orientable; the classical case
notFormalized.label: §6.4, p. 218; the opening of §6.5, p. 219
notFormalized.book: The text remarks that $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ is known to be non-orientable, though orientable over certain subsets. For a classical Fredholm map $f : U \to F$, the determinant line bundle of the $Df(x)$ is a smooth line bundle over $U$, with precisely two orientations if $U$ is contractible.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** (remarks, not used). The orientability over convex sets of Fredholm operators, which is what the chapter uses, is Proposition 6.26 (V6.30) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 26).

notFormalized.title: Proposition 6.28 (1): sc-smooth contractibility
notFormalized.label: §6.5, Proposition 6.28 (1), p. 220; Theorem 6.35, Definition 6.36, Theorem 6.37
notFormalized.book: The neighbourhood $U(x)$ of Proposition 6.28 is sc-smoothly contractible (by $r(ty)$ on $U = r(V')$, $V'$ convex), and Theorem 6.35, Definition 6.36 and property (∗) of Theorem 6.37 ask for sc-smoothly contractible neighbourhoods.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** As we read it, the proof does not establish (1) for $U$: it needs $r(V') \subseteq V'$, which is not stated. (1′) is proved instead (two sc-smooth paths in $U$ with the same end points are sc-smoothly homotopic in a larger $W$ with the end points fixed) and is what the proofs use (V6.32, V6.48, V6.50, V6.57) (Findings, Chapter 6, items 45, 53, 54, 72).

notFormalized.title: Lemma 6.30 as a statement about manifolds
notFormalized.label: §6.5, Lemma 6.30, p. 222
notFormalized.book: The solution set of $F = 0$ near $(t, \varphi(t), 0)$ is a smooth manifold with boundary with corners, $\pi : S \to [0, 1]$ is a submersion, its fibres $S_t$ are manifolds with boundary with corners, and $L$ is a smooth vector bundle over $[0, 1]$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** The kernels are formalized as a continuous family of subspaces of the model space (V6.34, V6.42), which is all the continuation of orientations needs (Findings, Chapter 6, item 48).

notFormalized.title: Property (P) of Lemma 6.29 for the slices $F_t$
notFormalized.label: §6.5, Lemma 6.29, p. 222
notFormalized.book: (P): for every fixed $t \in [0, 1]$, the section $F_t$ is at $(\varphi(t), 0)$ in general position to the boundary of $X \times \mathbb R^k$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** The general position of $F$ at the points $(t, \varphi(t), 0)$, which the text derives from (P) and which Lemmas 6.30, 6.31 use, is proved (V6.33). As we read it, (P) follows, since the tangent vectors of the family of zeros lie in $\ker F'$ and $\mathbb R^n$ has no boundary; this chart computation is not carried out (Findings, Chapter 6, item 47).

notFormalized.title: $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ as sc-Fredholm operators on every level
notFormalized.label: §6.1, Definition 6.1, p. 201
notFormalized.book: The operators in $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ are sc-Fredholm operators $T_xX \to Y_x$, all with the same Fredholm index.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** on every level: at a chart point the members are shown Fredholm on level $0$, with the index $\mathrm{ind}(f, x)$ of V3.98, which is what the determinant lines use (V6.1) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 40).

notFormalized.title: Paths and families on $[0, 1]$; $X \times [0, 1]$ as an M-polyfold
notFormalized.label: §6.5, pp. 220–230
notFormalized.book: Paths, homotopies and families are sc-smooth maps on $[0, 1]$, $[0, 1]^2$, $[0, 1]^n$, and $X \times [0, 1]$, $[0, 1] \times X \times \mathbb R^k$ are M-polyfolds with boundary (Proposition 6.28, Lemmas 6.29–6.34, Theorem 6.35, Remark 6.42).
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** as stated: they are read on $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb R^2$, $\mathbb R^n$ and $\mathbb R^n \times X$, of which only $[0, 1]$, $[0, 1]^2$, $[0, 1]^n$ matters (decision D2), as for Proposition 6.2 in Chapter 3 (V3.98); a path that does not extend sc-smoothly to $\mathbb R$ is not covered (Findings, Chapter 6, items 71, 102).

notFormalized.title: Remark 6.42 beyond a point
notFormalized.label: §6.5, Remark 6.42, p. 230
notFormalized.book: $\hat f(x, t) = f(x) + s(x, t)$ on $X \times [0, 1]$ has a natural orientation associated with $o$ and the standard orientation of $[0, 1]$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** beyond a point: that $(t, y) \mapsto \hat o$ is an orientation of $\hat f$ in the sense of Definition 6.40 (continuity over the orientable neighbourhoods of $\mathbb R \times X$, independence of the chart of the pull-back bundle), built from an orientation of $f$. At a point the remark is V6.62 (Findings, Chapter 6, item 97).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 6.41: the orientation of $S$ as a manifold
notFormalized.label: §6.5, Theorem 6.41, p. 229
notFormalized.book: The solution set $S$ is a smooth compact manifold with boundary with corners possessing a natural orientation.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** as an orientation of the abstract finite-dimensional manifold $S$ (of its tangent bundle in the charts of the induced structure). What is formalized is the tangent orientation at each zero and its continuity along the sc-smooth paths of zeros in a chart (V6.61) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 92).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 6.41: tangent orientations read in two charts
notFormalized.label: §6.5, Theorem 6.41, p. 229
notFormalized.book: $T_xS = \ker f'(x)$ is oriented by $o^f_x$, an object the text treats as independent of the chart.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized**: the compatibility of the tangent orientations read in two charts at the same zero. $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ itself is identified between charts (V6.53–V6.55) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 92).

notFormalized.title: The paragraph after Theorem 6.41: perturbed solution sets
notFormalized.label: §6.5, after Theorem 6.41, pp. 229–230
notFormalized.book: If $f$ is not generic, a small perturbation $s$ supported near the zero set gives $S_{f+s}$ a natural orientation coming from $o^f$, since $\det((f + s)'(x))$ is oriented from $\mathrm{DET}(f, x)$ for $x \in S_{f+s}$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized**: the perturbation, the orientation of $S_{f+s}$ coming from $o^f$, and the identification $\mathrm{Lin}(f + s, x) = \mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ for an sc⁺-section $s$ that it uses. The perturbations themselves are Theorem 5.18 (V5.38, V5.39) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 93).

notFormalized.title: Definition 7.4: the tangent $T\varphi$ as an sc-isomorphism
notFormalized.label: §7.1, Definition 7.4 and the paragraph before it, p. 227
notFormalized.book: For a smooth morphism $\varphi$, i.e. $\varphi \in \mathbf X_\infty$, there is an associated sc-isomorphism $T\varphi : T_{s(\varphi)}X \to T_{t(\varphi)}X$ defined by $T\varphi := T\hat\varphi(x)$; $T\varphi$ can be defined for $\varphi$ on level at least $1$ and gives a bounded linear isomorphism on level $0$, and only for smooth $\varphi$ is $T\varphi$ an sc-operator. Definition 7.4 associates with a smooth morphism $\varphi$ the local sc-diffeomorphism $\hat\varphi$ and its tangent $T\varphi$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** beyond the definition: `tangentMor` defines $T\varphi$ (V7.5), but that it is well defined, equal to $T\hat\varphi(s(\varphi))$, bijective, a bounded linear isomorphism on level $0$ for $\varphi \in \mathbf X_1$ and an sc-operator for smooth $\varphi$ is not formalized; the linearity needs the linear structure of the tangent spaces, which the project does not have (gap G.7). Not used in Chapter 7; deferred to Chapter 8 (Findings, Chapter 7, items 5, 110).

notFormalized.title: Propositions 7.9, 7.10: $\mathbf X^R$ Hausdorff and paracompact
notFormalized.label: §7.2, Propositions 7.9 and 7.10, pp. 242–244
notFormalized.book: Proposition 7.9: the reduced morphism set $\mathbf X^R$ has a natural M-polyfold structure. Proposition 7.10: every ep-groupoid $X$ possesses an associated reduced ep-groupoid $X_R$, and $X_R$ is effective. Since an M-polyfold is a paracompact Hausdorff space (Part I, Definition 2.8), these assert in particular that $\mathbf X^R$, with the quotient topology, is Hausdorff and paracompact, for every ep-groupoid $X$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** for a general ep-groupoid: as we read it, the proof of Proposition 7.9 gives neither property, and both are hypotheses (`[T2Space X.ReducedMor] [ParacompactSpace X.ReducedMor]`) of `reducedPolyfold` and so of Propositions 7.9 and 7.10 (V7.39, V7.40). They are discharged for effective $X$, and so for the trivial ep-groupoid of every M-polyfold, and paracompactness follows from regularity when $\mathbf X$ is second countable. Hausdorffness fails in general: for $\mathbb Z/2$ acting on the dimension-jumping retract of Part I's Remark 4.3, $\mathbf X^R$ is not Hausdorff (`Examples.exists_not_t2Space_reducedMor`, formalized after the round-trip audit). Not formalized: whether $\mathbf X^R$ is paracompact when it is Hausdorff, and whether Hausdorffness with $\mathbf X$ second countable suffices for paracompactness (Findings, Chapter 7, items 56, 60, 107, 111).

notFormalized.title: The filtration of $|X|$: the set $|X_\infty|$
notFormalized.label: §7.1, p. 228
notFormalized.book: Since $ml(x) = ml(y) = ml(\varphi)$ for every morphism $\varphi : x \to y$, the filtration of $X$ induces the filtration $|X| = |X_0| \supset |X_1| \supset \dots \supset |X_\infty| = \bigcap_{k \ge 0} |X_k|$ of the orbit space $|X| = X/\sim$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** beyond the levels: $|X_k| = \pi(X_k)$ is `orbitLevel k`, and $s$, $t$ preserve the levels (V7.6); the set $|X_\infty|$ and the identity $|X_\infty| = \bigcap_k |X_k|$, immediate as $ml$ is constant on classes, are not stated (Findings, Chapter 7, items 6, 112).

notFormalized.title: The density of $X_\infty$ in $X_k$
notFormalized.label: §7.1, p. 227
notFormalized.book: The M-polyfolds $X$ and $\mathbf X$ carry the filtrations $X = X_0 \supset X_1 \supset \dots \supset X_\infty = \bigcap_k X_k$; the set $X_\infty$ is dense in every space $X_k$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized**: the text states the density without proof; Part I proves it only for sc-Banach spaces (`ScBanach.denseRange_incl`), and its text does not state it for M-polyfolds or retracts. For a retract $O = r(U)$ it follows from the continuity of $r$ on level $k$ and the density of $U_\infty$ in $U_k$, which for $U$ open in a partial quadrant $C$ needs $C \cap E_\infty$ dense in $C \cap E_k$. Chapter 7 uses the filtration, never the density. Found by the round-trip audit (V7.6) (gap G.73; Findings, Chapter 7, item 116).
